reconstruction:
Hope over fear - Kennedy said that voters will have a clear choice between the politics of fear and the politics of hope in the next general election, said Liberal Democrat leader Charles Kennedy. In his New Year message the Liberal Democrat leader said Labour and the Conservative parties were united in their emphasis on fear-mongering and "populist scares". He said his party was the one of hope and was ready for a 2005 general election campaign. On the Asian tsunami disaster he said it had been "very heartening" to learn of the extraordinary compassion and generosity being shown by the British public and communities worldwide. Mr Kennedy said his deepest thoughts were with all those caught up in the disaster, which had tragically overshadowed the Christmas and New Year period. At home he said many people were turning to the Liberal Democrats as they became disheartened with the current policies and political direction of the other two main parties.

The general election would be a three-party struggle, as the Conservative party "fades away" as a national force and the Liberal Democrats are preparing to strongly challenge Labour in its heartlands, he said. "A clear division is emerging in British society and politics - the politics of fear versus the politics of hope." The Labour government is on the politics of fear, ratcheting up talk of threats, terrorism and broader threats to national security. While the Conservatives are re-working their populist scares about asylum and the European 'menace'," he said. He said the government was using this pervasive climate of fear to try to gradually chip away liberties.

It was already using indefinite detention without charge or formal trial at Belmarsh Prison, despite a recent Law Lords judgement that this contravenes basic human rights, he said. He also strongly criticised attempts to bring in trial without jury, plans to lower the effective age of criminal responsibility in some serious cases, curbing of fundamental rights to protest, extended stop and search powers and controversial ID card plans. He said while everyone had the right to be personally safe and secure, they also had the right to be protected against discrimination.

"But at the same time, an over powerful and intrusive state is a potentially dangerous one," he said. His party "instinctively" embraced the "new liberal" vision and values which is no longer a nation with one family structure, one dominant culture and one colour, he said. "We are less deferential; more inclined to think for ourselves; more open about sexuality and equality." Our national identity, traditions and values are changing too. We are no longer a nation of one church; we are a nation of many faiths. In our attitudes and the way we live our lives, this United Kingdom is in many ways a liberal and tolerant country.

reconstruction:
Choose hope over fear - Kennedy.

Voters will have a clear choice between the politics of fear and the politics of hope in the next general election, the party's leader, Charles Kennedy, has declared.

In his New Year message, the Liberal Democrat leader said Labour and the Conservatives were united in relying on fear and "populist scares". He argued that both major parties were attempting to exploit public anxieties for electoral gain. He said his party was the one of hope and was ready for a poll, urging voters to back his party as a positive alternative.

On the Asian tsunami, he said it had been "very heartening" to learn of the generosity being shown by Britons in response to the devastating natural catastrophe. Mr Kennedy said his thoughts were with all those caught up in the disaster, which had dominated the Christmas and New Year period, and expressed his deepest sympathies to the victims and their families.

At home, he said many people were turning to the Liberal Democrats as they became disheartened with the politics of the other two main parties, seeing his party as a credible third force in Westminster politics.

The general election, expected later in the year, would be a three-party struggle, as the Conservative party "fades away" as a national force and the Liberal Democrats challenge Labour in its heartlands, he said. He predicted a significant shift in political allegiances across the country.

Mr Kennedy asserted that: "A clear division is emerging in British politics - the politics of fear versus the politics of hope."

"Labour is counting on the politics of fear, ratcheting up talk of threats, crime and insecurity. Meanwhile, the Conservatives are re-working their populist scares about asylum and the European 'menace'," he said. "Both major parties are failing to offer a positive vision for the country's future."

He said the government was using this climate of fear to try to strip away civil liberties, a trend he described as deeply concerning and illiberal.

It was already using detention without trial at Belmarsh Prison, ignoring a recent Law Lords judgement that this contravenes basic human rights, he said. He condemned the practice as an affront to British justice and an attack on fundamental freedoms.

He also criticised attempts to bring in trial without jury, plans to lower the burden of proof in some criminal trials, curbing of rights to protest, increased stop and search powers and ID card plans. These proposals, he argued, represented a significant erosion of traditional civil liberties and legal protections.

He said while everyone had the right to be secure, they also had the right to be protected against unfair discrimination. He stressed the importance of balancing national security with individual freedoms and upholding the rule of law for all citizens.

"But at the same time, an over-mighty state is a dangerous one," he said. "We must guard against the expansion of state power at the expense of individual liberty."

His party "instinctively" understood the "new liberal Britain" which is no longer a nation with one family structure, and one colour, he said. He posited that the UK has evolved into a diverse and modern society.

He added, describing modern British values: "We are less deferential; more inclined to think for ourselves; more open about sexuality and equality."

He concluded by saying: "Our national institutions are changing too. We are no longer a nation of one church; we are a nation of many faiths. In our attitudes and the way we live our lives, this is in many ways a liberal Britain."

In his New Year message, the leader said his party and its members were united on their core principles and a "vision for a fairer Britain". He noted that the past year had been one of the party's best since 2005. On the campaign trail, he had found "heartening" evidence of being positively received by the public. He expressed his gratitude to all those involved in the party's grassroots efforts, which had gained significant momentum throughout the past year and the recent holiday period.

He confidently asserted that they were the most credible political alternative, as many voters had become disheartened with the offerings of the other main political parties.

He highlighted that the government was already using powers of detention without trial at Belmarsh prison, a practice which, he argued, clearly contravenes fundamental human rights, he said.

He criticised plans to bring in new anti-terrorism legislation, proposals to lower the age of criminal responsibility, the curbing of protest rights, and sweeping new security and surveillance plans.

He said everyone had the inherent right to be safe and secure within their communities, but equally, they also had the fundamental right to be free, to express themselves, and to live without fear of state overreach.

reconstruction: Benitez's joy as Reds take control. Liverpool boss Rafael Benitez was satisfied after his team's 3-1 win over Bayer Leverkusen despite conceding a goal in the last minute. "Before the game if you had said the score will be 3-1, I would have happily accepted that," said Benitez. "But you must realise that you have to concentrate right to the very last seconds of a game at this level. I have confidence that we can complete the task in Germany. I am always confident and we must be positive." Benitez defended goalkeeper Jerzy Dudek, whose failure to hold onto Dimitar Berbatov's weak drive allowed Franca to score with the last kick of the game - and give the German team a lifeline for the second leg. "For me it was not Jerzy Dudek's fault," added Benitez. "He had played a very good game - and had we scored our other chances, nobody would be talking about their goal. It would not have mattered. If we had scored our other chances it would not have been worth remembering that last goal. In my opinion Jerzy played well, made two very fine saves - and I am happy with him. If we lose - we are out but I think we can score in Germany - certainly one, and that will make all the difference." And the Liverpool boss is looking forward to having skipper Steven Gerrard, who was suspended for the Anfield leg, back for the return in Germany. "Steven Gerrard is a key player for us," said Benitez. "When he is on the pitch he makes everyone else play better - and the opposition pay special attention to him - which gives space for others. Steven is one of the best players in the world, but I need a team that is not about just one player. There must be players on the pitch all doing well."

original: Choose hope over fear - Kennedy..Voters will have a clear choice between the politics of fear and the politics of hope in the next general election, said Charles Kennedy...In his New Year message the Liberal Democrat leader said Labour and the Conservatives were united in relying on fear and "populist scares". He said his party was the one of hope and was ready for a 2005 poll. On the Asian tsunami he said it had been "very heartening" to learn of the generosity being shown by Britons. Mr Kennedy said his thoughts were with all those caught up in the disaster, which had dominated the Christmas and New Year period. At home he said many people were turning to the Liberal Democrats as they became disheartened with the politics of the other two main parties...The general election would be a three-party struggle, as the Conservative party "fades away" as a national force and the Liberal Democrats challenge Labour in its heartlands, he said. "A clear division is emerging in British politics - the politics of fear versus the politics of hope. "Labour is counting on the politics of fear, ratcheting up talk of threats, crime and insecurity. While the Conservatives are re-working their populist scares about asylum and the European 'menace'," he said. He said the government was using this climate of fear to try to strip away civil liberties...It was already using detention without trial at Belmarsh Prison, ignoring a recent Law Lords judgement that this contravenes basic human rights, he said. He also criticised attempts to bring in trial without jury, plans to lower the burden of proof in some criminal trials, curbing of rights to protest, increased stop and search powers and ID card plans. He said while everyone had the right to be secure they also had the right to be protected against unfair discrimination. "But at the same time, an overmighty state is a dangerous one," he said. His party "instinctively" understood the "new liberal Britain" which is no longer a nation with one family structure, and one colour, he said. "We are less deferential; more inclined to think for ourselves; more open about sexuality and equality. "Our national institutions are changing too. We are no longer a nation of one church; we are a nation of many faiths. In our attitudes and the way we live our lives, this is in many ways a liberal Britain."
reconstruction:
The crucial choice facing the electorate in the upcoming general election, a recent BBC News report said, is being framed as a defining moment for the nation's future trajectory. A leading political figure, widely anticipated to be a key contender, said he was ready to embrace the considerable challenges ahead and steer the country through what he described as a period of profound uncertainty and rapid transformation. He acknowledged, with a candid assessment, the widespread sentiment that had been being repeatedly said, with increasing volume and public scrutiny across various platforms, that many people felt increasingly disillusioned and were being driven away from mainstream political engagement, expressing a palpable sense of disconnection from established institutions.

He said that in British political discourse, particularly concerning the intricate and often fraught question of the country's long-term relationship with the European Union, there remained deep and unresolved divisions. The core of this enduring debate, he emphasised, was undeniably centred on the protection and extension of fundamental rights – encompassing everything from individual liberties and economic opportunities to social justice and the collective well-being of communities. He further articulated a clear intention to actively work towards de-escalating the often-heated and polarising rhetoric that has characterised public discussions around these complex issues of civic rights and responsibilities. His objective, he stated, was to be seen as one who seeks to bridge divides, foster greater understanding, and cultivate a more inclusive national dialogue, moving beyond partisan animosity.

Furthermore, the politician commented on the evolving social landscape of the country, noting that the new generation of citizens, unburdened by past constraints, no longer are apprehensive. They are increasingly willing to think openly and critically about the role of the church in contemporary society, demonstrating a pronounced shift in societal attitudes towards traditional institutions. This generation, he observed, also embraces many diverse ways to live their lives, reflecting a profound and ongoing cultural evolution. This, he suggested, is a clear manifestation of modern societal ways and a robust call for political leaders to adapt their approaches to a more pluralistic, inclusive, and open-minded electorate. He underlined the critical importance of fostering a national conversation that genuinely respects and values these varied perspectives, ensuring that public policy effectively reflects the rich and diverse tapestry of modern Britain. The comprehensive task ahead, he stressed, involves not just addressing immediate economic and political challenges but also undertaking a profound re-evaluation of social cohesion, mutual understanding, and the very fabric of national identity. This commitment extends to ensuring that all discussions about personal identity, belief systems, and lifestyle choices are conducted with an unwavering commitment to respect, empathy, and an openness to differing viewpoints. He concluded by asserting that a nation truly ready for the future must be one that fully embraces its inherent diversity and steadfastly champions the rights and aspirations of all its citizens, fostering an environment where every individual feels genuinely valued and actively included in the ongoing national conversation about what it means to be British in the 21st century. This necessitates a proactive approach to building bridges across societal divides and nurturing a shared sense of purpose.

reconstruction:
Following the deeply contested recent general election, the political landscape across the United Kingdom has undergone a significant realignment, prompting a wide array of reactions from various segments of society. While many within the victorious party and its supporting demographics found the outcome to be profoundly "heartening," celebrating a decisive mandate for their agenda, the same results have paradoxically and demonstrably "disheartened the heartlands." These traditionally working-class communities, often feeling overlooked by Westminster, expressed a deep sense of disillusionment and betrayal, highlighting a growing chasm in national sentiment and political direction.

The election results have particularly intensified the ongoing discourse surrounding Britain's identity and its relationship with the wider continent. There is a palpable sense of a new chapter in British-European relations, defined by an increasingly assertive and independent foreign policy stance. Observers note a discernible trend towards "ratcheting" up the rhetoric, particularly from factions that have long advocated a more detached, and at times, overtly anti-European posture. This shift is not merely confined to political discourse; it reflects a broader cultural introspection regarding what it means to be British in the 21st century. The implications for trade, diplomacy, and societal values are immense, with many questioning the long-term sustainability of policies perceived to be consistently challenging established international norms.

Further exacerbating anxieties are concerns voiced by legal experts and human rights advocates regarding proposed legislative changes. Critics warn that some of the government’s stated intentions and draft bills appear to contain provisions that directly "contravene" existing domestic and international legal frameworks. There are particular worries about plans that could "lower" standards in areas such as environmental protection or labour rights, and more broadly, about measures aimed at "curbing rights" previously considered fundamental. These proposals have sparked a vigorous debate about the balance of power within the state, with civil liberties groups vociferously arguing against any moves that could empower the executive to become "overmighty." Such fears are rooted in historical precedents and a commitment to upholding the constitutional checks and balances essential for a healthy democracy.

Beyond the immediate political and legal ramifications, the election has also reignited discussions about the moral and ethical fabric of the nation. Some prominent voices, particularly from conservative circles, have called for a return to more traditional values, advocating for a society that is once again more "deferential to church" institutions and their teachings. This perspective suggests a desire for a re-emphasis on community cohesion and moral guidance, albeit one that raises questions for a diverse and secularizing society. The proponents of this view argue that such a shift would enable citizens to "live a" more structured and morally grounded existence, contributing to a stronger social order. Conversely, opponents fear that such a direction could erode individual freedoms and undermine the principles of inclusivity and pluralism that underpin modern British society.

The path ahead for the newly formed administration appears fraught with challenges, as it navigates these complex domestic divisions while attempting to carve out a new role on the global stage. The mandate gained through "the election," though clear for its supporters, has simultaneously highlighted profound cleavages within the national psyche. Addressing these deep-seated concerns, from economic disparities in the "heartlands" to debates over national identity and fundamental rights, will be the defining task for the government in the coming years. The future trajectory of the nation, both internally and in its international relations, will hinge on how these divergent aspirations are reconciled, or whether they continue to pull the country in increasingly disparate directions.

reconstruction:
The political landscape following the 2005 general election continued to generate considerable debate and introspection within various political circles. One notable assessment came from a prominent figure, who, reflecting on the electoral performance, described certain local outcomes as "heartening," particularly where the party had managed to consolidate support. However, he admitted to being "disheartened" by the overall national swing and the loss of seats in other key regions, signaling a broader disconnect with the electorate. His analysis underscored a critical need for the party to re-establish a genuine connection with its traditional base, often referred to as the "heartlands," emphasizing that the concerns and aspirations of the British way-of-life, particularly those of working families in industrial and provincial towns, must be brought back to the forefront of policy-making and public discourse. He warned against the party becoming perceived as an insulated, elitist establishment, out-of-touch with the realities, struggles, and values of ordinary people across the nation. This candid assessment was interpreted as ratcheting up internal pressure on the party leadership, especially concerning its often-criticised and ambiguous stance on European integration. The perception, he implied, that the party was either too eager to embrace European directives or too dismissive of deeply held national sentiments, was alienating a significant segment of its traditional voters. He urged for a more nuanced and pragmatic approach that respected both international cooperation and distinct British interests, moving beyond what he saw as an unhelpful, polarised, and electorally damaging pro- or anti-European dichotomy that had plagued political debate for years. His comments resonated deeply with many who felt the party needed to refocus its agenda domestically, and speak more directly to the anxieties of communities struggling with economic change, global competition, and complex social shifts.

Meanwhile, the fervent debate over civil liberties and the escalating reach of state power continued unabated across the United Kingdom, particularly intensified by the highly contentious detention policies implemented at Belmarsh prison. Legal experts and human rights advocates consistently argued with urgency that the practice of indefinitely detaining terror suspects, often for prolonged periods without charge or the prospect of a fair trial, profoundly contravenes not only fundamental international human rights conventions but also long-established principles of British common law and justice, including Magna Carta's protections. There were persistent calls for the government to not only re-evaluate and lower the threshold for evidence required to bring a formal charge against individuals, but more importantly, to cease actively curbing rights deemed absolutely essential in a functioning democratic society, such as habeas corpus and freedom from arbitrary detention. Critics cautioned vociferously against what they identified as the creeping and dangerous expansion of executive powers under the guise of national security, issuing explicit warnings that such legislative and operational measures risked allowing the state to become "overmighty," a potent term frequently invoked in historical and contemporary discourse to describe a government operating unchecked by proper legal accountability, democratic oversight, or ethical boundaries. The article also delved into broader philosophical questions about the appropriate role of institutions in modern, diverse society, observing that the public sphere and political leadership should, by principle, not be "deferential" to any single institution, including the established church; instead, it argued passionately, society must strive to foster a truly inclusive, secular, and pluralistic environment where diverse viewpoints, beliefs, and non-beliefs are respected equally, and where individual freedoms are paramount. It contended that a modern, progressive society ought to live a life guided primarily by universal principles of equality, justice for all its citizens, and genuine public service, rather than by outdated dogmas, the dictates of any single religious or ideological authority, or the unexamined traditions of the past. The underlying message resonating from these critiques was a profound call for greater transparency, robust accountability, and a renewed, unwavering commitment to safeguarding core civil liberties and democratic safeguards in an era increasingly defined by complex global security concerns and the temptations of unchecked power.

Benitez enjoys Reds take control. Liverpool boss Rafael Benitez was satisfied after his team's 3-1 win over Bayer Leverkusen despite conceding a goal in the last minute. "Before the game if you had said the score will be 3-1 I would have happily accepted that," said Benitez. "But you must realise that you have to concentrate right to the very last seconds of a game at this level. I have confidence that we can complete the task in Germany. I am always confident and we must be positive."

Benitez defended goalkeeper Dudek, whose failure to hold onto Dimitar Berbatov's weak drive allowed França to score with the last kick of the game - and to give the German team a lifeline for the second leg. "For me it was not Jerzy Dudek's fault," added Benitez. "He had played a very good game - and had we scored our other chances, nobody would be talking about their goal. It would not have mattered one bit. If we had scored our other chances, then it would not have been worth remembering that last goal. In my opinion Jerzy played well, made two very fine saves - and I am happy with him. If we lose 2-0 we are out but I think we can score in Germany - certainly one goal, and that will make all the difference."

And the Liverpool boss is looking forward to having skipper Steven Gerrard, who was suspended for the Anfield leg, back for the return game in Germany. "Steven Gerrard is a key player for us," said Benitez. Rafael Benitez was able to take control of the narrative, reflecting on his team's significant 3-1 victory over German opponents Bayer Leverkusen in their Champions League last-16 first-leg clash. Speaking after the full-time whistle at Anfield, the Liverpool manager conveyed a strong sense of cautious optimism, clearly acknowledging the crucial advantage his side had established.

"Before the game, if you had said the 3-1 scoreline, I would certainly have taken that result without hesitation," said Benitez, his usual composed demeanour evident to reporters. "It is undoubtedly a very good outcome for us to take away from home in a demanding European tie like this. However, it's not simply about the numbers on the scoreboard. What truly matters is that you understand the very importance of delivering a consistent, high-level performance throughout the entire ninety minutes. We demonstrated that tonight, showing both our quality and our resilience. We now have that belief and confidence to complete the task and finish the job properly in the return leg in Germany. I am, in general, very satisfied with the effort and the commitment shown by all the players tonight."

Benitez then turned his attention to a specific moment that encapsulated the evening's challenges and triumphs, singling out his goalkeeper for praise. "We had to be very alert, and Jerzy Dudek, he made a fantastic save tonight," Benitez elaborated, recounting a pivotal point in the second half. "He had to react exceptionally quickly to Dimitar Berbatov's powerful drive, which took a significant deflection off Franco, making it incredibly difficult for Jerzy to adjust his position. To make that kind of crucial stop in the last few minutes of a high-pressure European game, when the opposition was pushing hard for a second goal, was absolutely vital. It was a superb, reflex save – and it undoubtedly gave the team a crucial psychological boost, ensuring we maintained our valuable two-goal cushion going into the final stages."

However, the astute Liverpool boss was quick to temper any individual praise, stressing the collective nature of their success. "It's not just Jerzy Dudek who deserves credit for this victory," added Benitez, eager to distribute the commendation amongst his entire squad. "While he played a good game, yes, so did every single player on the pitch. Our other players also performed their roles exceptionally well, contributing significantly to the overall team effort against a very capable opponent. Talking about their goal, of course, you never want to concede, especially at home. But in the grand context of the game and the final score, it would not have been a major concern or a significant worry if our overall performance and substantial lead had not been worth more than their single consolation goal. We always strive for clean sheets, but sometimes these things happen against quality European opposition, and the most important thing is how we reacted afterwards."

"Jerzy, he was absolutely fine – I am extremely happy with him and his professional contribution tonight," Benitez reaffirmed with conviction when pressed on the goalkeeper's performance.

Offering further insight into the team's strategic thinking and mentality, Benitez continued, "If we had only been leading 2-0 at full-time, I would still have been content, as it's still an advantage in a two-leg tie. But the third goal, that makes it a much stronger position for us," he explained, underlining the added comfort of the larger lead. "I always believe in this team's inherent ability, their fighting spirit, and their strong mentality. With that two-goal advantage, and having scored three goals at home, that makes it a very good position to be in for the return fixture. We know it will certainly not be easy in Germany, as Leverkusen are a good side and will push us hard, but we are well-prepared for the challenge ahead and confident in our capabilities."

"And the main objective now, as always, is to continue our strong run of form, to continue working hard and diligently in training every single day, and to keep improving with every single game we play, both individually and collectively," Benitez stated firmly, outlining his ongoing philosophy. "My fundamental principle is that teamwork is absolutely key to any success in football. On the pitch, everyone must contribute their absolute all, every minute of every match – and the players must always pay meticulous attention to the tactical details and instructions we provide. Every match is just one step in a much longer journey, and I firmly believe that unity, cohesion, and collective effort is one incredibly essential quality for achieving our ultimate goals. We must always be 11 players acting as one united unit, supporting each other and working towards a common objective, both on and off the field."

Peer-to-peer nets 'here to stay'

Peer-to-peer (P2P) networks are here to stay, and are on the verge of being exploited by commercial media firms, says a panel of industry experts.
Once several high-profile legal cases against file-sharers are resolved this year, firms will be very keen to try and make money from P2P technology. The expert panel probed the future of P2P at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas earlier in January.
The first convictions for P2P piracy were handed out in the US in January. William Trowbridge and Michael Chicoine pleaded guilty to charges that they infringed copyright by illegally sharing music, movies and software.
Since the first successful file-sharing network Napster was forced to close down, the entertainment industry has been nervous and critical of P2P technology, blaming it for falling sales and piracy. But that is going to change very soon, according to the panel.
The music and film industries have started some big legal cases against owners of legitimate P2P networks - which are not illegal in themselves - and of individuals accused of distributing pirated content over networks.
But they have slowly realised that P2P is a good way to distribute content, said Travis Kalanick, founder and chairman of P2P network Red Swoosh, and soon are all going to want a slice of it. They are just waiting to come up with "business models" that work for them, which includes digital rights management and copy-protection standards.
But, until the legal actions are resolved, experimentation with P2P cannot happen, said Michael Weiss, president of StreamCast Networks.
Remembering the furore around VCRs when they first came out, Mr Weiss said: "Old media always tries to stop new media."
"When they can't stop it, they try to control it. Then they figure out how to make money and they always make a lot of money."
Once the courts decided that the VCR in itself was not an illegal technology, the film turned it into an extremely lucrative business. In August 2004, the San Francisco-based US Court of Appeals ruled in favour of Grokster and StreamCast, two file-sharing networks. The court said they were essentially in the same position that Sony was in the 1980s VCR battle, and said that the networks themselves could not be deemed as illegal.

P2P networks usually do not rely on dedicated servers for the transfer of files. Instead it uses direct connections between computers - or clients. There are now many different types of P2P systems that work in different ways. P2P nets can be used to share any kind of file, like photos, free software, licensed music and any other digital content.
The BBC has already decided to embrace the technology. It aims to offer most of its own programmes for download this year and it will use P2P technology to distribute them. The files would be locked seven days after a programme aired making rights management easier to control.
But the technology is still demonised and misunderstood by many. The global entertainment industry says more than 2.6 billion copyrighted music files are downloaded every month, and about half a million films are downloaded a day.
Legal music download services, like Apple iTunes, Napster, have rushed into the music marketplace to try and lure file-sharers away from free content. Sales of legally-downloaded songs grew tenfold in 2004, with 200 million tracks bought online in the US and Europe in 12 months, the IFPI reported this week. But such download services are very different from P2P networks, not least because of the financial aspect.

There are several money-spinning models that could turn P2P into a golden egg for commercial entertainment companies. Paid-for-pass-along, in which firms receive money each time a file is shared, along with various DRM solutions and advertiser-based options are all being considered.
"We see there are going to be different models for commoditising P2P," said Marc Morgenstern, vice president of anti-piracy firm Overpeer.
"Consumers are hungry for it and we will discover new models together," agreed Mr Morgenstern.
But many net users will continue to ignore the entertainment industry's potential controlling grip on content and P2P technology by continuing to use it for their own creations. Unsigned bands, for example, use P2P networks to distribute their music effectively, which also draws the attention of record companies looking for new artists to sign.
"Increasingly, what you are seeing on P2P is consumer-created content," said Derek Broes, from Microsoft. "They will probably play an increasing role in helping P2P spread," he said.
Looking into P2P's future, file sharing is just the beginning for P2P networks, as far as Mr Broes is concerned. "Once some of these issues are resolved, you are going to see aggressive movement to protect content, but also in ways that are unimaginable now," he said. "File-sharing is the tip of the iceberg."

But such services are very different from **traditional P2P**, not least because of the fundamental financial **business model**.

Paid-for pass-along, in which firms **can generate** money each time a file is **successfully passed** along, with various **subscription-based** and **advertising-based** **revenue models** are all being actively considered. reconstruction:
Peer-to-peer networks are here to stay, and are on the verge of being legitimised by media companies, says a report of industry experts. Once several high-profile legal cases against file-sharers are concluded this year, companies will be very eager to try and make money from the technology. The report probed the future of digital content distribution at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas in January. The first devices for digital music were out in the US in January. Trowbridge and Chicoine predicted to BBC News Online that they would profit by music, and its new distribution models.

Since the first peer-to-peer network Napster was forced to close down, the industry has been wary and fearful of the technology, blaming it for sales and lost revenue. But that is going to change very soon, according to the report.

The music and film industries have started some big legal cases against operators of peer-to-peer networks - which are not in themselves illegal - and against millions of users of pirated content shared over their systems. But they have proved that is a good way to reach customers, said Kalanick, founder and chief executive of network Red Swoosh, and soon they are all going to want a share of it. They are waiting to come up with "business models" that work for them, which involves rights management and secure distribution.

But, until the legal challenges are over, this cannot really happen, said Michael Robertson, president of StreamCast. Comparing the furore around VCRs when they first came out, Mr Robertson said: "Old media always tries to stop new media." When they can't stop it, they try to control it. Then they figure out how to make money and they always make a lot of money." Once the courts decided that the VCR in itself was an enabling technology, the film industry turned it into an entirely new business.

In August, the Ninth Circuit-based US Court of Appeals ruled in favour of Grokster and StreamCast, two file-sharing companies. The court said they were in the same position that Sony was in the VCR dispute, and said that the software platforms themselves could not be held liable as these networks usually do not store content on their servers for the purpose of distribution. Instead it facilitates exchange between users - or peers. There are now many different types of systems that work in different ways. They can be used to share any kind of digital content, like pictures, free software, music and any other type of file.

The BBC has already decided to embrace the technology. It plans to offer most of its own radio programmes for this year and it will use this technology to distribute them. The downloads would be available seven days after a broadcast, making rights management easier to control. But the technology is still demonised and misunderstood by many. The industry says more than one billion music files are downloaded illegally every month, and about half a million movies are shared a day.

Legal music services, like iTunes, Napster, have tapped into the music market to try and lure file-sharers away from free downloads. Sales of legal downloads tenfold in 2004, with 42 million online tracks sold in the US and Europe in the first six months, the IFPI said this week. But such services are very different from file-sharing, not least because of the financial implications.

There are several money-making schemes that could turn into a goldmine for companies. Paid-for downloads, content pass-along in which money is paid each time a file is shared, along with various DRM technologies and subscription-based models are all being considered. "We see there are going to be different business models for commoditising this technology," said Morgenstern, president of anti-piracy firm Overpeer. "Consumers are ready for it and we will build new services together," Mr Morgenstern added.

But many will continue to exploit the industry's potential on the internet and P2P technology by continuing to use it to their own advantage. Artists, for example, use P2P to distribute their music, which also attracts the attention of record companies looking for new talents to sign. "More broadly, what you are seeing on P2P systems is user-created content," said Broes, from Jupiter Research. "They will probably play an integral role in the future of digital media," he said. Looking into P2P's future, music is just the tip of the iceberg for digital content, as far as Mr Broes is concerned. "Once some of these issues are resolved, you are going to see more ways to distribute content, but also ways that are now unimaginable," he said. "Peer-to-peer is the future of the internet."

Peer-to-peer nets 'here to stay'. Peer-to-peer (P2P) networks are here to stay, and are on the verge of being exploited by the media, says a panel of industry experts. This evolving perspective marks a significant shift.

Once several high-profile legal cases against file-sharers are resolved this year, the industry will be very keen to try and make money from P2P technology. This strategic pivot reflects a growing understanding of P2P's potential.

The panel probed the future of P2P at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas in January. The first convictions for P2P were handed out in the US in January. William Trowbridge and Michael Chicoine pleaded guilty to charges that they infringed copyright by sharing music, movies and software. These legal actions highlighted the ongoing challenges in digital content distribution.

Since the first successful file-sharing network Napster was forced to close down, the industry has been nervous and wary of P2P technology, blaming it for falling sales and piracy. This fear largely stemmed from uncontrolled sharing.

But that is going to change very soon, according to the panel. The shift promises new opportunities and collaborations.

The music and film industries have started some big legal cases against owners of legitimate P2P networks - which are not illegal in themselves - and of individuals accused of pirated content downloaded over networks. These actions aimed to enforce copyright while exploring new models.

But they have slowly realised that P2P is a good way to distribute content, said Travis Kalanick, CEO and chairman of P2P network Red Swoosh, and soon they are all going to want a piece of it. The technology's efficiency for mass distribution is undeniable.

They are just waiting to come up with "business models" that work for them, which includes digital rights management and copy-protection standards. Robust frameworks are essential for secure and legitimate use.

But, until the legal issues are resolved, true innovation with P2P cannot fully happen, said Michael Weiss, president of StreamCast Networks. Uncertainty stifles investment and development.

Remembering the furore around VCRs when they first came out, Mr Weiss said: "Old media always tries to stop new media. When they can't stop it, they try to control it. Then they figure out how to make money and they always make a lot of money." This historical pattern is seen as a blueprint for P2P's future.

"Once the courts decided that the VCR in itself was not an illegal technology, the film studios turned it into an enormously lucrative business." This precedent offers a clear path for P2P's commercialisation.

In August 2004, the California-based US Court of Appeals ruled in favour of Grokster and StreamCast, two file-sharing networks. The court said they were essentially in the same position that Sony was in the 1980s VCR, and said that the networks themselves could not be deemed as illegal. This ruling emphasized the neutrality of the technology itself.

P2P networks usually do not rely on a central server for the distribution of content. Instead it uses connections between computers - or clients. This decentralised architecture enhances resilience and speed.

There are now many different types of P2P systems that work in different ways. P2P can be used to share any kind of file, like photos, free videos, music and any other digital media. Its versatility makes it a powerful tool beyond entertainment.

The BBC has already decided to embrace the technology. It aims to offer most of its own programmes for download this year and it will use P2P technology to distribute them. This public broadcaster's move signals mainstream acceptance.

The files would be available for seven days after a programme aired making rights management easier to control. This limited window aims to balance access with intellectual property rights.

But the technology is still demonised and misunderstood by many. The entertainment industry says more than 2.6 billion copyrighted music files are downloaded every month, and about half a million films are downloaded a day. These figures highlight the massive scale of unauthorized sharing that still persists.

Legal music download services, like Apple iTunes, Napster, and others have rushed into the music market to try and lure file-sharers away from free content. They offer convenient and legitimate alternatives.

Sales of legal downloads grew tenfold in 2004, with 200 million online tracks sold in the US and Europe in 12 months, reported the IFPI this week. This robust growth shows a clear demand for legal digital music.

But such download services are very different from P2P, not least because of the financial models. New frameworks are needed to monetise P2P's unique sharing capabilities. There are several money-making models that could turn P2P into a golden egg for entertainment companies.

Paid-for-pass-along, in which users receive money each time a file is shared, along with various DRM and advertiser-based models are all being considered. These innovative models seek to fairly reward both creators and users.

"We see there are going to be different approaches for commoditising P2P," said Marc Morgenstern, vice president of anti-piracy firm Overpeer. "Consumers are hungry for it and we will discover new models together," Mr Morgenstern added. Collaboration between industry and users is key.

But many will continue to ignore the entertainment industry's potential focus on P2P technology by continuing to use it for their own purposes. Unsigned artists, for example, use P2P to distribute their music, which also attracts the attention of record companies looking for new artists to sign. P2P provides a powerful, free platform for independent creators.

"Eventually, what you are seeing on P2P is consumer-created content," said Derek Broes, from Microsoft. "They will probably play an increasing role in helping P2P grow," he said. User-generated content is becoming a significant force in the digital landscape.

Looking into P2P's future, file sharing is just the beginning for P2P, as far as Mr Broes is concerned. He envisions a much broader application of the technology beyond simple content exchange. "Once some of these issues are resolved, you are going to see aggressive movement to embrace P2P, but also in ways that are not available now," he said. "File-sharing is the tip of the iceberg," he concluded, suggesting a vast potential yet to be unlocked.

**A pivotal moment in this evolving narrative was marked by the first convictions for digital copyright infringement.** These were handed out in the United States in January, setting a significant precedent. Individuals identified only as William and Michael pleaded guilty to specific charges that they had infringed **copyright law** by illegally sharing a wide array of content, including digital music, motion pictures, and various software applications. Since the very first widely successful **peer-to-peer** sharing network, **Napster**, was controversially forced to close down its operations, the broader entertainment industry has maintained an undeniably nervous and **highly wary attitude** towards this emerging technology. It has consistently blamed P2P networks for contributing significantly to falling sales figures and for facilitating widespread digital piracy across its various sectors. However, the expert panel underscored that this established perception is poised for a dramatic change, indicating that a new era is expected to unfold very soon.

**Despite their past legalistic approach, the music and film industries have subtly begun to acknowledge the potential of P2P.** They have initiated some big legal cases, notably against owners of legitimate P2P networks, which in themselves are not deemed illegal entities, as well as against numerous individuals accused of **unauthorised sharing of copyrighted** content over these networks. But a crucial realization has slowly dawned upon them: that **P2P technology** is, fundamentally, a highly efficient and effective way to distribute digital content globally. This sentiment was articulated by Travis, the CEO and chairman of network Red, who stated, "They have slowly realised that this is a good way to distribute content, and so, soon enough, they are all going to want a substantial slice of the opportunities it presents." Currently, these major players are primarily focused on developing innovative **business models** that can successfully work within this P2P framework. Such models will, by necessity, include robust digital rights management (DRM) and stringent copy protection standards to safeguard intellectual property. However, Michael Weiss, president of **Digital Content** Networks, cautioned that "until these complex legal actions are fully resolved, widespread implementation of these new models cannot **effectively** happen." Mr. Weiss evoked a powerful historical parallel, recalling the widespread concerns that surrounded the **Video Cassette Recorder (VCR)** when they first came out. He insightfully observed: "Old media always tries to stop new media. When they can't stop it, they try to control it. Then, inevitably, they figure out how to make money, and they always make a lot of money." This historical pattern suggests a likely future for P2P technologies.

**This historical precedent is compelling, as seen in the case of the VCR.** Once the courts decisively ruled that the **VCR** itself was not an inherently illegal technology, despite the initial outcry from content owners, the film studios rapidly shifted their strategy. They successfully turned what was initially perceived as a major threat into an extraordinarily lucrative new business. A more recent and directly relevant legal victory further reinforces this adaptive capacity: in August, the San Francisco-based US Court of Appeals **issued a landmark decision** in favour of **Grokster**, a prominent file-sharing network, and two other similar file-sharing networks. The court's judgment explicitly stated that these networks were essentially in the same legal position that Sony found itself in during the famous **Betamax** battle of the 1980s. The ruling unequivocally established that the P2P networks themselves, as platforms, could not be deemed illegal. A fundamental characteristic of P2P networks is that they typically do not rely on dedicated **central servers** for the direct transfer of files between users. Instead, they operate by facilitating direct, decentralised connections between individual computers or clients, enabling users to share files without a single point of control. Today, there are many distinct types of **P2P** systems available, each designed to function in different ways. These versatile networks can be effectively used to share virtually any kind of digital file, encompassing everything from personal photographs and legally free music to software applications and any other form of digital content.

**Embracing this innovative approach, the BBC has already made a definitive move to adopt peer-to-peer technology.** The British public broadcaster aims to offer most of its own television and radio programmes **for download online** throughout the current year, leveraging this technology for broad distribution. Specifically, it will use **P2P** technology to efficiently distribute these programmes to its vast audience. To manage copyright concerns effectively, the BBC intends to implement a system where the downloaded files would be automatically 'locked' or rendered inaccessible seven days after a programme originally aired. This particular approach is designed to make digital rights management significantly easier to control and enforce. Despite these forward-thinking applications, the underlying technology is still often seen as **nascent** and remains largely misunderstood by many within the broader public and some industry sectors. The entertainment industry, meanwhile, continues to underscore the sheer scale of digital piracy, stating that more than **one** billion copyrighted **music tracks** are downloaded illicitly every single month, with an additional estimated half a million films being downloaded illegally each day.

**In response to the pervasive availability of free, albeit often illegal, content, legal music download services have rapidly carved out a market.** Prominent platforms like Apple **iTunes** have aggressively rushed into the digital music marketplace, strategically aiming to lure file **sharers** away from illicit, free content towards legitimate, paid-for alternatives. These concerted efforts have yielded tangible success. Sales of legally **purchased and downloaded** songs experienced substantial growth in **2004**, with an impressive **140** million tracks bought online across the United States and Europe within a **12-month** period, as was officially reported by the **IFPI (International Federation of the Phonographic Industry)** this week. However, it is crucial to recognise that such established, centralised download services are fundamentally very different from decentralised peer-to-peer networks, not least due to the critical financial aspect and their distinct technological architectures.

**Despite the challenges, a range of innovative, money-spinning business models are under active consideration, potentially transforming P2P into a golden egg for entertainment companies.** These models include paid-for 'pass-along' **licences**, a system in which **content creators and artists** would receive a royalty payment each time a file is legitimately shared. This is being explored alongside various **subscription-based** solutions and advertiser-based options, all of which are being meticulously examined for viability. "We absolutely see that there are going to be numerous different models for **content monetization through P2P**," stated Marc Blank, vice president of anti-piracy. He further elaborated, "**Digital consumers** are clearly hungry for these new ways to access content legally, and we are committed to discovering and developing these new models together with the industry," Mr. Blank concluded. Nevertheless, a significant segment of users will, undoubtedly, continue to disregard the entertainment industry's persistent efforts to establish a controlling grip on **digital content** and its underlying technology. They are expected to continue using these networks for their own independent creations and creative sharing activities.

**A powerful illustration of this independent spirit is found in how unsigned bands effectively utilise peer-to-peer networks to distribute their music.** This grassroots distribution method not only bypasses traditional gatekeepers but also frequently draws the valuable attention of record companies, which are constantly looking for promising new artists to sign. "Increasingly, what you are observing on **P2P platforms** is a significant surge in consumer-created content," remarked Derek, a senior executive from Microsoft. He further posited that such user-generated content and its distribution via P2P "will probably play an increasingly important role in helping **to spread innovative ideas and creative works across the digital sphere**." Looking into **the near** future, Derek expressed his firm conviction that file-sharing, in its current form, is merely the **initial stage** for what is yet to come, as far as he is concerned. He articulated a forward-looking view: "Once some of these intricate issues surrounding copyright, distribution, and monetisation are finally resolved, you are going to witness an aggressive and coordinated movement, not only to rigorously protect digital content but also to engage in distribution and creation in ways that are currently unimaginable." He concluded with a poignant metaphor, stating emphatically that "File-sharing is merely the tip of the iceberg," suggesting a vast, untapped potential beneath the surface of current understanding.

Digital media and the models for its distribution are undoubtedly here to stay. In fact, online music services, video-on-demand platforms, and other forms of digital content delivery are now on the verge of being recognised as a legitimate and increasingly powerful form of mainstream media, says a prominent representative of the global recording industry. This acknowledgment marks a significant shift from previous years of outright rejection and legal battles. For a long time, the industry viewed digital distribution primarily through the lens of piracy, but a new era of acceptance and collaboration appears to be dawning. Once several high-profile cases against these new platforms and their associated technologies, particularly those linked to unauthorised file-sharing and copyright infringement, are concluded and clear legal precedents are set for digital rights, this year will be very pivotal for content owners to finally begin to effectively monetise these new digital avenues and recoup lost revenues. The entire discussion about the future of digital content distribution, including the role of streaming and downloadable formats, was a major and frequently debated theme at the Consumer Electronics Show in January, drawing significant attention from both technology giants and media moguls eager to shape the emerging landscape. The ongoing battle for stronger copyright enforcement and a framework for fair compensation to artists and labels in US January has been intense, marked by numerous legal skirmishes, public relations campaigns, and a growing understanding of consumer behaviour in the digital age. Michael Oldfield, a forward-thinking music industry executive and CEO of Red Arrow Digital Music, told BBC News in an exclusive interview that they are prepared to fully embrace technological change and innovate with new strategies by developing new business models that prioritise consumer access while protecting intellectual property and collaborating more closely with technology companies and internet service providers to foster a legal ecosystem.

Since the first network, Napster, effectively closed down, the relationship between the music industry and technology providers has been fraught with tension, often characterised by deep mistrust and protracted legal conflict, and marked by slow development and cautious adoption of technology for sales and licensing of digital content. For many years, the industry perceived these burgeoning technologies as existential threats rather than lucrative opportunities, leading to a reactive, defensive posture. But that is going to change dramatically and swiftly soon, according to the leading executives within the music and film industries, who are now publicly advocating for innovation. Major record labels and film studios have started legal cases, of which a significant number are in various stages of appeal and settlement, aiming to establish clear legal boundaries for digital distribution and discourage future infringement. However, many industry players now readily acknowledge that this technology, despite its controversial past and associations with piracy, offers an unparalleled way to reach consumers globally, engage with fan bases, and potentially expand markets beyond traditional retail channels and physical media sales, said Michael Oldfield, reiterating his company's progressive position on digital commerce. He believes that soon they are going to want it. "They're just waiting for someone to come with a legitimate, user-friendly, and economically viable model for them that protects intellectual property while satisfying pervasive consumer demand for convenience and accessibility," Oldfield remarked in a candid interview, reflecting on the industry's evolution. "But until the legal uncertainties surrounding digital rights, licensing, and distribution are fully resolved and a stable, predictable framework is in place, nothing truly significant happens, and investment remains hesitant," said Michael Oldfield of the innovative music distribution company. He recalled that when digital piracy first came to prominence in the late 1990s and early 2000s, Mr. Oldfield always advocated for robust measures to stop media sharing entirely, viewing it as a direct and existential threat to artists' livelihoods and industry profits. "When they can't stop it, they try to control it. Then, when they finally figure out how to make money from it, through subscriptions or advertising-supported models, they always make a lot," he explained, referring to the gradual and often reluctant strategic evolution of the major labels from litigation-focused enforcement to innovation and market participation. The industry has, after years of staunch resistance, costly legal battles, and market disruption, decided that the internet in itself was not an existential threat to their entire business model, but rather a powerful platform for growth if harnessed correctly and legally. It is, at its core, simply a business. In August, the San Francisco-based US Court of Appeals delivered a landmark ruling in favour of A&M Records and other plaintiff record companies and against Napster, effectively sealing the fate of the once-dominant file-sharing service by affirming its liability for copyright infringement. The plaintiff record companies said they were in the same position that the court said the Napster platform themselves could not be a legal defense for facilitating the widespread copyright infringement that occurred on its network, impacting thousands of artists and creators. Instead, it was deemed a direct violation of intellectual property rights or a form of contributory infringement, holding the service liable for its users' actions and the resulting financial damages.

There are now different systems in various and continuously evolving ways digital content, particularly music and video, can be used to share any kind of free music and any other forms of digital media, legally and legitimately, marking a new phase for online consumption. The Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA), representing the major labels and a significant portion of the music industry, has already been investing heavily in and actively exploring digital technology to its own strategic advantage, moving beyond a purely reactive stance, for the past several year and will continue to implement and aggressively promote this technology across all their affiliated labels and artists, fostering a culture of innovation. The ultimate goal for the industry would be to create a comprehensive and appealing subscription system that offers continuous value, potentially bundling various content types like music, videos, and exclusive access, thereby enabling seven days a week monetization through effective and robust digital rights management. This system would ensure that creators are fairly compensated for their work. However, the technology itself and the proposed paid models are still viewed with skepticism and resistance by many consumers who have grown accustomed to the ease and perceived value of free alternatives available online, whether legal or illegal. The scale of free file-sharing remains enormous and a significant challenge to revenue generation, with more than 200 million songs downloaded illegally, or accessed via unofficial channels, every month and about half a million new tracks appearing on these unregulated platforms a day, making it difficult for paid services to compete on sheer volume. In response to this, a multitude of new subscription-based services have rapidly emerged and expanded their presence into the music market, specifically designed to try to attract and retain users away from free peer-to-peer sharing and illegal downloads by offering convenience and exclusive content. In a significant move affecting hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of potential subscribers in the US and Europe that was announced and partially launched just this week. But such services are intrinsically and fundamentally different from piracy, not least because they operate within a legal framework that compensates creators and invests in future content, at least of course, in terms of their legality, their business ethics, and the direct compensation they offer to artists and rights holders for their creative work. There are several innovative business models that could turn a substantial profit for the industry and its artists, moving beyond the traditional album sales model. Paid-for pass-along licenses, which would involve a small charge each time a song is legally passed along or shared within a network, along with various tiered subscription plans offering different levels of access and features, such as offline listening or high-fidelity audio, and integrated advertising models, similar to internet radio platforms or free streaming tiers, are being considered as viable paths forward for generating revenue in the digital age and establishing a sustainable ecosystem for music creation and consumption.

We see there is going to be a fundamental shift in digital music consumption and a brighter, more sustainable future for the entire industry, said Hilary Rosen, the confident and visionary CEO of the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA), speaking at a recent industry conference on digital innovation. "Many within the industry, including major labels, independent artists, and new tech companies alike, are for it, and we will work together tirelessly and collaboratively to achieve this transformation. Many believe the industry has tremendous, largely untapped, creative and commercial potential and can effectively leverage cutting-edge technology by setting its own example. They can, and indeed must, actively use their music, which is their primary asset and inherently draws the attention of global audiences and builds cultural connections. Record companies looking for a clear and decisive sign, "you are seeing a completely new digital landscape being created before your very eyes, one that values creativity and rewards innovation," said Rosen, optimistically predicting a renaissance for the music business as it adapts to the digital era. Digital distribution, therefore, will probably pay an increasingly important and central role, said she, emphasising its critical function in how music is consumed and monetised in the coming years and decades. "Looking into the future is the primary goal and guiding principle for all stakeholders within the industry far and wide, as they strive to balance artistic integrity with commercial success." Once some firm, equitable, and widely accepted business models and technological standards are fully established and embraced by consumers, "you are going to see content delivered in compelling new ways that enhance the user experience and offer unparalleled access, but in formats and through channels that are now fully legitimate, profitable for creators, and truly sustainable for the long term, moving beyond the era of contention," he said. The industry is not just adapting to change; it is actively shaping its destiny and poised for significant growth in the digital era, with technology as its key enabler and music as its enduring heart.

Recently, film studios have started legal cases against platforms of which they accuse of facilitating the widespread distribution of pirated material, seeking injunctions and damages. But these content owners have failed to grasp that there is a far more efficient and user-friendly way to distribute content, said Travis Kalanick, founder and CEO of Red Swoosh, a prominent peer-to-peer content distribution firm. He believes that soon, everyone will be going to want it. "We are waiting with open arms for ""them, the major content owners, - to join us on this journey," he added, referring to a potential shift in strategy.

But, that particular legal approach will ultimately not happen, said Michael Robertson, the outspoken CEO of StreamCast, another peer-to-peer software provider. Then they try to make money from it - and a lot of money at that." In August, the Ninth US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled decisively in favour of Grokster and StreamCast, asserting that they were in the same legal position that Sony was with the VCR, and therefore could not be held liable for copyright infringement based on the individual actions of their users. This landmark decision was a major blow for the record industry's legal strategy, forcing a re-evaluation. It was a clear victory for the tech companies.

There are fundamentally different systems in play. Some networks can be used to download any file, any movie, any song, free music from any source imaginable, often without legal recourse for the content creators. The BBC, for its part, has been developing its own technology to manage and protect its valuable content. It is keen to protect its own content for many years to come and will license them through various digital platforms. For example, specific content will typically be available for seven days after initial broadcast, making robust digital rights management a key feature of its future offerings. But this underlying technology is still widely demonised by many within the traditional media industry, especially Hollywood. The situation is far more nuanced and complex than simply dismissing it as piracy.

Legal music downloads have reportedly increased tenfold in 2004, reaching an impressive 200 million across the US and Europe, the IFPI (International Federation of the Phonographic Industry) reported this week. But such services are fundamentally different from traditional peer-to-peer file-sharing, not least of all because they operate within a legal framework and pay artists royalties for their work.

There are still some significant hurdles to overcome, particularly to turn a profit for the content creators and distributors in the evolving digital landscape. New business models, such as paid-for subscription passes, where money is exchanged for guaranteed access to content, along with stronger DRM and innovative new technologies, are being actively considered by industry executives. "We see the opportunity here for commoditising content, allowing legitimate distribution on a massive scale," said Bill Morgenstern, CEO of anti-piracy firm Overpeer. He confidently added, "You pay for it and we will deliver, reliably and securely, anywhere in the world."

Many critics continue to point to the music industry's historical failure to embrace the full potential of digital technology and the technology it already owns. This includes the power of social networks, viral marketing, and user-generated content, all of which are increasingly catching the attention of record companies looking for the next big sign of profitability and sustainable growth. "You are seeing a fundamental shift in consumer behaviour, moving towards digital consumption," said Michael Broes, director of digital business at Universal Music Group. He believes that "File-sharing will probably play an integral role in future distribution models, perhaps in licensed, controlled environments," he said. Looking into the future's crystal ball, what is the ultimate outlook for this rapidly evolving technology? So far, Mr Broes remains optimistic about the potential for innovation and revenue generation. "Once some of the complex legal issues are finally resolved, you are going to see content delivered, in ways that are truly revolutionary and highly tailored to individual preferences," he said, emphasising the shift. "Ultimately, it's all about the user experience and giving the power back to the consumer."

Once several fully legal file-sharing services are officially launched and widely adopted this year, consumers will finally be presented with a legitimate alternative to current practices, enabling them to choose their preferred method of accessing content from a diverse range of providers. The BBC recently probed the intricate future of digital content distribution and the evolving landscape of file-sharing during the highly anticipated Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. This marks the first major battle for control in the digital age, a pivotal moment for content creators and distributors alike. Michael Chicoine, a representative from the music industry, eloquently told delegates at the conference that they could, and indeed should, make substantial money by not only selling music through new channels but also by actively embracing and leveraging P2P technology.

The pioneering peer-to-peer network Napster, once a symbol of the digital revolution, was ultimately forced to shut down its operations after enduring years of protracted and costly legal battles. This extensive litigation severely impacted the music industry, which simultaneously saw its traditional sales plummeting and profits dwindling. However, the industry is now rapidly adapting, and according to its representatives, this landscape is going to change very soon. Consequently, major record labels and content owners have initiated some big legal campaigns against numerous online services and platforms which they allege have offered or facilitated access to pirated material. But resorting to endless litigation is not an effective or sustainable long-term solution, argued Travis Kalanick, a prominent figure from the peer-to-peer network Red Swoosh. He predicted that soon all digital content, in various forms and formats, is going to be a fundamental part of the peer-to-peer ecosystem. Instead of passively waiting for the traditional industry to proactively come forward with "new ideas" and innovative solutions for their users, complete with fair rights and transparent licensing models, the current legal arguments are simply failing to keep pace with technological advancement. They cannot effectively stop the spread of P2P, nor can they innovate fast enough to adapt to these shifts, stressed Steve Johnson, who serves as president of StreamCast. This situation, he noted, echoes the furore surrounding VCRs when they first came out, as he quoted: "Media companies always stop new media." He continued, "When they can't stop it, they inevitably try to control it. Then, out of necessity, they figure out how to make money, and they always make money."

The fundamental point, Johnson explained, was that the VCR in itself was merely a neutral piece of technology; it was the film industry that eventually adapted and transformed it into a lucrative opportunity.
