UK bank Standard Chartered seals major South Korean deal.

UK-based bank Standard Chartered has announced it will pay $3.3bn (£1.8bn) to buy one of South Korea's main lenders, Korea First Bank (KFB). The acquisition marks a significant strategic move for the emerging markets-focused bank, expanding its presence in a crucial Asian economy.

Standard Chartered said Korea First Bank (KFB), a cornerstone for building its strategic presence in the region, is currently South Korea's third largest bank by total assets. The announcement led to a fall in Standard Chartered's shares, which dropped 3% in early London trading. To finance the substantial deal, the bank revealed plans for a rights issue, intending to raise £1bn ($1.8bn) by issuing new shares. This represents approximately 10% of its current share capital, potentially diluting existing shareholders but providing the necessary capital for the acquisition. Standard Chartered anticipates that Korea First Bank will contribute significantly to its overall performance, expecting about 16% of the group's future pre-tax earnings to come from the new South Korean operations.

Furthermore, the South Korean bank is projected to account for 22% of the group's total risk-weighted assets, highlighting its immediate impact on Standard Chartered's balance sheet. This acquisition is particularly noteworthy as it comes a year after US banking giant Citigroup successfully outbid Standard Chartered for KorAm Bank, another major South Korean lender. This earlier defeat had underscored Standard Chartered's strong ambition to penetrate the South Korean market. This latest move, therefore, represents a major victory for Standard Chartered and is poised to become the largest foreign takeover of a financial institution in South Korea's history, signalling growing international interest in the country's banking sector. Sources close to the deal suggest that this time around, Standard Chartered is thought to have moved with exceptional speed and decisiveness to secure the agreement, learning from its previous experience. KFB is currently the fifth largest bank in South Korea, boasting a substantial customer base of 3 million individuals and commanding approximately 6% of the country's competitive retail banking market. It also operates an extensive branch network across the nation, providing a strong platform for Standard Chartered's expansion.

South Korea's banking market is considerably large, estimated to be three times the size of Hong Kong's, with total financial assets valued at an impressive $44bn. This scale presents significant growth opportunities for international players. Standard Chartered, despite having its headquarters firmly established in London, conducts a substantial portion of its global operations - specifically two-thirds of its business - across the vibrant economies of Asia. Much of the remaining third is focused on the high-growth markets of Africa and the Middle East, reflecting its unique emerging markets focus and diverse geographical footprint. Addressing concerns about the acquisition price, Standard Chartered's chief executive, Mervyn Davies, confidently stated at a London press conference: "We're comfortable with the price paid. The key here has been speed and decisiveness in making sure that we won this strategic asset." He emphasized the bank's long-term commitment to South Korea. Mr Davies further praised KFB, describing it as a "well-managed, conservatively run bank with a strong brand identity" and a "leading position in a dynamic growth market". These characteristics, he noted, align perfectly with Standard Chartered's investment criteria.

Back in London, the announcement of the rights issue, which involves the issuance of 118 million new shares to finance the acquisition, put pressure on Standard Chartered's stock. Its share price declined, contributing to a 0.3% fall in the benchmark FTSE 100 index. By midday, Standard Chartered's shares were trading 28p lower at 925p, reflecting investor concerns about dilution and the significant outlay for the Korean asset. Some financial analysts and market observers immediately questioned whether Standard Chartered had overpaid for KFB, given the competitive bidding process and the bank's previous attempt. Concerns about integration challenges also surfaced. The acquisition, which remains subject to final regulatory approvals from both UK and South Korean authorities, is anticipated to be formally completed by April 2005. Standard Chartered expects the deal to be earnings accretive - meaning it will add to earnings per share - by 2006, indicating a relatively quick turnaround for profitability. It also emerged that British banking rival HSBC, a global powerhouse based in London and with strong ties to Hong Kong, was also in the running for KFB. HSBC had reportedly been keen to expand its footprint in South Korea. Standard Chartered is widely understood to have sealed the deal through swift negotiations, reportedly bringing together key executives from all parties during the Chuseok holiday break – a major public holiday in South Korea. This strategic timing allowed them to outmanoeuvre competitors.

''They were able to move so quickly, sewing it up by Friday evening,'' the Financial Times quoted an anonymous analyst in its report as saying, highlighting the rapid pace of the negotiations. With KFB now off the market, attention will undoubtedly turn to the next South Korean bank in line for a sale. Analysts speculate that this is most likely to be Woori Bank, another significant lender that is also currently under the ownership and control of a US private equity group, awaiting privatisation. Standard Chartered confirmed it was acquiring 100% of KFB's equity, a move that would fully integrate the bank into its global operations. This acquisition is significant as it will bring an end to Korea First Bank's long-standing nationalised status, a legacy of the Asian financial crisis. Prior to this deal, the South Korean government held a controlling stake of 51.4% in KFB. The remaining shares, along with significant operational and strategic control, were in the hands of the US private equity group Newbridge Capital, which had been seeking an exit for some time.

Newbridge originally acquired its stake in KFB during the tumultuous period of the government's widespread nationalisation of several distressed lenders in the immediate aftermath of the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis. This period severely crippled South Korea's financial sector, leading to widespread reforms. Looking at the broader economic picture, South Korea's economy is forecast to grow by a robust 4.5% this year, reflecting a strong recovery and stable outlook. While South Korea has often been thought of primarily as an industrial powerhouse, renowned for its manufacturing and exports, its service sector has experienced significant and sustained growth in the last decade or so, transforming the economic landscape. Services now make up approximately 40% of the country's economy, with financial services and information technology (IT) having emerged as particularly important drivers of growth and innovation. In the aftermath of the Asian financial crisis, the South Korean government actively encouraged the growth of consumer credit as a means to stimulate domestic demand. However, this policy unfortunately led to severe problems; notably, LG Card, the country's largest credit card company, has been subject to a protracted workout programme for many months, following massive and unsustainable losses from delinquent borrowers. Despite these past challenges, many financial analysts believe South Korea's financial services industry is still in its relative infancy, presenting substantial opportunities for innovation and the introduction of new, sophisticated financial products and services.

Standard Chartered's management highlighted their strategic vision, stating they see "the immense opportunity to create significant value by the cross-selling of more diverse products and services" to KFB's existing customer base and beyond. Since 1999, KFB itself has undergone a significant transformation. It has been restructured from what was largely a corporate-focused bank into a more dynamic retail bank, with a strong focus on consumer lending. This segment now proudly makes up 45% of its entire loan portfolio, showcasing its successful pivot.

Standard Chartered expects about 16% of future group revenue to come from KFB...The South Korean bank will also make up 22% of the group's total assets. The move, a year after Citigroup beat Standard Chartered to buy Koram bank, would be the South Korean financial sector's biggest foreign takeover. This time around, Standard Chartered is thought to have beaten HSBC to the deal. KFB is South Korea's seventh largest bank, with 3 million retail customers, 6% of the country's banking market and an extensive branch network...The country's banking market is three times the size of Hong Kong's with annual revenues of $44bn. Standard Chartered has its headquarters in London but does two thirds of its business in Asia, and much of the rest in Africa. Mobile data services such as GPRS and MMS are still struggling to gain widespread adoption in the UK, despite an increase in the number of GPRS-enabled handsets. This is according to the latest report from the Mobile Data Association (MDA). The report highlights a significant gap between the availability of these technologies and their actual use by consumers.

By 2005, the MDA projects that 75% of all new handsets sold will be GPRS-enabled, indicating a strong push from manufacturers and networks to make the technology ubiquitous. However, the association warns that this alone will not be enough to drive uptake.

A survey conducted by the MDA found that while approximately 53% of handsets currently in the market are GPRS-enabled, actual usage is significantly lower. The MDA stated that average GPRS usage sessions often last for only around 30 seconds, indicating casual or limited engagement with the 'always-on' data service. GPRS, which stands for General Packet Radio Service, is often referred to as 2.5G technology, bridging the gap between older 2G mobile networks and the newer, faster 3G services. It allows for continuous connection to the internet, enabling quicker browsing, email access, and the download of various types of mobile content.

The report noted that services like ringtones are popular, and campaigns that promote data usage, such as the recent Band Aid-ringtone download initiative, have helped raise awareness. According to the MDA, such campaigns are crucial for educating consumers about the benefits of GPRS. Despite this, the conversion from awareness to active usage remains a significant challenge for the industry.

When it comes to MMS (Multimedia Messaging Service), the data reveals a similar pattern of slow but steady growth. The report indicates that 32% of new handsets are capable of sending and receiving MMS messages, which can include pictures, video clips, and sound files. However, only 14% of mobile phone users in the UK have actually sent an MMS message.

This figure represents a modest increase from previous years. The MDA states that the adoption rate for MMS has grown by 36% since 2003, when only 7% of users had sent an MMS. While this growth is positive, it suggests that MMS is still far from becoming a mainstream communication tool for most mobile users.

One of the primary factors that has been hindering the widespread adoption of MMS has been interoperability issues. Users have often found it difficult to send multimedia messages between different mobile networks or between handsets from different manufacturers. These technical barriers can frustrate users and deter them from regularly using the service, despite its rich media capabilities. The industry is working towards resolving these interoperability challenges to ensure a smoother user experience and drive future MMS growth.

His comments come in a BBC documentary called 'No More Mr Nasty'.

TV presenter Anne Robinson said as home secretary he gave the impression he would "like to kick your cat". Ms Robinson, a friend of the Tory leader, also revealed that as a Cambridge student Mr Howard was "much loved by women and he was a courteous and kind and rather dashing lover" - although she denied having personal experience. "I wasn't at Cambridge - and it's not personal experience - but I know people who were."

Documentary maker Michael Cockerell was given behind-the-scenes access to Mr Howard for his film portrait. The Tory leader was asked to respond to people who said that if there had been a quota on immigration and asylum in the 1930s, his parents might not have been allowed into the country.

He replies: "What is the inference of that? That if you reach the view that you need to control immigration in the interests of the country you're not allowed to put a view forward if you happen to be descended from immigrants? That seems to me an absolutely extraordinary proposition? It would certainly mean no-one from immigrant parents could be prime minister."

Ms Robinson, who presents The Weakest Link, tells Cockerell that she despaired at his hardline image when he was home secretary in John Major's government. "I used to have to sit on my hands because he'd get on television and give a passable impression of someone who'd like to kick your cat or would put your baby in prison if he cried. I mean it was very, very Draconian."

The film shows Mr Howard laughing at Rory Bremner's impression of him as Dracula, which he calls "good fun", apart from the serious falsehood of a comment suggesting he wants fewer black people in the UK. The film shows the private side of the Tory leader watching television at home or playing table tennis with his wife, ex-model Sandra. Asked if she enjoys a game of ping pong she confesses: "Yeah, it would be more enjoyable if I could win occasionally too, but otherwise it's quite fun."

Former Downing Street communications chief Alastair Campbell, now working on Labour's election campaign, says a "touchy-feely" image does not fit Mr Howard. He says Tony Blair was not worried by his opponents' early performance in their Commons clashes because Mr Howard lacked a "big strategy", including on issues like Iraq. The Tory leader brands such criticisms as "absolutely rubbish", arguing that he has been consistent on his support for the war but critical of Mr Blair's failure to tell the truth on intelligence.

Former Tory chancellor Ken Clarke says Mr Howard has a bigger problem changing perceptions of the Tory party than his personal image. Mr Clarke says the party is improving and it is "conceivable" it could win the next election. But he adds: "It has got to change itself a bit and broaden its appeal."

Michael Portillo, the widely recognised former Conservative cabinet minister, has gone on the defensive in a new television documentary, directly responding to people who have, at various points in his career, questioned or cast aspersions on his family origins. In the programme, Mr Portillo spoke openly and candidly about his late father, Luis Gabriel Portillo, a Spanish Republican exile, whose Spanish Republican parents, his grandparents, he says, would have been considered "no one of any particular significance" by some elements within his extended British family. This background, he suggests, profoundly shaped his own political views and personal identity, offering him a unique perspective on British society.

In a new More4 TV documentary, provisionally titled "Portillo's Progress," for which he gave extensive behind-the-scenes access to his life and thoughts, Mr Portillo recounted in detail how his father, who was also a student in Britain at the time, was significantly helped by various compassionate women after his initial arrival in the country. He described his father with evident affection as "a kind and rather shy" man, navigating a new culture with quiet dignity. The film focuses not only on his having personal experience with these sensitive themes of migration and integration but also includes insights from other individuals who were in strikingly similar situations, offering a broader perspective on the challenges faced by immigrants. The documentary was about to air when he was confronted by a commentator who suggested that if there had been a more stringent immigration law on the statute books at that historical time, his father might not have been allowed into the United Kingdom at all.

"What is the true implication of that?" Mr Portillo asked rhetorically in a particularly impactful segment of the film, challenging the underlying premise. He continued, articulating his strong concern that such a viewpoint suggests "that if you yourself believe you need greater control in the area of immigration, then you are simply not allowed to put your view forward, purely because you happen to be from an immigrant background yourself?" He dismissed this notion vehemently, stating, "That seems to me utterly absurd, illogical, and deeply unfair." Veteran journalist Michael Cockerell rebuts recent criticism regarding his approach to historical narratives. Mr Cockerell has offered a detailed response to observations made by some people of Caribbean origin, particularly those whose parents themselves, having immigrated to the UK, would one day become leading and influential figures in British public and professional life. His assistant, working on the forthcoming documentary series 'More Mr. Cockerell', stated as he elaborated on his own viewpoint, that he "liked to" see the programme feature a broader spectrum of diverse voices and experiences. A close friend, who is also a student mentored by Mr Cockerell, echoed this sentiment, adding that he "had a similar and rather insightful perspective" on the importance of inclusive storytelling – although Mr Cockerell himself was quick to clarify that he was not speaking from direct personal experience on this particular matter. He elaborated, "I wasn't – it's not my personal experience – but I certainly know people who have been through this, and their stories deserve to be heard and understood."

For his new series, Michael Cockerell was afforded extensive behind-the-scenes access, enabling him to explore complex historical and social issues. During a recent interview promoting the series, he was pressed specifically about comments he had made pertaining to individuals who posited that if there had been a more progressive and open stance on issues of race and immigration in Britain during the 1930s, the country would have been in a much better and more harmonious state by the post-war era. Mr Cockerell responded with a rhetorical question, challenging the premise of personal experience as a prerequisite for commentary. He asked pointedly: "Is it the case that if you genuinely believe that you need to be an intrinsic part of the specific group or community you're discussing, then you're only allowed to put forward your considered views if you happen, by accident of birth or circumstance, to be precisely from that background yourself?" He concluded his thought with a strong affirmation of his discomfort with such a restrictive viewpoint, stating: "That seems to me an utterly absurd and frankly illiberal notion. Would no one whose own parents were themselves not British citizens by birth, for example, then be legitimately allowed to speak on matters concerning the country's past or future?"

Michael Cockerell, known for his incisive political journalism, vividly recalled a period of his life where he confronted entrenched ideological positions. He particularly despaired of the fervent hardliners he encountered during his time as a student at St John's College, describing their views and methods with palpable disapproval. Recounting those challenging days, he stated: "We used to have to *deal with them* on *our hands* on an almost daily basis, because *they'd* get *extremely aggressive and agitated* if challenged, and quickly give a passable *justification for anyone* who'd like *to put* your *head* in *a metaphorical guillotine* if *they had the slightest opportunity or power to do so*. I *personally found* it very, very Draconian, and utterly antithetical to open debate and intellectual freedom."

In related news, the forthcoming film by satirist Rory Bremner, which Michael Cockerell recently praised as "good" and commendable, reportedly seeks to rigorously dispel the falsehood of insidious claims suggesting that Mr Bremner harbours views intending for black people to leave or be expelled from the UK. The documentary aims to present a more rounded and personal portrait of the public figure. It shows him in various relaxed settings, such as at home or playing with his children and other family members, highlighting his private life beyond his public persona. Asked by an interviewer if she thought her father, Mr Bremner, was 'more Mr. Serious' in private compared to his on-screen comedic image, his daughter replied candidly: "Yeah, he can definitely be more reserved and thoughtful too, especially when he's focused on serious topics, but honestly, it's quite fun having him around and seeing both sides of his personality."

In a separate segment of the documentary, a former prominent political figure, understood to be former Labour leader Neil Kinnock, reflects on his own experiences with media scrutiny. His original selection for a major television interview in the past was, by many observers, widely seen as a "feel-good" factor for his party at the time, generating positive publicity. However, Mr Kinnock himself later conveyed that he was not entirely impressed by his own performance in what he described as Mr Cockerell's "big" interview, an extensive sit-down including searching questions like "what was your greatest defeat, and how did it impact you personally?". Interestingly, Mr Kinnock also recalled that he had previously been on another of Cockerell's programmes, broadcast just the week before, where he was able to tell the full, unvarnished story of his political career and personal motivations, which perhaps contrasted with the more challenging "big" interview. Former Labour leader Mr Kinnock subsequently discussed his personal motivations and the sacrifices made during his long tenure in politics. Mr Kinnock, ever forthright, says his party and its future chances of electoral success "could" be significantly enhanced with proactive reform. He concluded with an emphatic statement: "It has got to change itself a bit, from the grassroots upwards. It's absolutely essential for its long-term viability and to reconnect with the electorate."

The documentary series, 'No More Mr. Cockerell', is scheduled for broadcast on BBC2 on 12 February, commencing at 2005 GMT.

Butler launches attack on Blair. Former civil service chief Lord Butler has criticised the way Tony Blair's government operates, accusing it of being obsessed with headlines. He also attacked the way the Iraq war was "sold" to the public, with important warnings on the strength of the intelligence left out. Tory leader Michael Howard said Lord Butler had given the "most damaging testimony" he could remember. But Downing Street said Mr Blair should be judged by results, not his style.

Lord Butler said Mr Blair bypassed the Cabinet and relied instead on small, informal groups of advisers to help him make decisions. The prime minister's official spokesman said the Cabinet was still used to achieve a consensus on important issues. But he added: "You cannot, in a modern government, take every decision in Cabinet. It's just not possible."

Lord Butler said the government had too much freedom to "bring in bad Bills" and "to do whatever it likes" and it relied too much on the advice of political appointees. The former cabinet secretary said in an interview with The Spectator magazine: "I would be critical of the present government in that there is too much emphasis on selling, there is too much central control and there is too little of what I would describe as reasoned deliberation which brings in all the arguments." Mr Howard described Lord Butler's intervention as "very important". "This is from someone who was an insider at the very heart of the Blair government." "It is certainly the most damaging testimony I can ever remember from someone in such an eminent position."

Lord Butler's report earlier this year into Iraq intelligence said the government's September 2002 weapons dossier did not make clear that intelligence about claims that Saddam Hussein had stockpiles of chemical and biological weapons was "very thin". The reason for this is that it would have weakened ministers' case for war, Lord Butler said in his Spectator interview, which was conducted by the magazine's editor, Conservative MP Boris Johnson. He said: "When civil servants give material to ministers, they say these are the conclusions we've drawn, but we've got to tell you the evidence we've got is pretty thin." Similarly, if you are giving something to the United Nations and to the country, you should warn them.

Asked why he thought the warnings were not there, Lord Butler said: "One has got to remember what the purpose of the dossier was. The purpose of the dossier was to persuade the British why the government thought Iraq was a very serious threat."

When asked whether he thought the country was well-governed on the whole, he replied: "Well. I think we are a country where we suffer very badly from Parliament not having sufficient control over the executive, and that is a very grave flaw." "We should be breaking away from the party whip. The executive is much too free to bring in a huge number of extremely bad Bills, a huge amount of regulation and to do whatever it likes - and whatever it likes is what will get the best headlines tomorrow." "All that is part of what is bad government in this country." Lord Butler's assessment was backed by his predecessor as Cabinet Secretary, Lord Armstrong. Lord Armstrong told BBC Two's Newsnight: "I agree ... there doesn't appear to be the sort of informed collective political judgement brought to bear on decision-making that those affected by decisions are entitled to expect." Liberal Democrat deputy leader Menzies Campbell said he thought Lord Butler's comments were "well justified" and Mr Blair's style of leadership was "corrosive of the whole system of government". But Labour former minister Jack Cunningham accused Lord Butler of basing his comments on the first eight months of the incoming Labour administration, when he was cabinet secretary. Mr Cunningham told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "Taken together, Robin Butler's comments are partial, inaccurate and cannot be taken as anything other than politically biased against the Labour government."

reconstruction:
Lord Butler launches scathing attack on Tony Blair's government

Lord Butler, the former head of the Home Civil Service, has launched a wide-ranging and significant attack on the operational style of Prime Minister Tony Blair's government. He criticised the administration for its perceived over-reliance on media management, accusing it specifically of being 'obsessed with headlines' in its decision-making processes.

Lord Butler's criticisms extended particularly to the crucial period leading up to the Iraq war. He specifically highlighted concerns about how the case for military action was presented or 'sold' to the British public. He revealed that vital warnings regarding the true strength and reliability of the intelligence underlying the claims of Saddam Hussein's weapons programmes were deliberately withheld or omitted from public discourse.

The Conservative Party leader, Michael Howard, swiftly responded to Lord Butler's outspoken remarks, describing them as profoundly damaging to the government. Mr Howard stated that the former civil service chief had delivered 'the most damaging testimony I can ever remember' from someone in such a senior and informed position, underscoring the gravity of the allegations.

However, Downing Street was quick to defend the Prime Minister and his government's practices. A spokesperson for Mr Blair countered Lord Butler's criticisms by asserting that the Prime Minister's performance should ultimately 'be judged by results, not his style' of leadership or internal operating procedures, implying that effectiveness outweighed the process.

Elaborating on his critique of the government's operational methods, Lord Butler asserted that Prime Minister Blair frequently bypassed the traditional structures of collective Cabinet decision-making. Instead, according to Lord Butler, Mr Blair 'relied instead on small, informal groups of advisers' to formulate and execute key policy decisions, a method which he suggested undermined established governmental processes.

In a direct response to this particular point, the Prime Minister's official spokesman maintained that the Cabinet remained an active and integral part of governance, insisting that it 'was still used to achieve a consensus on important issues.' The spokesman further elaborated on the practicalities of modern governance, stating: 'You cannot, in a modern government, take every decision in Cabinet. It's just not possible,' thereby defending the need for flexible decision-making structures.

Lord Butler also voiced significant concerns about the perceived unchecked power of the executive. He argued that the government possessed 'too much freedom to bring in bad Bills' and an inclination 'to do whatever it likes,' implying a lack of proper scrutiny. He further criticised its heavy reliance 'on the advice of political appointees,' suggesting a politicisation of advice. In an extensive interview published in The Spectator magazine, the former cabinet secretary explicitly stated: 'I would be critical of the present government in that there is too much emphasis on selling, there is too much central control and there is too little of what I would describe as reasoned deliberation which brings in all the arguments.'

Reiterating his earlier comments, Mr Howard emphasised the profound significance of Lord Butler's intervention. He highlighted Lord Butler's unique perspective, stating: 'This is from someone who was an insider at the very heart of the Blair government.' The Tory leader underscored the unprecedented nature of the critique, adding: 'It is certainly the most damaging testimony I can ever remember from someone in such an eminent position,' suggesting the comments could seriously undermine the government's credibility.

Earlier this year, Lord Butler had chaired an official inquiry into the intelligence surrounding the Iraq war. His report from that inquiry concluded that the government's key September 2002 dossier, which presented the case for war, failed to adequately convey crucial caveats. Specifically, it 'did not make clear that intelligence about claims that Saddam Hussein had stockpiles of chemical and biological weapons was "very thin",' a detail that, if revealed at the time, could have significantly altered public and parliamentary perception.

Lord Butler elaborated on the rationale behind this omission during his interview with The Spectator, which was notably conducted by the magazine's editor, Conservative MP Boris Johnson. He suggested that the reason for not explicitly stating the thinness of the intelligence was pragmatic: 'it would have weakened ministers' case for war,' implying a deliberate choice to present a stronger, albeit less qualified, argument.

Further elucidating the principles of civil service integrity, Lord Butler explained the expected standard of advice. He stated: 'When civil servants give material to ministers, they say these are the conclusions we've drawn, but we've got to tell you the evidence we've got is pretty thin.' He extended this principle to international relations, adding: 'Similarly, if you are giving something to the United Nations and to the country concerned, you should warn them' about the reliability of the information.

When pressed on why these vital warnings were absent from the public presentation, Lord Butler offered his perspective on the dossier's primary objective. He remarked: 'One has got to remember what the purpose of the dossier was.' He then clarified his understanding: 'The purpose of the dossier was to persuade the British public why the government thought Iraq was a very serious threat,' suggesting a focus on persuasion over full disclosure of intelligence limitations.

Shifting to a broader assessment of the state of governance in the UK, Lord Butler was asked for his overall view on whether the country was well-governed. He responded candidly: 'Well, I think we are a country where we suffer very badly from Parliament not having sufficient control over the executive, and that is a very grave flaw.' His comments pointed to a fundamental imbalance of power.

Lord Butler advocated for a significant reform in parliamentary practice, stating: 'We should be breaking away from the party whip.' He argued that the executive branch has become 'much too free to bring in a huge number of extremely bad Bills, a huge amount of regulation and to do whatever it likes.' He critically linked this autonomy to media management, adding: '—and whatever it likes is what will get the best headlines tomorrow.' He concluded his scathing assessment by declaring: 'All that is part of what is bad government in this country,' painting a stark picture of current political failings.

Significantly, Lord Butler's robust assessment found support from his own predecessor as Cabinet Secretary, Lord Armstrong. Speaking on BBC Two's Newsnight programme, Lord Armstrong echoed similar concerns. He stated: 'I agree that there doesn't appear to be the sort of informed collective political judgement brought to bear on decision-making that those affected by decisions are entitled to expect,' thus lending considerable weight to Lord Butler's critique of the government's decision-making culture.

The Liberal Democrat deputy leader, Menzies Campbell, also weighed in on the controversy, expressing his agreement with Lord Butler's analysis. He asserted that Lord Butler's comments were 'well justified' and went on to describe Mr Blair's distinctive style of leadership as 'corrosive of the whole system of government,' indicating a broad concern across the opposition benches about the Prime Minister's approach.

However, not all reactions were supportive of Lord Butler. Labour's former minister Jack Cunningham launched a counter-attack, accusing Lord Butler of grounding his criticisms in an outdated period. Mr Cunningham suggested that Lord Butler was unfairly basing his comments 'on the first eight months of the incoming Labour administration, when he was cabinet secretary,' a period now well over a decade in the past. Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Mr Cunningham delivered a strong condemnation: 'Taken together, Robin Butler's comments are partial, inaccurate and cannot be taken as anything other than politically biased against the Labour government,' casting doubt on the impartiality of the former civil service chief's remarks.

Attack on Blair: Former service chief Lord Butler has launched a scathing attack on the way Tony Blair's government operates, accusing it of being obsessed with central control, with presentation and with spin. He also severely criticised the way the case for war in Iraq was presented to the public, saying important caveats on the limits and reliability of the intelligence were left out. Conservative leader Michael Howard said Lord Butler had given the most damning indictment of the government's style he could remember. But a Downing Street spokesman said Mr Blair should be judged by results and achievements, not merely by his style of government.

Lord Butler said Mr Blair had increasingly bypassed the traditional decision-making processes of the Cabinet and instead relied on small, informal groups of trusted advisers and aides to help him make crucial decisions. The prime minister's official spokesman, however, insisted that the Cabinet was still very much used to take collective decisions on all important issues. But he added: 'You cannot in a modern government take every single decision in Cabinet. It's just not practically possible.'

Lord Butler said he felt the government had accumulated too much power, making it too easy to bring in bad legislation and to do whatever it wished, and that it focused far too much on the short-term calculations of political advantage rather than long-term strategy. The former cabinet secretary elaborated on his concerns in an interview with The Spectator magazine, stating: 'I would be profoundly critical of the present government in that there is far too much emphasis on presentation, there is far too much central control and there is far too little of what I would describe as proper collegiality, which brings in all the different views and opinions before decisions are made.'

Mr Howard described Lord Butler's remarks as extremely significant and very important. 'This is from someone who was an insider, who was at the very heart of the government and saw how it worked from the inside. It is the most damning indictment I can ever remember from someone in such a senior and privileged position,' Mr Howard added.

Lord Butler's independent report earlier this year into the quality of pre-war intelligence on Iraq said the government's September 2002 dossier did not make sufficiently clear the significant doubts that existed about the intelligence that Iraq possessed chemical and biological weapons, and that it was deliberately very vague. He explained that the reason for this lack of clarity was that it would have significantly weakened the public case for war against Iraq at the time.

Lord Butler said in his interview with The Spectator, which was written up by the Conservative MP Boris Johnson: 'When civil servants give advice to ministers, their duty is to say 'these are the facts as we believe them to be, but we've got to tell you that the evidence we've got is pretty flimsy'. If you are giving something to the United Nations Security Council and to the country as a whole, you should tell them the full, unvarnished truth about the intelligence.'

Asked why he thought those crucial warnings about the intelligence's weaknesses were not included in the public dossier, Lord Butler said: 'One has got to remember what the fundamental purpose of that dossier was. The primary purpose of the dossier was to convince the British public why the government thought Iraq was a very serious and imminent threat, justifying military action.'

When asked whether he thought the country was well governed on the whole, Lord Butler replied with a critical assessment: 'Well, I think we are a country where we have moved very, very far from the traditional checks and balances, from not having proper control over the executive, and that is a very dangerous and unhealthy path for a democracy.' He added: 'We should be moving away from the notion of party over principle and the excessive power of the executive. The executive is much too free to bring in a huge number of bad laws, to promote a huge amount of spin and to do whatever it wants, and whatever it thinks is what will get the best headlines tomorrow. All that is an integral part of what is fundamentally bad government in this country.' Lord Butler's analysis was strongly supported by his predecessor as Cabinet Secretary, Lord Armstrong.

Lord Armstrong told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he agreed with Lord Butler's sentiments: 'I believe there ought to be the proper exercise of informed political judgement brought to bear on decision making that those governed by, the citizens, are surely entitled to expect.' He further said he thought Lord Butler's criticisms were well founded and that Mr Blair's style of government was symptomatic of a wider problem within the whole system of government. Meanwhile, Conservative leader Michael Howard referred to his own analysis of the first eight months of the Labour government, which he conducted when he was shadow cabinet secretary. Mr Howard told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: 'Taken together, Lord Butler's findings are absolutely devastating and cannot be taken as anything other than a damning and comprehensive indictment against the government.'

The attack on Iraq has in many ways undermined this government, it has done away with established protocols and processes of decision-making. Also the way the intelligence was presented was deliberately misleading to the public, with important caveats and qualifications of the intelligence left out. Lord Butler said this was the "most difficult" period he could remember in government. But Sir Jeremy Greenstock said he himself would be judged by results, not his intentions. Lord Butler bypassed the conventional civil service and established channels, and instead relied on small, informal groups to help him make decisions. The 'official' advice of the Joint Intelligence Committee was sometimes used in parallel with or superseded by these small groups on important issues. He said: "You cannot, in a modern government, take intelligence in isolation. It's just too complex a business to be handled by a select few."

Lord Butler said the government had received much "bad" or incomplete intelligence and pursued a "do whatever it takes" attitude, and it relied heavily on the advice and opinions of political appointees rather than expert civil servants. The report noted in a damning section: "The way of government in that period was far too ad hoc and reactive, there is too much central control focused on the Prime Minister's office and there is a lack of what would normally be expected in terms of formal structure and collective decision-making, which all contributed to the serious problems identified." Mr Blair's role in the lead-up to war was described as "very important". "He is who was at the very heart of government during this crucial period." It is most important for us to hear from everyone involved in an inquiry of this magnitude.

Lord Butler's report, released this year into the intelligence surrounding the Iraq war, said the government's September 2002 dossier did not make it sufficiently clear about chemical and biological stockpiles and was "very misleading" in its overall impression. The reason for this particular presentation of the intelligence is that it would not have strengthened the public case for war, Lord Butler said. His report also suggested that the intelligence assessment was greatly undermined by the intelligence services' weaknesses and their lack of critical assessment. He said: "When you give advice to politicians, you have to be very clear. You can say these are the possibilities, but 'we've got to tell you the unvarnished evidence we've got, the raw intelligence.'", especially if you are giving something to the United Nations Security Council and the country you are about to confront militarily.

Asked what he thought the public's reaction and perception of the report was, Lord Butler noted: "It has to be seen in the context of what the public's perception of the situation was at the time. The whole point of this report was to provide a transparent account and to inform the British public why the government was acting as it did in the critical period before the war." When asked whether he thought the government was well-equipped on the whole to handle such crises, Lord Butler replied: "We are a country not over the brink, but there are serious issues to address. There should be a definite move away from the politicisation of intelligence, where it becomes an instrument of policy. It gives too much freedom to bring in a huge amount of bad intelligence, a huge capacity to do it – whatever happens, what will happen tomorrow without proper scrutiny. And that is precisely part of what is wrong with the current system."

Lord Butler's report outlined his critical findings and recommendations. Lord Butler told Newsnight in a subsequent interview: "I think there's got to be the strongest possible political judgement brought to bear on decision-making, particularly on those issues that are critical decisions of state and national security." He said the 'spin' surrounding the intelligence was "unprecedented" in its scale and reach, and "the responsibility of the whole of government" rather than just a few individuals. Tony Blair, the former prime minister, spent months under intense fire from the inquiry, particularly when he was being questioned by the committee. He said: "It was a serious strategic mistake, and cannot be regarded as anything other than a grave misjudgement."

A significant point of contention was how the public, with its important concerns and legitimate questions, was often deliberately kept out of the loop on key decisions, he said, describing it as the most egregious example he could remember in his long career of public service and observation. But Mr. Street said emphatically that the true measure of success should be solely by results, not by the public statements of the peer or the Prime Minister, nor by the carefully crafted narratives presented to the media. And instead, he lamented, crucial decisions were made by an insulated, tight-knit small group of advisers, concentrating all power to the Prime Minister to make the final, unchallenged calls on matters of national importance, leading to a profound lack of accountability. The official said the centralized decision-making structure that was used even for the most important issues. He cannot fathom how such an archaic system can persist in a modern democratic state and remain functional, let alone effective. He just said the government had much that was inherently bad about its internal workings and its approach to governance, and it appeared determined to do whatever it pleased, without genuine accountability or broader consultation. And it was all driven entirely on the altar of political expediency, often at the expense of sound policy and the public good.

There is too much central control and micromanagement emanating from Downing Street, stifling innovation and critical thinking. There is little of what would traditionally be considered proper ministerial responsibility or genuine delegated authority, which, in all, the peer, as someone intimately involved and very important, is particularly concerned about, as this critique comes directly from someone who was at the very heart of government and witnessed these practices first-hand, often with grave concerns.' It is the most searing and personally challenging criticism I can ever remember from someone in a high-ranking position within the governing establishment this year. In his extensive statement, he said the government's September fiscal announcement, or budget, did not make clear about the full economic implications of its proposals and indeed offered very little in the way of reassuring detail or transparent justification for its drastic measures, leaving many questions unanswered and anxieties unaddressed.

The reason for this significant lack of transparency, he suggested, is that it would have significantly complicated or even undermined the case for the peer's firmly held position on the matter. The peer said his own firm stance and subsequent decisions were entirely guided by the incontrovertible facts and figures of the situation, rather than political messaging. He then passionately added: 'When given the opportunity to say these things, and I feel compelled to do so now, but I've got to tell you, the evidence we've got is, if you're giving something significant to the United Kingdom and the country, you absolutely have a right to expect full accountability, honesty, and complete transparency in return from your leaders.' Asked, though, he thought then that the real issue was not simply about what the precise nature of the challenge or crisis facing the nation was, nor of what its immediate or long-term ramifications was to the British electorate, but more fundamentally, why the government was not taking it serious enough to implement effective, coherent policies and to truly grasp the gravity of the situation at hand.

When asked whether he thought the overall condition of the country was well, on the whole, he offered a stark assessment, responding grimly: 'I think our country, we are suffering immensely and tragically from not having consistently strong, clear, and decisive leadership at the very top over the strategic direction and core values of the nation, and I believe strongly that we should be moving decisively away from the pernicious belief that the executive branch of government is much too free to bring in a huge and damaging number of bad policies, to implement huge and disruptive structural changes, and to do it whatever they whimsically please, without any proper deliberation or genuine consideration for the potential consequences for what will unfold tomorrow. That is part of what is fundamentally and catastrophically wrong with our current approach to government, eroding trust and stability.'

Labour chooses Manchester. The Labour Party's leadership has chosen the city as the venue for its main gathering, marking a significant departure from its long-standing tradition of holding conferences in seaside towns. The Labour Party will hold its 2006 autumn conference in Manchester and not Blackpool, it has been confirmed. The much-trailed decision was ratified by Labour's ruling National Executive Committee, in a break with the traditional choice of a seaside venue. Sources close to the party suggested that the decision reflected a desire to project a more contemporary image and access to modern conference facilities. It will be the first time since 1917 that the party has chosen Manchester to host its annual event. Blackpool will get the much smaller February spring conference instead, in what will be seen as a placatory move.

For years, the main political parties have rotated between Blackpool, Bournemouth and Brighton. Blackpool, with its grand ballrooms and ample accommodation, has historically been a popular choice for all major parties, particularly Labour. And the news that the much larger annual conference is not to gather in Blackpool will be seen as a significant blow for the coastal resort. Local businesses are expected to lose millions of pounds in revenue during the week-long event. In 1998, the party said it would not return to Blackpool but did so in 2002, following a strong campaign by local hoteliers. The following year, Bournemouth hosted the event before the party signed a two-year deal for Brighton to host the autumn conference.

Colin Asplin, of the Blackpool Hotel Association, said: "We have tried very hard to make sure they come back to Blackpool. Obviously, we have failed in that. I just hope Manchester can handle the crowds. It amazes me that the Labour Party, which is a working-class party, doesn't want to come to the main working-class resort in the country."

The exact cost to Blackpool in terms of lost revenue for hotel accommodation is not yet known, but it is thought that block bookings will be taken at the major Manchester hotels after the official announcement.

original: Goldsmith denies war advice claim..The attorney general has denied his statement to Parliament about the legality of the Iraq war was drafted by Downing Street officials...Lord Goldsmith said Lord Falconer and Baroness Morgan played no part in drafting the answer. He added the answer represented his view that the war was legal, but was not a summary of his advice to the PM. The government has resisted calls to publish the full advice, saying such papers are always kept confidential...In a statement, Lord Goldsmith said: "I was fully involved throughout the drafting process and personally finalised, and of course approved, the answer." He said the answer had been prepared in his office with the involvement of Solicitor General Harriet Harman, two of his own officials, three Foreign Office officials, a QC, Christopher Greenwood and the then Lord Chancellor, Lord Irvine of Lairg..."No other minister or official was involved in any way." He suggested the claim that Lord Falconer and Lady Morgan had drafted the answer were the result of a mis-transcription of his evidence to the Butler Inquiry into pre-war intelligence. "As I have always made clear, I set out in the answer my own genuinely held, independent view that military action was lawful under the existing (UN) Security Council resolutions," he said. "The answer did not purport to be a summary of my confidential legal advice to government." Former foreign secretary Robin Cook said Lord Goldsmith's admission that his parliamentary answer was not a summary of his legal opinion suggested Parliament may have been misled. "The attorney general may never have presented his answer as a summary, but others certainly did," he said. "What is clear from his statement today is that he does not believe that it was a full, accurate summary of his formal opinion."..Earlier, Tony Blair dismissed questions about the attorney general's advice, and said his Parliamentary statement had been a "fair summary" of his opinion. "That's what he (Lord Goldsmith) said and that's what I say. He has dealt with this time and time and time again," Mr Blair told his monthly news conference in Downing Street. He refused to answer further questions on the issue...On the question of whether such papers have always been kept confidential, Tory MP Michael Mates, who is a member of the Commons intelligence and security committee and was part of the Butler inquiry, told the BBC: "That, as a general rule, is right, but it's not an absolute rule." He said there had been other occasions when advice had been published, most recently regarding Prince Charles's marriage plans. The government could not pick and choose when to use the convention, he said. Mr Mates added: "This may be one of those special occasions... when it would be in the public interest to see the advice which the attorney general gave to the prime minister."..The claims about Lord Falconer and Baroness Morgan's involvement were made in a book published this week by Philippe Sands QC, a member of Cherie Blair's Matrix Chambers. He also says Lord Goldsmith warned Tony Blair on 7 March 2003 that the Iraq war could be illegal without a second UN resolution sanctioning military action...A short statement about Lord Goldsmith's position presented in a written parliamentary answer on 17 March 2003 - just before a crucial Commons vote on the military action - did not suggest this. Former minister Clare Short, who resigned from the government over the Iraq war, said the ministerial answer was the same statement that was earlier shown to the cabinet as it discussed military action. She said the full advice should have been attached, according to the ministerial code, and demanded a Lords inquiry into the matter. The Conservatives and Liberal Democrats say they still want the publication of the full legal advice given by the Attorney General. Lib Dem foreign affairs spokesman Sir Menzies Campbell said Lord Goldsmith's statement still did not clear up the outstanding issues. "If his original advice of 7 March accepted that military action might be illegal, how was it that he resolved any such doubts by the time the Parliamentary answer was published on 17 March?" he said. "Only the fullest disclosure will now do."

Goldsmith denies war advice claim. The attorney general has denied his statement to Parliament about the legality of the Iraq war was drafted by Downing Street officials. Lord Goldsmith said Lord Falconer and Baroness Morgan played no part in drafting the answer. He added the answer represented his view that the war was legal, but was not a summary of his advice to the PM. The government has resisted calls to publish the full advice, saying such papers are always kept confidential.

In a statement, Lord Goldsmith said: "I was fully involved throughout the drafting process and personally finalised, and of course approved, the answer." He said the answer had been prepared in his office with the involvement of Solicitor General Harriet Harman, two of his own officials, three Foreign Office officials, a QC, Christopher Greenwood and the then Lord Chancellor, Lord Irvine of Lairg. "No other minister or official was involved in any way." He suggested the claim that Lord Falconer and Lady Morgan had drafted the answer were the result of a mis-transcription of his evidence to the Butler Inquiry into pre-war intelligence. "As I have always made clear, I set out in the answer my own genuinely held, independent view that military action was lawful under the existing (UN) Security Council resolutions," he said. "The answer did not purport to be a summary of my confidential legal advice to government."

Former foreign secretary Robin Cook said Lord Goldsmith's admission that his parliamentary answer was not a summary of his legal opinion suggested Parliament may have been misled. "The attorney general may never have presented his answer as a summary, but others certainly did," he said. "What is clear from his statement today is that he does not believe that it was a full, accurate summary of his formal opinion."

Earlier, Tony Blair dismissed questions about the attorney general's advice, and said his Parliamentary statement had been a "fair summary" of his opinion. "That's what he (Lord Goldsmith) said and that's what I say. He has dealt with this time and time and time again," Mr Blair told his monthly news conference in Downing Street. He refused to answer further questions on the issue.

On the question of whether such papers have always been kept confidential, Tory MP Michael Mates, who is a member of the Commons intelligence and security committee and was part of the Butler inquiry, told the BBC: "That, as a general rule, is right, but it's not an absolute rule." He said there had been other occasions when advice had been published, most recently regarding Prince Charles's marriage plans. The government could not pick and choose when to use the convention, he said. Mr Mates added: "This may be one of those special occasions... when it would be in the public interest to see the advice which the attorney general gave to the prime minister."

The claims about Lord Falconer and Baroness Morgan's involvement were made in a book published this week by Philippe Sands QC, a member of Cherie Blair's Matrix Chambers. He also says Lord Goldsmith warned Tony Blair on 7 March 2003 that the Iraq war could be illegal without a second UN resolution sanctioning military action.

A short statement about Lord Goldsmith's position presented in a written parliamentary answer on 17 March 2003 - just before a crucial Commons vote on the military action - did not suggest this. Former minister Clare Short, who resigned from the government over the Iraq war, said the ministerial answer was the same statement that was earlier shown to the cabinet as it discussed military action. She said the full advice should have been attached, according to the ministerial code, and demanded a Lords inquiry into the matter.

The Conservatives and Liberal Democrats say they still want the publication of the full legal advice given by the Attorney General. Lib Dem foreign affairs spokesman Sir Menzies Campbell said Lord Goldsmith's statement still did not clear up the outstanding issues. "If his original advice of 7 March accepted that military action might be illegal, how was it that he resolved any such doubts by the time the Parliamentary answer was published on 17 March?" he said. "Only the fullest disclosure will now do."

This appointment, to be formally announced later today, sees Mr. Campbell move into a significant international sporting role. He also expressed personal anticipation, adding, "I am also very much looking forward to going back to New Zealand for the later stages of the tournament, particularly as the crucial knockout rounds approach, should the formidable All Blacks progress as is widely expected by fans and commentators alike."

His appointment evokes vivid memories of the contentious media environment that has historically surrounded major sporting events, particularly recalling the heated atmosphere during the British & Irish Lions tour of Australia in 2001. During that memorable series, a prominent New Zealander, Graham Henry, was then coach of Wales, a key component of the Lions management, adding an interesting dynamic to the tour's overarching narrative. We must have robust processes, clear structures, and meticulous plans in place to effectively manage that considerable attention and all the attendant challenges that will inevitably come with such a high-stakes global spectacle and national celebration."

He then drew a direct parallel to his previous illustrious career in UK politics, reflecting: "My primary focus and responsibility was to the government in the crucial year leading up to the pivotal 2005 general election, a period of extraordinarily intense media management and political campaigning, culminating successfully in the May general election itself." The intricate tapestry of Britain's political history from 2003 faced renewed scrutiny today as fresh revelations emerged from a high-profile memoir, triggering a series of intense exchanges within the Houses of Parliament. Lord Falconer, a key figure in the Labour government of the era and former Lord Chancellor, found his actions and recollections placed squarely under the spotlight, particularly regarding decisions surrounding significant national and international policy. His recently published book has become a lightning rod for critics, prompting a vigorous defence from the peer himself against accusations of historical inaccuracy or political expediency.

During a particularly animated session, Lord Falconer added that the specific arrangements surrounding a critical policy implementation had not yet been "finalised," contrary to some media speculation and opposition claims. He elaborated that while plans were advanced, the ultimate sign-off required further procedural steps. Furthermore, Lord Falconer confirmed that an individual identified as Mr Lairg had been "involved" in preliminary consultations and background work related to the policy. However, he carefully avoided providing extensive details on Mr Lairg's specific remit or the precise stage at which his involvement concluded, leading to further questions from the benches about transparency and the full list of contributors to such consequential decisions. The implication was that while Mr Lairg played a part, his precise influence or the nature of his contribution remained, for now, a matter for internal governmental record.

Defending his professional integrity and the principles that guided his tenure, Lord Falconer delivered a strong rebuttal to his detractors. "Always, I take the action that I purport is my duty, and I do so transparently and in the best interests of the nation," he stated with conviction. This declaration was an attempt to assert control over the narrative, implying that his decisions were always driven by genuine commitment to public service and established protocols, rather than partisan motives. He further asserted that "my actions" were always in line with the responsibilities entrusted to him, rejecting any insinuation of hidden agendas or personal gain. The former Lord Chancellor emphasised that accountability was paramount to him, and he stood by every decision made during his time in office, despite the retrospective criticism. He said "it's not" for others to second-guess these decisions without full context.

The parliamentary debate took a pointed turn when Lord Falconer engaged directly with one of his most persistent questioners. He interjected with a challenging query: "Is he not a member of the public? What time is it, Mr Speaker? Has he been, when had he been, most recently, the leader of the opposition?" This highly personal and rhetorical line of questioning, delivered with visible frustration, was widely interpreted as an attempt to highlight the perceived hypocrisy of an opposition leader now scrutinising decisions made when they were in a position of power or influence, or perhaps drawing a distinction between public servants and those operating from outside the government's direct chain of command. The Speaker was compelled to intervene, reminding members to address their remarks through the chair and to maintain decorum amidst the charged atmosphere. This exchange underscored the deeply partisan nature of the debate, moving beyond policy specifics to the credibility and past roles of the individuals involved.

The wider implications of the discussions revolved around the need for governmental transparency and the right of the public generally to understand the processes behind critical national decisions. Advocates for greater openness argued that the passage of time only amplified the need for full disclosure, especially concerning events that had long-term ramifications for the country's standing and its citizens. The concept of "public general" knowledge and access to information was a recurring theme among those pressing for more comprehensive answers.

Further fuelling the ongoing political firestorm is Lord Falconer's book, which notably includes references to Cherie Blair, the barrister and wife of then-Prime Minister Tony Blair. The specific nature of these mentions has become a significant talking point among political analysts and the media, with speculation rife about what insights they might offer into the inner workings of the Blair administration. While the text has yet to reveal any entirely new, explosive facts, the very inclusion of Mrs Blair, described as a "member Cherie" within the wider political and social circles of the time, and the context in which she appears, has prompted renewed interest in the personal and professional dynamics at the top of government during that pivotal period. Critics are keen to establish whether her role extended beyond that of a private citizen, particularly concerning the issues discussed in the memoir.

Central to the book's controversial narrative is its account of the sanctioning of a highly significant action on 1 July 2003. This particular date has swiftly emerged as a critical reference point in the ongoing historical re-evaluation, as it marks a key moment in a series of decisions widely understood to pertain to the United Kingdom's involvement in military operations in the Middle East. The controversy stems from conflicting accounts and interpretations of the precise timeline and the individuals responsible for giving the ultimate go-ahead for this action. Lord Falconer's book, written about this critical sanctioning, explicitly details the events leading up to this point. Manchester United avoided an FA Cup upset by edging past Exeter City in their third round replay. Cristiano Ronaldo scored the opener, slipping the ball between Paul Jones' legs after just nine minutes. United wasted a host of chances to make it safe as Jones made some great saves, but Wayne Rooney put the tie beyond doubt late on with a cool finish. Exeter had chances of their own, Sean Devine twice volleying wide and Andrew Taylor forcing Tim Howard to save. United boss Sir Alex Ferguson was taking few chances after their goalless draw in the first game and he handed starts to Paul Scholes and Ryan Giggs as well as Ronaldo and Rooney.

Exeter began brightly with Devine and Steve Flack seeing plenty of the ball, but it did not take United long to assert their authority and the hosts soon found themselves a goal down. Scholes played a lovely pass into Ronaldo on the left-hand side of the six-yard box and the Portuguese winger slid the ball between the legs of Jones to open the scoring. United sensed a chance to finish the tie as a contest early on and Ronaldo blazed over before Jones saved well from Scholes and then Rooney. The visitors' pressure by now was incessant and Rooney had another shot blocked while Ronaldo slammed well over the bar again from a good position. Just before the break Giggs had a golden chance to double the advantage, but the Welshman dragged a left-foot effort badly wide from just a few yards. In stoppage time Exeter created their best chance as Alex Jeannin swung in a cross from the left that Devine managed to flick goalwards, but the ball flew wide of Howard's goal.

The Grecians came out after the break in determined fashion and Howard had to show safe hands to collect two searching crosses into the United box. Rooney looked like he might have sealed the result with a turn and shot but the ball stuck in the St James Park mud and Jones raced back to gather on the goalline. Moments later Devine had the chance to make himself a hero, but he could only volley Jeannin's brilliant cross wide of Howard's goal after being left unmarked six yards out. After Rooney had completely messed up a free-kick from a promising position, Taylor showed him how it should be done, his stunning drive from distance forcing a flying stop from Howard. The home crowd were baying for a goal and they did get the ball into the net only for Devine's low effort to be ruled out for an obvious offside. The persistent Rooney eventually rounded Jones with three minutes to go and slotted into an empty net to book a home tie with Middlesbrough in the fourth round.

original: Goldsmith denies war advice claim..The attorney general has denied his statement to Parliament about the legality of the Iraq war was drafted by Downing Street officials...Lord Goldsmith said Lord Falconer and Baroness Morgan played no part in drafting the answer. He added the answer represented his view that the war was legal, but was not a summary of his advice to the PM. The government has resisted calls to publish the full advice, saying such papers are always kept confidential...In a statement, Lord Goldsmith said: "I was fully involved throughout the drafting process and personally finalised, and of course approved, the answer." He said the answer had been prepared in his office with the involvement of Solicitor General Harriet Harman, two of his own officials, three Foreign Office officials, a QC, Christopher Greenwood and the then Lord Chancellor, Lord Irvine of Lairg..."No other minister or official was involved in any way." He suggested the claim that Lord Falconer and Lady Morgan had drafted the answer were the result of a mis-transcription of his evidence to the Butler Inquiry into pre-war intelligence. "As I have always made clear, I set out in the answer my own genuinely held, independent view that military action was lawful under the existing (UN) Security Council resolutions," he said. "The answer did not purport to be a summary of my confidential legal advice to government." Former foreign secretary Robin Cook said Lord Goldsmith's admission that his parliamentary answer was not a summary of his legal opinion suggested Parliament may have been misled. "The attorney general may never have presented his answer as a summary, but others certainly did," he said. "What is clear from his statement today is that he does not believe that it was a full, accurate summary of his formal opinion."..Earlier, Tony Blair dismissed questions about the attorney general's advice, and said his Parliamentary statement had been a "fair summary" of his opinion. "That's what he (Lord Goldsmith) said and that's what I say. He has dealt with this time and time and time again," Mr Blair told his monthly news conference in Downing Street. He refused to answer further questions on the issue...On the question of whether such papers have always been kept confidential, Tory MP Michael Mates, who is a member of the Commons intelligence and security committee and was part of the Butler inquiry, told the BBC: "That, as a general rule, is right, but it's not an absolute rule." He said there had been other occasions when advice had been published, most recently regarding Prince Charles's marriage plans. The government could not pick and choose when to use the convention, he said. Mr Mates added: "This may be one of those special occasions... when it would be in the public interest to see the advice which the attorney general gave to the prime minister."..The claims about Lord Falconer and Baroness Morgan's involvement were made in a book published this week by Philippe Sands QC, a member of Cherie Blair's Matrix Chambers. He also says Lord Goldsmith warned Tony Blair on 7 March 2003 that the Iraq war could be illegal without a second UN resolution sanctioning military action...A short statement about Lord Goldsmith's position presented in a written parliamentary answer on 17 March 2003 - just before a crucial Commons vote on the military action - did not suggest this. This fueled accusations of selective disclosure. This distinction remained a central point of controversy.
