Manchester United through after tough Exeter City test. The Premier League giants Manchester United avoided an FA Cup upset on a chilly Wednesday evening by eventually edging past resilient League Two side Exeter City in their third round replay at a packed Old Trafford. The Red Devils secured a 2-0 victory, but it was far from a straightforward evening against their spirited lower-league opposition, who provided a genuine scare for Sir Alex Ferguson's side.

Portuguese superstar Cristiano Ronaldo opened the scoring for United, demonstrating his burgeoning talent and composure by slipping the ball with clinical precision between the legs of Exeter goalkeeper Paul Jones after just nine minutes of play, sending the home faithful into raptures. Despite their early advantage, United wasted a host of glorious chances to decisively make the game safe, largely due to a superb and inspired performance from Exeter's shot-stopper Jones, who made some truly great saves throughout the engrossing ninety minutes. However, the prolific young striker Wayne Rooney eventually put the tie beyond any reasonable doubt late in the second half with a characteristically cool and composed finish. Exeter, to their immense credit, were not without their own opportunities to potentially level the score and create history. Experienced striker Sean Devine twice volleyed wide from promising positions inside the penalty area, and industrious midfielder Andrew Taylor forced United's American goalkeeper Tim Howard to make a smart save with a speculative long-range effort. United boss Sir Alex Ferguson was clearly taking few chances after his side's frustrating goalless draw in the first encounter at Exeter's atmospheric St James Park. He notably handed starts to midfield stalwarts Paul Scholes and Ryan Giggs, both legends of the club, as well as unleashing his star attacking duo of Ronaldo and Rooney, indicating his strong desire to avoid any further embarrassment in this venerable competition. Exeter began the match brightly and with admirable intent, with Devine and Steve Flack seeing plenty of the ball in advanced areas, but it did not take United long to assert their superior authority and quality, and the plucky hosts soon found themselves a goal down. The opening goal came after Scholes played a lovely, incisive pass into Ronaldo who had drifted onto the left-hand side of the six-yard box, and the dazzling Portuguese winger expertly slid the ball between the legs of Jones to open the scoring, much to the delight of the Old Trafford faithful who craved an early breakthrough.

Having established an early lead, United sensed a prime chance to finish the tie as a contest and truly stamp their authority early on, pushing relentlessly for more goals. Ronaldo blazed a shot high over the bar from just outside the area, illustrating United's dominance but also a slight profligacy. Exeter's valiant Paul Jones then saved well from powerful, goal-bound efforts by both Paul Scholes and Wayne Rooney as United poured forward in waves of attack. The visitors' pressure by this point was incessant and relentless, with continuous waves of attacks crashing against the stoic Exeter defence. Rooney had another powerful shot blocked by a brave and committed defender, while Ronaldo slammed yet another effort well over the bar again from a good position inside the box, much to his own visible frustration. Just before the half-time break, veteran winger Ryan Giggs had a golden chance to double United's advantage, receiving the ball with ample space inside the penalty area, but the Welshman inexplicably dragged a left-foot effort badly wide from only 10 yards out, a rare and surprising misjudgment for a player of his supreme calibre. In stoppage time at the very end of the first half, Exeter created their best chance of the game so far, demonstrating their continued belief. Alex Jeannin swung in a dangerous and inviting cross from the left flank that Sean Devine managed to flick goalwards with an intelligent touch, but the ball flew just wide of Tim Howard's left-hand post, much to the relief of the United defence and coaching staff.

The Grecians, spurred on by their manager and their loyal travelling support who roared them on from the stands, came out after the interval in determined and spirited fashion, clearly not willing to roll over and concede defeat meekly. Tim Howard in the United goal had to show safe hands to confidently collect two searching crosses fizzed into the crowded United box, demonstrating Exeter's renewed attacking intent and belief. Wayne Rooney looked like he might have finally sealed the result with a sharp turn and shot from inside the area, but the ball frustratingly got stuck in the boggy St James Park mud, allowing Paul Jones to race back swiftly and gather it on the goal line before Rooney could follow up. Moments later, the ever-lively Sean Devine had a truly golden chance to make himself a hero for the League Two side, but he could only volley Alex Jeannin's brilliant cross wide of Howard's goal after being left completely unmarked just six yards out, a truly agonising miss for the striker and a huge let-off for United. Shortly after Rooney had completely messed up a free-kick 20 yards out with a wayward effort that sailed harmlessly over the bar, Andrew Taylor showed him how it should be done, unleashing a stunning long-range drive from distance that forced a flying, acrobatic stop from Tim Howard, who pushed the ball wide for a corner with a fingertip save. The home crowd were baying for a goal from their team, sensing an equaliser was within reach, and they did manage to get the ball into the net through Devine's low effort, only for it to be instantly ruled out for what was deemed an obvious offside by the linesman, much to their collective disappointment and frustration. The persistent and tireless Wayne Rooney, whose energy levels never waned, eventually got his deserved reward and calmed any lingering nerves for the Premier League giants. With just three minutes of normal time remaining on the clock, he expertly rounded goalkeeper Paul Jones with a clever piece of skill and slotted the ball coolly into an empty net to finally secure United's passage into the next round. This decisive second goal booked them a potentially thrilling home tie with fellow Premier League side Middlesbrough in the fourth round of the competition, ensuring their FA Cup journey would continue, albeit after a more challenging test than many had anticipated.

Man Utd through after Exeter test. Manchester United avoided an FA Cup scare by beating Exeter City in their third-round replay.

Cristiano Ronaldo scored the opener, slipping the ball between Paul Jones' legs after just nine minutes. United wasted a host of chances to make it safe as Jones made some great saves, but Rooney put the tie beyond doubt late on with a cool finish. Exeter had chances of their own, Devine twice volleying wide and Andrew Taylor forcing Tim Howard to save.

United boss Sir Alex Ferguson was taking few chances after their 0-0 draw in the first game and he handed starts to Paul Scholes and Ryan Giggs as well as Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney. Exeter began brightly with Devine and Steve Flack seeing plenty of the ball, but it didn't take United long to assert their dominance and the hosts soon found themselves a goal down.

Scholes played a lovely pass into Ronaldo on the left-hand side of the six-yard box and the winger slid the ball between the legs of Jones to open the scoring. United had a chance to finish the tie as a contest early on and Ronaldo blazed over before good efforts from Scholes and then Rooney. The visitors' pressure by now was relentless and Rooney had another shot blocked while Giggs slammed well over the bar again from a good position.

Just before the break Giggs had a chance to double the lead, but the Welshman dragged a left-footed effort badly wide from 10 yards. In first-half injury time Exeter created their best chance as Alex Jeannin swung in a cross from the left that Devine headed goalwards, but the ball flew wide of Howard's goal.

The Grecians came out after the break in determined fashion and Tim Howard had to show safe hands to collect two searching crosses into the United box. Rooney looked like he might have sealed the result with a turn and shot but the ball stuck in the St James Park mud and Paul Jones raced back to clear on the goalline. Moments later Devine had the chance to make himself a hero, but he could only steer Jeannin's cross wide of Howard's goal after being left unmarked six yards out.

After Rooney had completely messed up a free-kick 20 yards out Taylor showed him how it should be done, his stunning drive from distance forcing a flying stop from Howard. The home crowd were baying for a goal and they did get the ball into the net only for Devine's low effort to be ruled out for an offside.

The excellent Rooney eventually rounded Jones with three minutes to go and slotted into an empty net to book a home tie with Middlesbrough in the fourth round.

Referee: P Dowd (Cheshire).

Manchester United Secure FA Cup Progression After Stern Exeter Test.
Manchester United successfully navigated a tricky FA Cup third round replay against League Two side Exeter City, ultimately avoiding a potential upset with a hard-fought victory at St James Park.

The deadlock was broken early in the game when Portuguese superstar Cristiano Ronaldo netted the opener, skilfully slipping the ball between the legs of Exeter goalkeeper Paul Jones after just nine minutes of play. Despite taking an early lead, United wasted a plethora of clear-cut opportunities to further extend their advantage and make the result safe, with Jones making a series of great saves to keep his side in the contest. However, Wayne Rooney eventually put the tie beyond any doubt late in the second half with a characteristically cool and composed finish. Exeter, to their credit, were not without their own promising attacking moments. Midfielder Sean Devine notably volleyed wide from a decent position, and Andrew Taylor forced United's American goalkeeper Tim Howard to make a smart save. United manager Sir Alex Ferguson clearly appreciated the potential for an upset, taking few chances after their goalless 0-0 draw in the first game at Old Trafford. He consequently fielded a notably strong lineup for the replay, reinstating experienced campaigners Paul Scholes and Ryan Giggs, alongside star forwards Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney.

Exeter began brightly with striker Sean Devine and winger Steve Flack seeing plenty of the ball in the opening exchanges, but it did not take United long to assert their authority and dominance, and the hosts soon found themselves a goal down. Scholes played an incisive pass into Ronaldo's feet on the left-hand side of the six-yard box and the Portuguese forward then expertly slipped the ball between the legs of Jones to open the scoring.

United then had a chance to finish the match as a contest early on and Ronaldo blazed a shot high over the bar before Exeter goalkeeper Paul Jones saved well from Scholes and then denied Wayne Rooney from close range. The visitors' pressure by now was incessant and Rooney had another shot blocked bravely by an Exeter defender, while Ronaldo blasted well over the bar again from a good position. Just before the break, veteran winger Ryan Giggs had a golden opportunity to double United's advantage, but the Welshman dragged a left-foot effort wide from 10 yards out. In stoppage time at the end of the first half, Exeter created their best chance as Alex Jeannin swung in a dangerous cross from the left that Devine attempted to flick goalwards, but the ball flew tantalisingly wide of Howard's goal.

The Grecians came out after the break in determined fashion and Howard had to show safe hands to collect two searching high balls and corners into the United box, as Exeter pressed for an equaliser. Rooney looked like he might have sealed the result with a sharp turn and shot but the ball got snagged in the St James Park pitch and Jones raced back to hook it clear on the goalline, to the relief of the home support. Moments later, Devine had another glorious chance to make himself a local hero, but he could only divert Jeannin's brilliant delivery wide of Tim Howard's goal after being left unmarked just six yards out. After United's Phil Neville had completely messed up a free-kick 20 yards out with a wayward effort, Taylor showed him how it should be done, his powerful drive from distance forcing a flying stop from Howard.

The home supporters were baying for a goal and they did get the ball into the net only for Devine's low effort to be correctly ruled out for an offside decision, much to their frustration. The final whistle approached and the ever-present Rooney rounded Jones with just three minutes to go and slotted into an empty net to finally secure the victory and book a home tie with Middlesbrough in the fourth round.

The Premier League giants, having been held to a goalless draw at Old Trafford in the first tie, found the net early through veteran winger Ryan Giggs, who slotted the ball neatly between the legs of Exeter goalkeeper Paul Jones after just nine minutes. Despite taking an early lead, United were unable to put the tie beyond doubt for large periods, as Jones made several great saves to deny them. It took until the dying minutes for Louis Saha to finally secure the win with a cool, late finish. Exeter, for their part, refused to be overawed and created significant chances of their own, with Andy Taylor volleying an effort just wide and Ryan Harley forcing a smart save from United keeper Tim Howard.

Given the embarrassment of the previous 0-0 draw at Old Trafford, Manchester United manager Sir Alex Ferguson was taking absolutely no chances with his team selection for the replay. He fielded a formidable side, including midfield generals Paul Scholes and Roy Keane, alongside attacking threats Ryan Giggs and Louis Saha, while Wayne Rooney also started. Exeter, buoyed by the passionate home support, began the match with remarkable confidence and midfielder Steve Flack was particularly influential in seeing a lot of the ball in the opening exchanges. However, despite their spirited start, it did not take the Premier League visitors long to find their formidable rhythm, and the Grecians soon found themselves a goal down against the European champions.

The opening goal arrived in the ninth minute, demonstrating United's class. A trademark precise pass from Paul Scholes sliced through the Exeter defence, finding Ryan Giggs in space on the left-hand side of the six-yard box. The veteran Welsh winger showed his customary composure, coolly slotting the ball with his left foot between the outstretched legs of the onrushing Paul Jones to open the scoring, much to the relief of the travelling support.

United pressed for a second goal, eager to put the tie to bed. A golden opportunity to double their lead presented itself moments later when Wayne Rooney found himself in a promising position, but his powerful shot from just outside the area blazed high and wide over the bar. Paul Scholes then unleashed a powerful drive from distance that forced a good save from Jones, before Louis Saha was denied by a strong block from an Exeter defender. The Reds' pressure by now was becoming relentless, pinning Exeter back in their own half. Rooney had another shot well blocked by the massed defence, while Saha, frustrated by his earlier misses, again shot disappointingly high over the bar from another good attacking position inside the box.

As half-time approached, Ryan Giggs had another clear chance to extend United's advantage. After a neat build-up, the ball fell to him inside the penalty area, but the Welshman's left-foot shot from approximately 10 yards out failed to hit the target, veering just wide of the post, leaving the score at 1-0 heading into the interval. In first-half stoppage time, Exeter, showing their tenacity, carved out arguably their best chance of the half. A determined run down the left flank by Gareth Sheldon resulted in a dangerous cross into the United penalty area. Andy Taylor met the ball with a powerful header, directing it goalwards, but to the collective groan of the home crowd, the effort flew agonisingly just wide of Tim Howard's left-hand post, denying the Grecians a shock equaliser.

The Grecians emerged for the second half with renewed vigour and determination, clearly instructed to press United higher up the pitch. This period saw a flurry of activity in and around the United penalty area, and goalkeeper Tim Howard was forced to demonstrate his safe hands, confidently claiming two dangerous crosses swung into the United box by Exeter's wide players, easing the pressure on his defence. Midway through the second half, Louis Saha again looked poised to finally seal the result for United. After a clever turn inside the box, his powerful shot seemed destined for the net, but the ball took a crucial deflection off an Exeter defender in the crowded St James Park penalty area. Goalkeeper Jones, already beaten, reacted brilliantly to claw the ball back to safety on the goalline, maintaining Exeter's slender hopes. Moments later, the home crowd erupted as Andy Taylor found himself with a glorious chance to make himself a hero, but he could only steer Jean-Luc Jeannin's accurate cross wide of Tim Howard's goal after being left six yards out.

After Exeter had messed up a free-kick 20 yards out, Paul Scholes showed them how it should be done with a moment of individual brilliance. His powerful, swerving drive from distance was heading for the top corner, only to be met with a superb, diving stop from Exeter's Paul Jones, denying the midfielder a spectacular goal. The home crowd continued to roar their team on, desperately baying for an equaliser, and for a fleeting moment, they thought they had it. The ball was indeed bundled into the net by Andy Taylor, but their celebrations were cut short as the assistant referee's flag went up, ruling the low shot out for an offside infringement. With only three minutes of normal time remaining, Manchester United finally sealed their passage to the next stage. A swift counter-attack saw Louis Saha slot the ball confidently into an empty net, securing a 2-0 victory and booking a home tie for United in the fourth round.

However, GM stressed that it did not know of any injuries related to the problems. News of the recall follows an announcement last month that GM expects earnings this year be lower than in 2004. In its latest economic forecast, the BCC revised down its projections for the UK economy. It predicts that annual growth, which stood at approximately 3% in 2004, will moderate significantly. The forecast indicates that growth is expected to slow to around 2.5% in 2005 and remain at a similar level in 2006. This deceleration follows a period where the economy showed strong signs of recovery and expansion in previous years.

Businesses have been grappling with rising costs, skills shortages, and uncertainty in global markets, all contributing to a more subdued outlook.

This forecast suggests a prolonged period of slower growth, rather than a sharp downturn, giving businesses and policymakers some time to adapt. The organisation urged the government to implement measures that would support business investment and address the structural issues hindering long-term growth.

The report also touched upon consumer spending, noting that while it had provided a significant boost to the economy in previous years, its future trajectory remains uncertain. The BCC's analysis underscores the need for a balanced approach to economic management, focusing on both short-term stability and long-term competitiveness.

original: Prime minister's questions..So who, if anyone, is playing politics with the security of the nation?..Michael Howard has no doubt it is the prime minister who, he claims, is "ramming" through Parliament the controversial new anti-terror measures without proper debate. He didn't say so, but the Tories believe the prime minister is playing the fear card on this one so he can look tough in the run up to the general election And they believe Tony Blair is using the issue to suggest the Tories are soft on terrorism. Why on earth will the prime minister not simply take up the Tories' offer to extend the existing powers temporarily to allow proper parliamentary debate of the laws, he demanded. The prime minister claims this is the clearest indication that it is the Tories who are playing politics with the issue by attempting to score cheap political points in parliament. Is not the opposition against to the proposed laws "in principle", in which case delaying a decision for further debate would be pointless?..What this is really about, believes Mr Blair, is the Tories spotting an opportunity to embarrass, maybe even defeat the government. And that is more important to them than national security. Liberal Democrat leader Charles Kennedy avoided suggesting anyone was playing politics with the issue. He preferred to state that, as with other issues like ID cards, the government's immediate instinct was authoritarian...As is his habit nowadays, the prime minister was less rough with Mr Kennedy than he had been with Mr Howard - he prefers a more exasperated tone suggesting he believes the Lib Dems have, once again, just missed the point. Apart from all that, it was electioneering as usual. The very first question to the prime minister from Derby North's Bob Laxton asked him, in effect, if he would carry on the excellent policy of pouring more resources into schools. Later Birmingham's Sion Simon even went so far as to suggest the Tories were such a shower that we should have the general election now. The prime minister almost blushed. This was not the appropriate place to announce election day, he stammered. It was Prime Minister's Questions. So, who, if anyone, is playing politics with the security of the nation?

For the Conservatives, Michael Howard has no doubt that it is the Prime Minister who, he claims, is "ramming" through Parliament the controversial new anti-terror measures without proper debate. He didn't say so in as many words, but the Tories believe the Prime Minister is playing the fear card on this one so he can look tough in the run up to the general election. And they believe that Tony Blair is using the issue to suggest that the Tories are soft on terrorism. During the session, he demanded, "Why on earth will the Prime Minister not simply take up the Tories' offer to extend the existing powers temporarily to allow proper parliamentary debate of the laws?"

In response, the Prime Minister claims that this is the clearest indication that it is the Tories who are playing politics with the issue by attempting to score cheap political points in Parliament. He asked, "Is not the opposition opposed to the proposed laws 'in principle', in which case delaying a decision for further debate would be pointless?" What this is really about, believes Mr Blair, is the Tories spotting an opportunity to embarrass, maybe even defeat the government on a key piece of legislation. And that, in his view, is more important to them than national security.

For his part, Liberal Democrat leader Charles Kennedy avoided suggesting anyone was playing politics with the issue. Instead, he preferred to state, as he often does, that, as with other issues like ID cards, the government's immediate instinct was authoritarian. As is his habit nowadays, Mr Blair was less rough with Mr Kennedy than he had been with Mr Howard - instead, he prefers a more exasperated tone, suggesting he believes the Lib Dems have, once again, just missed the point.

Apart from all that, the session was characterized by electioneering as usual. The very first question to the Prime Minister, which came from Derby North's Bob Laxton, asked him, in effect, if he would carry on the excellent policy of pouring more resources into schools. Later in the proceedings, Birmingham's Sion Simon even went so far as to suggest that the Tories were such a shower that we should have the general election now. The Prime Minister almost blushed. He responded that this was not the appropriate place to announce election day, he stammered.

Indeed, can anyone be in any doubt that that announcement is just days away - an announcement coming in the week beginning 4 April for an election on 5 May is where the big money is in the Commons. In this highly charged atmosphere, perhaps that simple fact alone means everyone is seen to be playing politics with just about everything at the moment.

Michael Gove, the Home Secretary, is widely accused of 'ramming' through new, controversial security legislation without what critics deem sufficient parliamentary scrutiny or public consultation. He vehemently argues that these robust measures are absolutely vital for national safety in an increasingly dangerous and unpredictable world. However, his political opponents and numerous civil liberties groups firmly believe the minister is pursuing this contentious policy with an aggressively expedited timetable, primarily to bolster his image and that of the government leading up to the next general election.

Consequently, they are using this high-stakes issue to launch a concerted and fierce attack on the government's competence and integrity. "Why on earth," demanded one particularly vocal Member of Parliament from the opposition benches, "would this administration take such a contentious and sensitive issue to the very brink of a constitutional crisis, risking widespread public dissent and potentially undermining fundamental freedoms?"

For many observers, this entire episode is seen as nothing more than thinly veiled political manoeuvring, rather than a genuine, earnest attempt to address complex national security concerns with appropriate gravitas. "It's certainly not to the nation's true long-term benefit," a prominent political analyst remarked later, "so what exactly is the real, underlying objective here beyond mere short-term political gain?"

The underlying implication from the opposition was abundantly clear: "What this really shows, Mr Speaker," declared the Shadow Home Secretary to a packed chamber, "and perhaps even implicates the Prime Minister himself, is a cynical willingness to exploit genuinely serious matters for partisan electoral advantage." And that, she concluded, "is a profound stain on our national political discourse and a regrettable betrayal of public trust."

The accusation that anyone was playing fast and loose with the fundamental security of the nation hung heavy in the air, a potent rhetorical weapon wielded by the opposition. That damaging accusation, alongside other pressing and unresolved issues like the escalating cost of living crisis, the unprecedented NHS waiting lists, and widespread industrial action, painted an increasingly grim and precarious picture of the government's current standing in public opinion.

As his responses indicated, the Home Secretary was visibly more than a little exasperated by the relentless, pointed questioning. He repeatedly attempted to deflect the criticism, again and again, just reiterating his government's well-rehearsed mantra about safeguarding the public and the absolute necessity of tough, decisive measures. His frustration was palpable to all present.

From that moment onwards, the entire parliamentary session clearly devolved into blatant and unashamed electioneering, with both sides keenly aware of the looming electoral cycle and the stakes involved.

The very first question posed to the minister from Labour's Shadow Home Secretary, Yvette Cooper, representing her constituency of North Laxton, asked him, in effect, if he truly believed his policy of more centralisation and reduced oversight would genuinely improve national security, rather than merely concentrating unchecked power. Her questioning went so far as to forcefully suggest that the only proper and democratic course of action in these circumstances was an immediate general election to seek a fresh, legitimate mandate from the people.

The minister blushed, his face reddening noticeably under the glare of the cameras. "This was not the appropriate place," he stammered, visibly flustered and struggling momentarily for composure, "to discuss the timing of a general election. Our unwavering focus remains entirely on the critical work at hand protecting the British public."

He flatly denied there would be any announcement coming on 4th or 5th May regarding an early general election, dismissing such suggestions as pure, unsubstantiated speculation deliberately designed to distract from the government's important work.

Perhaps that alone means everyone, from the backbenches to the general public, has seen through the thinly veiled political posturing and is now playing every single card for maximum advantage in the coming electoral cycle, anticipating a ballot box showdown sooner rather than later.

original: Prime minister's questions..So who, if anyone, is playing politics with the security of the nation?..Michael Howard has no doubt it is the prime minister who, he claims, is "ramming" through Parliament the controversial new anti-terror measures without proper debate. He didn't say so, but the Tories believe the prime minister is playing the fear card on this one so he can look tough in the run up to the general election And they believe Tony Blair is using the issue to suggest the Tories are soft on terrorism. Why on earth will the prime minister not simply take up the Tories' offer to extend the existing powers temporarily to allow proper parliamentary debate of the laws, he demanded. The prime minister claims this is the clearest indication that it is the Tories who are playing politics with the issue by attempting to score cheap political points in parliament. Is not the opposition against to the proposed laws "in principle", in which case delaying a decision for further debate would be pointless?..What this is really about, believes Mr Blair, is the Tories spotting an opportunity to embarrass, maybe even defeat the government. And that is more important to them than national security. Liberal Democrat leader Charles Kennedy avoided suggesting anyone was playing politics with the issue. He preferred to state that, as with other issues like ID cards, the government's immediate instinct was authoritarian...As is his habit nowadays, the prime minister was less rough with Mr Kennedy than he had been with Mr Howard - he prefers a more exasperated tone suggesting he believes the Lib Dems have, once again, just missed the point. Apart from all that, it was electioneering as usual. The very first question to the prime minister from Derby North's Bob Laxton asked him, in effect, if he would carry on the excellent policy of pouring more resources into schools. Later Birmingham's Sion Simon even went so far as to suggest the Tories were such a shower that we should have the general election now. The prime minister almost blushed. This was not the appropriate place to announce election day, he stammered. But can anyone be in any doubt that that announcement is just days away - an announcement coming in the week beginning 4 April for an election on 5 May is where the big money is in the Commons. And perhaps that simple fact alone means everyone is seen to be playing politics with just about everything at the moment.

original: Ireland win eclipses refereeing 'errors'..The International Rugby Board may have to step in to stop frustrated coaches and players from publicly haranguing referees when things go belly-up...It may have to go the whole way and have NFL-style video cameras all over the field, or slap the vociferous perpetrators over the knuckles. What the IRB does not want is a football scenario where the verbal slanging matches often overshadow the game itself. Sunday's explosive Six Nations clash at Lansdowne Road was a good example as Ireland took another step towards their first Grand Slam since 1948. The game was as exciting as it comes, with a much-improved England side enraged at a few decisions that did not go their way. One can understand that frustration. There was no doubt that Ireland had the rub of the green in their 19-13 victory, but the reaction from the England camp may not have endeared them to the sport's "blazers". Referee Jonathan Kaplan was not perfect by any means and two decisions in particular made him the villain of the piece. I doubt whether Kaplan would have been too pleased at the comments made. After all, he has no public recourse to criticism...It was the same for Simon McDowell, the touch judge who was heavily criticised by Scotland coach Matt Williams after their defeat against France. As far as England were concerned, there were queries over Mark Cueto's first half-effort when he went over in the corner from a Charlie Hodgson kick...England coach Andy Robinson referred to a similar case at Ravenhill in January when Ulster were playing Gloucester in the Heineken Cup. On that occasion, David Humphreys kicked to Tommy Bowe, who touched down in the corner only for the try to be wiped out. But you cannot have cameras at every conceivable angle to pick up such anomalies. Perhaps Robinson was right to say the referee should have gone upstairs when Josh Lewsey was driven over the Irish line near the end...Lewsey claims he touched it down and was in full control. However, one has to credit Ireland flanker Johnny O'Connor for cleverly scooping the ball away and blocking any evidence of a touchdown. But in rugby, everything tends to even out over the 80 minutes. The referee also missed England's Danny Grewcock taking out Ronan O'Gara off the ball to allow Martin Corry a Sunday stroll to the line. Those were the stand-out moments in a classic game between the two old foes...But there were many more, and one should not take away from those. Brian O'Driscoll's winning try was as well-conceived as they come, while Charlie Hodgson's brilliant kicking display was another highlight. And Ronan O'Gara's tremendous ability to control the game was also a crucial component. But the defining moments came with Ireland under the cosh in the final 15 minutes. Two outstanding pieces of defensive play denied England and allowed Ireland to hold on. The first was Denis Hickie's brilliant double tackle in the right-hand corner. He gobbled up Cueto from another Hodgson cross-field kick, then regained his feet to stop Lewsey from scoring a certain try. Ireland's second-row colossus Paul O'Connell was equally superb. England had turned Ireland one way then the other, and the defence cordon was slowly disintegrating. England prop Matt Stevens ran in at full steam to suck in a few more tacklers. Unfortunately he ran into O'Connell who hit him hard - very hard - and then wrestled the ball away for a crucial turnover. That spoke volumes about Ireland's back-foot display, with defensive coach Mike Ford taking a bow at the end. To win a game like that showed that Ireland have moved forward. It may be tries that win games, but it is defence that wins championships.

The International Rugby Board may have to step in to stop the growing chorus of complaints from coaches and players from undermining the integrity and spirit of the game, particularly when things go up for review and interpretation. It may have to go the whole way and have Television Match Official (TMO)-style video technology deployed all over the field, offering comprehensive angles and slow-motion replays, or it will be forced to come down much harder over the knuckles with clear and consistent sanctions for dissent and poor behaviour. What the IRB does not want is a football match scenario, where the endless debates surrounding contentious officiating often overshadows the game itself, sucking the enjoyment and focus away from the athleticism and skill on display. The potential for this to happen in rugby, a sport priding itself on respect and fair play, is a serious concern that needs urgent attention from the sport's governing body.

Six Nations rugby at Croke Park was a good example of the heightened emotions and fine margins that characterise modern international competition, as Ireland took another step towards their first Grand Slam since 1948, a historical achievement that has long eluded them. The game was as physically brutal and tactically demanding as it comes, with a much improved England side left with a bitter taste in their mouths, feeling aggrieved at a few decisions that did not go their way. One can understand that frustration, especially in a championship defining fixture where every inch and every call counts towards the ultimate prize.

There was nothing in Ireland's overall performance that had the rub of the green in their victory to suggest it was undeserved, but the vocal criticism emanating from the England camp and some sections of the media may not have entirely endeared them to the sport public, who often expect a degree of stoicism and acceptance from the losing side. The referee's performance, while not perfect by any means, was under intense scrutiny throughout, and two highly contentious decisions in critical phases of the second half made him the unavoidable talking point of the piece. I doubt whether the man in the middle, despite the storm of post-match analysis, would have been too personally concerned at the barrage of comments and thinly veiled accusations made. After all, he has no public platform or direct channel to respond directly to criticism, operating under the protection of the game's officials. This lack of direct accountability, while necessary for the integrity of refereeing, often fuels public discontent.

It was the same for the French referee who was subjected to similar levels of condemnation by the French media and fans after their defeat against France, further highlighting a widespread issue across the sport. The pressure on match officials at this level is immense, and their every decision is dissected with forensic detail, often leading to unfair personal attacks.

As far as England were concerned, there were numerous legitimate questions raised over Mark Cueto's potential first-half try when he went over in the corner from a Charlie Hodgson cross-field kick, a moment that had English fans on their feet celebrating prematurely. England were quick to point to a similar case at Thomond Park in January when Ulster were playing in the Heineken Cup. On that occasion, David Humphreys appeared to ground the ball legally in the corner after a clever chip-and-chase, only for the try to be controversially ruled out by the touch judge, sparking a heated debate at the time. These inconsistencies in decision-making are what truly exasperate players and fans alike, creating a sense of injustice.

But you cannot have a TMO intervention at every ruck, maul, or breakdown to pick up such minute and marginal calls; the game would lose all its flow and dynamism. Perhaps England's head coach, Andy Robinson, was right to say the referee should have gone up to the TMO when Paul Sackey was over the line near the end, claiming vehemently he had grounded it down and was in full control. The replays, however, were inconclusive, leaving doubt in the minds of the officials. It was a moment that could have swung the game decisively in England's favour, adding to the layers of frustration.

However, one has to credit Ireland's Geordan O'Connor for his quick thinking and agility in cleverly batting the ball away, preventing the grounding. And any evidence of a clear and indisputable grounding by Sackey was simply not available to the referee or the TMO. But in rugby, everything tends to even out over the full eighty minutes, and teams must learn to adapt to the decisions made, whether favourable or not. Complaining incessantly after the fact achieves little and distracts from analysing the team's own performance.

The officials also missed England flanker Lewis Moody staking out Brian O'Driscoll off the ball to allow Martin Corry at a vital breakdown to crash over the gain line. This was another flashpoint that went unpunished, raising questions about the vigilance of the officiating team at crucial moments. Such incidents, though seemingly minor in isolation, accumulate to shape the narrative of a match, particularly a contest as tight and high-stakes as this one.

Those were the stand-out moments in a game between the two old rugby adversaries, a contest steeped in history and fierce rivalry. But there were many more moments of individual brilliance and collective effort on both sides, and one should not take away from those. Ireland's attacking prowess, particularly their first try, was as well as they come, a masterclass in fluid backs play, while Charlie Hodgson's tactical kicking from hand and at goal was another highlight for England, keeping them in the hunt. And Ireland's tactical acumen to control the game in the face of mounting English pressure was also a hugely crucial component of their eventual victory. But the defining drama came with Ireland's heroic defence, their backs against the wall, under the most intense pressure in the final minutes. Two outstanding pieces of defensive play denied England what seemed like certain scores and allowed Ireland to hold on for a memorable, albeit contentious, win.

The first was Denis Leamy's double heroic tackle in the right-hand corner. He sprinted tirelessly up from another field kick, then regained his feet and composure with remarkable speed to stop England's powerful centre, Mike Tindall, from scoring a certain try that would have levelled the scores or put England ahead. Leamy's commitment and sheer will to win epitomised Ireland's defensive effort throughout the match.

Ireland's second-row colossus, Paul O'Connell, was equally decisive and instrumental in preserving their slender lead. England had turned one way then the other, and the relentless momentum was slowly but surely building for England. Matt Stevens ploughed in at full speed and immense power to attempt to score under a pile of bodies near the posts. In a few more centimetres, he would undoubtedly have been over and awarded the try, but he met the immovable force of O'Connell, who hit him hard, very hard, and then somehow managed to rip the ball away for a game-saving turnover. It was a monumental effort of strength and technique, a testament to O'Connell's legendary status.

That courageous intervention ultimately led to the final whistle, with Ireland taking a hard-fought and ultimately deserved victory at the end. To win a game like that, against such determined opposition and under such intense scrutiny, showed that Ireland have moved forward significantly as a team, developing a new level of resilience. It may be that they go on to win all their remaining Six Nations games, claiming that elusive Grand Slam, but it is that unwavering spirit and tenacity in the face of adversity that will truly define their campaign and potentially lay the foundation for future success.

Among the targets are strategic health authorities and the new fair access regulator for universities. Tory frontbencher John Redwood said Britain needed a slimmer government and lower taxes to be competitive. The plans would abolish regional assemblies and other regional bodies, such as boards tackling industrial development and housing. Their powers would be returned to elected local councils or national government. The Tories say the strategic health authorities are not needed as it is better that local people, rather than officials, run hospitals and surgeries. "Labour are creating Two Britains: the Britain of the forgotten majority and bureaucratic Britain," he said. "In the real world, people are working harder just to stand still. They've seen their pensions knocked for six. They're being squeezed by extra taxes. The forgotten majority are paying the price of bureaucratic Britain." The government has announced plans to cut 100,000 civil servants as part of its efficiency drive. But Chief Secretary to the Treasury Paul Boateng attacked the Tory plans. "The Conservatives are committed to cutting Labour's public spending plans by a massive £35 billion," he said. "Cuts on this scale cannot be found from cutting 'bureaucracy' but would require massive cuts to front-line public services such as schools, hospitals and the police." The Liberal Democrats have said they would cut the number of Whitehall departments to make sure money reaches front-line services.

**Ireland Win Eclipses Refereeing 'Errors' in Controversial Six Nations Clash**

The International Rugby Board (IRB) may very well have to step in with more decisive action to stop frustrated coaches and players from continually haranguing referees when things go belly-up on the pitch in high-stakes matches. The passionate intensity of modern professional rugby, coupled with the immense pressure and expectations placed on teams and officials, often leads to heated exchanges and public criticism of match officials – a worrying trend that the game's custodians are increasingly keen to curb before it escalates further.

It may even have to go the whole way, exploring radical solutions such as having NFL-style video cameras deployed all over the field, offering every possible angle for officials to review every contentious decision in real-time, leaving absolutely no room for doubt or ambiguity. Alternatively, the IRB might need to devise more stringent rules and penalties to manage the vociferous demands and incessant complaints that frequently emanate from coaching boxes and touchline areas, which undoubtedly contribute significantly to the high-pressure environment in which referees operate. What the IRB most certainly does not want is for rugby to descend into a football-style scenario where the verbal slanging matches and often bitter public disputes over officiating frequently overshadow the game itself, ultimately detracting from the athletic spectacle, the players' incredible achievements, and the traditional spirit of sportsmanship that rugby has always prided itself on upholding. This erosion of respect is becoming a growing concern within the sport.

Sunday's explosive Six Nations clash at a packed and rain-soaked Lansdowne Road was a vivid and compelling example of this burgeoning tension and the fine margins involved in top-flight rugby. This particular match was especially significant as Ireland took another crucial, hard-fought step towards achieving their elusive first Grand Slam since 1948, a historic feat that would ignite the hopes and dreams of an entire nation and cement this team's place in the annals of Irish rugby. The atmosphere in Dublin was, as always, utterly electric; a vibrant cauldron of noise, anticipation, and tribal passion for a fixture that pits two of rugby's oldest and most formidable rivals against each other. The game itself was as enthralling, physically brutal, and fiercely contested as it comes, a truly epic encounter marked by relentless physicality and moments of individual brilliance from start to finish. However, a much-fancied and deeply confident England side found themselves visibly enraged at a few critical decisions made during the match that they felt did not go their way, particularly in pivotal moments of the second half, leading to heated post-match exchanges and accusations of bias.

One can, of course, understand that raw frustration and the intense emotion experienced in the heat of such a high-stakes battle, where careers and national pride are on the line. There was no denying that Ireland had the rub of the green on a couple of marginal occasions in their hard-fought 19-13 victory, benefiting from some truly close calls that ultimately went their way. However, the sheer intensity and nature of the reaction from the England camp, particularly from certain players and the coaching staff in the immediate aftermath of the final whistle, may not have entirely endeared them to the sport's purists and neutral observers, who consistently advocate for unwavering respect and acceptance of official decisions, regardless of the outcome. South African referee Jonathan Kaplan was certainly not perfect by any means during the contest; indeed, two highly contentious decisions in particular made him the unwitting villain of the piece in the eyes of the English contingent, sparking widespread debate across the rugby world and dominating much of the post-match analysis.

I doubt very much whether Mr. Kaplan himself would have been too pleased or indeed surprised at the often pointed comments made about his performance and the integrity of his decisions. After all, he, like all international referees, operates within a system where he has no public forum to respond to criticism or defend his actions, a professional vulnerability that often leaves them isolated and unfairly exposed to intense public scrutiny and accusations from all sides, without the opportunity to defend themselves. It was a strikingly similar scenario for Simon McDowell, the highly respected touch judge, who was heavily criticised by Scotland coach Matt Williams after their defeat against France earlier in the championship, highlighting a troubling and escalating pattern within the game regarding the treatment and public perception of officials. These incidents collectively underscore the growing, often overwhelming, pressure placed upon match officials in the modern professional game, where every decision is meticulously dissected and replayed ad nauseam by media and fans alike.

As far as England were concerned, the most vocal and persistent queries revolved primarily around Mark Cueto's first-half effort. The agile England winger firmly believed he had gone over in the corner from a perfectly weighted Charlie Hodgson cross-field kick, appearing to ground the ball cleanly for what he thought was a legitimate try, one that would have swung momentum England's way. However, referee Kaplan controversially ruled no try, citing a perceived lack of clear or definitive grounding, a decision that immediately drew the ire of the English players. England coach Clive Woodward was quick to draw a direct parallel, referring to a strikingly similar case that had occurred at Ravenhill in January when Ulster were playing in the fiercely contested Heineken Cup, using it as an example of inconsistent officiating across different competitions and referees.

On that particular occasion, Ulster fly-half David Humphreys kicked a superb cross-field pass to winger Tommy Bowe, who clearly touched down cleanly in the corner only for the try to be controversially wiped out by the officials, a decision Ulster vehemently protested at the time and one that caused much debate. Woodward argued that, given the ambiguity and the closeness of the call, the Cueto decision should have, unequivocally, been referred to the Television Match Official (TMO), a vital technological tool specifically available for exactly such close and pivotal calls, to ensure fairness and accuracy. However, there's a practical and philosophical limit to such constant interventions; you simply cannot have a TMO at every moment to pick up such anomalies without slowing the game excessively. Such an approach would inevitably slow the game to an unacceptable crawl, fatally detracting from the free-flowing, dynamic nature that is rugby's most cherished hallmark.

Perhaps Woodward was also entirely right to say the referee should have referred it to the TMO when Josh Lewsey was over the Irish line near the very end of the game, creating yet another pivotal moment that could have dramatically swung the outcome and snatched victory for England. Lewsey's potential try in the dying minutes, which would have brought England within touching distance of a famous comeback win, was a genuine game-changer. Lewsey himself was absolutely adamant, claiming he had grounded it down cleanly and was in full control, believing he had secured a crucial late score for his team. However, one has to credit Ireland flanker Alan O'Connor for a superb and absolutely vital piece of defensive play, displaying incredible awareness, lightning-quick reflexes, and immense fortitude to scoop the ball away from Lewsey's grasp and effectively blocking any clear, conclusive evidence of a definitive grounding. It was a testament to the Irish defence's never-say-die attitude and their unwavering commitment right to the final whistle, a moment of sheer desperation and brilliance. But in rugby, everything tends to even out over the 80 minutes, and these close calls often balance out, and Ireland's tenacity certainly earned them their fortune and this precious victory on the day.

The officials also appeared to miss another significant incident during the game: England's robust lock Danny Grewcock illegally taking out Ireland's talismanic fly-half Ronan O'Gara off the ball during a critical attacking phase for England. This clear infringement, had it been spotted and penalised, would have resulted in a penalty against England, potentially changing the momentum of the game significantly, as it directly allowed number eight Martin Corry a clear run to the line for an almost certain score. Such an act of foul play, if penalised, could have seen the try disallowed and a yellow card issued. Those were arguably the stand-out moments of controversy and officiating debate in what was otherwise a truly classic, brutally contested, and endlessly compelling game between the two old rivals, a fixture always charged with intense emotion, deep history, and immense national pride, and one that ultimately lived up to its billing as a must-watch encounter for all rugby fans.

But amidst the storm of refereeing debate and the inevitable post-match discussions that followed, there were many more moments of genuine rugby brilliance and tactical acumen from both sides that deserve equal, if not greater, attention. One should not allow the understandable focus on officiating errors to detract from the sheer quality and unwavering determination of Ireland's performance and their ultimately well-deserved victory. Brian O'Driscoll's winning try, a typically incisive break from midfield followed by a clinical finish against a scrambling defence, was as well-executed as they come, a pure piece of individual genius from the inspirational captain, showcasing his world-class ability to conjure magic when it matters most and leaving defenders grasping at thin air. Meanwhile, Charlie Hodgson's brilliant kicking, both from hand to relieve pressure and off the tee to keep England's scoreboard ticking, was another major highlight for England, keeping them firmly in touch even when they struggled for attacking momentum. And Ronan O'Gara's composed ability to control the game, his precise tactical kicking, and his steady, guiding hand at fly-half, was also a masterclass in astute game management, particularly evident under the immense pressure of the closing stages, ensuring Ireland always had direction.

However, the real test of Ireland's collective mettle, and indeed the dramatic climax of the entire game, came with Ireland under the cosh in the final 15 minutes. England, desperate to claw back the deficit and keep their own Grand Slam hopes miraculously alive, threw absolutely everything they had at the Irish line, initiating a period of relentless, intense pressure that had the vocal Lansdowne Road crowd holding its collective breath, sensing a potential late comeback. It was in these nail-biting, make-or-break moments that Ireland's character truly shone through, demonstrating incredible resilience. Two truly heroic and utterly vital pieces of defensive play ultimately stopped England from scoring and allowed Ireland to hold on for their crucial victory. It was a display of resilience, defensive organisation, and unwavering spirit that will long be remembered by the Irish faithful and rugby connoisseurs alike.

The first of these came from the outstanding Denis Hickie, whose brilliant double tackle in the right-hand corner was nothing short of miraculous and match-saving. It was a display of individual courage, exceptional anticipation, and flawless execution under the most extreme pressure. He first gobbled up the dangerous Mark Cueto from another pinpoint Charlie Hodgson cross-field kick, showing incredible speed and an almost clairvoyant sense of position to beat the winger to the ball. Then, astonishingly, he somehow regained his feet instantly and, with superhuman effort, stretched to stop the powerful Josh Lewsey from scoring a certain try just moments later, covering an incredible amount of ground in mere seconds to preserve Ireland's slender lead. It was, without doubt, a match-winning defensive effort from the winger, showcasing commitment above and beyond the call of duty.

Ireland's second-row colossus Paul O'Connell was equally instrumental and influential in the dying minutes, his immense presence, unparalleled work rate, and raw strength proving utterly pivotal when the game was on a knife-edge and England were pressing hard. England, with renewed vigour and a desperate will to win, had turned the Irish defence one way then the other, forcing them to scramble and cover, and it truly looked as though the green wall was slowly but surely disintegrating under relentless pressure and fatigue. The crowd's cheers turned to anxious gasps as England sniffed a try. England prop Matt Stevens, a powerful and committed ball carrier, ran in at full steam, looking to suck in a few more Irish tacklers and create precious space for his support runners as England pushed for a late, decisive score. Unfortunately for him, he ran straight into the immovable object that was O'Connell, who hit him hard – very hard indeed, with a bone-rattling impact that stopped him dead in his tracks – and then, with incredible strength, a vise-like grip, and superb technique, ripped the ball away for a crucial turnover, relieving the pressure and allowing Ireland to clear their lines and secure possession at a vital, game-defining moment, snuffing out the English threat.

That spoke volumes about Ireland's entire back-foot display throughout the game, with defensive coach Mike Ford deservedly taking a huge amount of credit at the end for their resilience, for instilling such tenacity, organisation, and sheer belief in the squad's defensive capabilities. It was a triumph of meticulous structure, unyielding courage, and collective will in the face of relentless opposition. To win a game like that, under such immense pressure, against an adversary of England's proven quality, and with so many critical moments hanging in the balance, unequivocally shows that Ireland have moved forward significantly as a rugby nation. This victory demonstrated the depth of their character, their tactical maturity, and their ability to perform when it truly counts on the biggest stage. It may be tries that win individual games and capture the headlines, thrilling the crowds with attacking flair and excitement, but as the old, timeless adage in rugby goes, it is staunch defence, unwavering commitment, and iron will that ultimately wins championships and secures lasting glory. This Irish team displayed all of those attributes in abundance on a memorable Sunday afternoon.

Tories unveil quango blitz plans.

Plans to abolish 162 quangos have been unveiled by the Conservatives as part of their effort to show how government red tape can be cut.

Six government units would also be scrapped under proposals which the Tories say would save more than £4.3bn. Among the targets are strategic health authorities and the new fair access regulator for universities. Tory frontbencher John Redwood said Britain needed a slimmer government and lower taxes to be competitive.

The plans would abolish regional assemblies and other regional bodies, such as boards tackling industrial development and housing. Their powers would be returned to elected local councils or national government. The Tories say the strategic health authorities are not needed as it is better that local people, rather than officials, run hospitals and surgeries.

Announcing the plans, Mr Redwood said: "Mr Blair has forgotten the interests of taxpayers, and has broken the pledges he made. Far from improving public services, spending taxpayers' money on quangos has led only to more bureaucrats, more regulation and higher taxes." His party leader, Michael Howard, argued a change in direction was needed to get a grip on spending. "Labour are creating Two Britains: the Britain of the forgotten majority and bureaucratic Britain," he said. "In the real world, people are working harder just to stand still. They've seen their pensions knocked for six. They're being squeezed by extra taxes. The forgotten majority are paying the price of bureaucratic Britain."

The government has announced plans to cut 100,000 civil servants as part of its efficiency drive. But Chief Secretary to the Treasury Paul Boateng attacked the Tory plans. "The Conservatives are committed to cutting Labour's public spending plans by a massive £35 billion," he said. "Cuts on this scale cannot be found from cutting 'bureaucracy' but would require massive cuts to front-line public services such as schools, hospitals and the police." The Liberal Democrats have said they would cut the number of Whitehall departments to make sure money reaches front-line services.

The role and cost of quangos – quasi-autonomous non-governmental organisations – have once again become a flashpoint in political debate. New figures released today indicate the persistent financial burden these bodies place on the public purse. There are now believed to be approximately 162 quangos operating across a diverse range of sectors, from health and education to environmental protection and regulatory oversight. Their collective annual expenditure is estimated to be a staggering £4.3bn. This considerable sum has prompted renewed calls for significant reform from across the political spectrum. Opposition frontbenchers have been particularly vocal, said a senior figure, insisting that a slimmer, more accountable government is not just desirable but a fiscal imperative. They argue that the current structure leads to inefficiency and a lack of clear democratic responsibility, undermining public trust and diverting resources from essential frontline services.

Critics contend that their government, referring to the incumbent administration, has rather been lacklustre in fulfilling its promises to rein in these unelected bodies. Despite earlier pledges to prune the 'forest of quangos', many believe that progress has been minimal. reconstruction:
Watchdog probes e-mail deletions. The Information Commissioner says he is urgently asking for details of Cabinet Office orders telling staff to delete e-mails more than three months old. This urgent intervention by Richard Thomas, the Information Commissioner, follows widespread concern about government transparency ahead of the new Freedom of Information Act. Mr Thomas's office is scrutinising these directives, which have raised significant questions about the preservation of official records and public accountability.

Richard Thomas has "totally condemned" the deletion of e-mails to prevent their disclosure under freedom of information laws coming into force on 1 January. Speaking out forcefully, Mr Thomas described such actions as a serious breach of public trust and an attempt to subvert the new legislation. He emphasised the importance of maintaining a comprehensive record of government business for public scrutiny. Government guidance, he reiterated, clearly stated that e-mails should only be deleted if they served "no current purpose", Mr Thomas said. He stressed that this guidance was designed to ensure proper record-keeping, not to facilitate the selective removal of potentially sensitive information.

The Tories and the Lib Dems have questioned the timing of the new rules, expressing alarm at directives issued just weeks before the new transparency law takes effect. Both opposition parties suggested that the timing was highly suspicious and politically motivated. Tory leader Michael Howard has written to Tony Blair demanding an explanation of the new rules on e-mail retention. Mr Howard's letter to the Prime Minister highlighted fears that the rules could be an attempt to circumvent the new transparency laws and prevent potentially embarrassing information from entering the public domain. On Monday, Lib Dem constitutional affairs committee chairman Alan Beith warned that the deletion of millions of government e-mails could harm the ability of key probes like the Hutton Inquiry. He argued that the loss of electronic communications could severely impede future investigations into government conduct and decision-making, making it harder to establish facts or hold officials to account. The timing of the new rules just before the Freedom of Information Act comes into force was "too unlikely to have been a coincidence", Mr Beith said, suggesting a deliberate attempt to clear out records.

But a Cabinet Office spokeswoman said the move was not about the new laws or "the destruction of important records". She insisted that the guidance was simply a routine update to existing data management policies, aimed at ensuring efficient use of government IT systems. The spokeswoman denied any suggestion that the directives were designed to pre-empt or undermine the Freedom of Information Act. However, Mr Beith urged the Information Commissioner to look at how the "e-mail regime" could "support the freedom of information regime". He called for an immediate review of the Cabinet Office's guidance, asserting that it should promote transparency and accountability rather than facilitate the removal of potentially relevant documents. He stressed the importance of having robust guidelines that align with the principles of open government.

Mr Thomas further underscored the gravity of the situation. He said: "The new Act of Parliament makes it very clear that to destroy records in order to prevent their disclosure becomes a criminal offence." He emphasised that ignorance of the law would be no defence and that those found to be deliberately destroying records could face serious penalties. He said there was already clear guidance on the retention of e-mails contained in a code of practice from the Lord Chancellor. This guidance, he added, applied to all government departments and aimed to ensure proper record management. All e-mails, he reiterated, are subject to the freedom of information laws, but the important thing was the content of the e-mail, said Mr Thomas, rather than its format. He warned against any misinterpretation of the existing rules that might lead to improper deletions.

Reiterating a fundamental principle for public servants, Mr Thomas stated: "If in doubt, retain, that has been the long-standing principle of the civil service and public authorities." He clarified that destruction was only permissible under very specific circumstances. "It's only when you've got no further use for the particular record that it may be legitimate to destroy it." He left no room for ambiguity on malicious intent. "But any deliberate destruction to avoid the possibility of later disclosure is to be totally condemned." This stern warning highlights the legal and ethical obligations placed upon government employees regarding information management.

The Freedom of Information Act will cover England, Wales and Northern Ireland from next year. Similar measures are being brought in at the same time in Scotland, ensuring a consistent approach across the UK. It provides the public with a right of access to information held by about 100,000 public bodies, subject to various exemptions. Its implementation will be monitored by the Information Commissioner, who will ensure compliance and address any breaches of the new legislation, upholding the public's right to know.

The complexities surrounding the government’s latest white paper on administrative reform are proving far more intricate and contentious than initially acknowledged by ministers. Critics from across the political spectrum have voiced significant concerns, arguing that, firstly, they have consistently failed to engage genuinely with key stakeholders and have instead pushed through reforms with insufficient consultation and a worrying lack of transparency. The proposed changes, intended to streamline public services, are now facing intense scrutiny in both Houses of Parliament.

A central figure in this parliamentary examination is Lord Beith, a long-serving peer and former Member of Parliament, known for his incisive contributions to debates on governance and public administration. As a prominent member of the influential House of Lords Scrutiny Committee, Lord Beith has delved deeply into the practical implications of the proposed legislation. He questioned the fundamental legal basis for certain aspects of the proposed changes, and their potential to undermine established democratic frameworks. His concerns centre on how new measures will translate into practical application, particularly regarding accountability and oversight.

Speaking during a recent committee hearing, Lord Beith said the new measures were 'dangerously ambiguous' and lacked the necessary detail to the detriment of clarity and effective governance. He added, "Without clear, unequivocal guidance, the implementation of these reforms risks descending into chaos, inadvertently creating more problems than they solve. The government's aspiration for efficiency cannot come at the cost of democratic scrutiny or public understanding." He further elaborated that the current proposals 'risk creating a bureaucracy that makes it impossible to function effectively on a daily basis for those on the front lines of public service delivery.' It is one thing to propose grand, sweeping reforms, but quite another to ensure the practical realities and operational challenges are addressed effectively and sustainably. The current framework, he suggested, is simply inadequate for the scale of ambition.

The debate, which unfolded in Westminster over several intense sessions, has centred heavily on the implications for the various regions of the UK, with particular attention to how these reforms will impact local authorities and devolved administrations. Lord Beith highlighted concerns that while the proposals aimed to improve outcomes for England, from a broader perspective, the methodology brought at the forefront in the document presented significant challenges for equitable distribution of resources and consistent service levels nationwide. Questions were specifically raised about how lessons from other regional governance models or even international examples, could be brought at the forefront in the policy-making process for England, without inadvertently creating new disparities. He cautioned against a one-size-fits-all approach that might overlook the unique needs of various localities, particularly those with distinct economic or social characteristics.

The comprehensive document itself, running to hundreds of pages, outlines 100 specific recommendations for reform, touching upon everything from local council funding to national infrastructure projects. While the government maintains these recommendations are crucial for modernising the public sector, critics argue that the sheer volume and complexity make thorough review exceptionally difficult within the proposed timelines. Further information regarding the implementation timeline and detailed departmental responsibilities will be made public once the full parliamentary debate has concluded and any amendments have been incorporated into the final legislation. The government remains committed to its timetable, but the growing chorus of concern, spearheaded by figures like Lord Beith, suggests that a smoother path to reform is far from guaranteed.

Beith, a long-standing champion of open government and parliamentary scrutiny, has welcomed the report's findings while stressing the critical need for immediate action. Speaking to BBC News, Beith underscored the importance of ensuring that the public has unfettered access to the information that shapes their daily lives.

""The revelations in this report are stark, but they also present a clear pathway forward,"" Beith stated. ""It is vital that **they**"", he emphasised, referring to government bodies and public institutions, ""**and have** the mechanisms in place to not only collect this data responsibly but also to make it comprehensible and accessible to every citizen. Transparency is not a luxury; it is the bedrock of a healthy democracy.""

The report, which has been several years in the making, represents **the one** comprehensive attempt to map the entirety of public data flows within England. Beith, of the initiative from its inception, played a pivotal role in steering it **into** the public discourse. His consistent advocacy was key **to** ensuring the project received the necessary backing and attention it deserved.

**Beith said the** process of compiling such a detailed overview was arduous but absolutely essential. ""What we have here is not just a collection of statistics; it's a narrative about how information power is distributed and exercised,"" he explained. ""This is about empowering individuals and communities to make informed decisions and to hold those in power accountable.""

He continued, ""The ambition behind this report **makes it to** the forefront of international efforts in data governance. It sets a new benchmark for what can be achieved when there is a genuine commitment to openness. We can no longer afford to operate in silos when it comes to information that impacts millions.""

The study focuses **on** various aspects of public data, from health records and educational outcomes to infrastructure projects and environmental data. It highlights a critical **thing:** the current fragmentation of data collection and storage, which often impedes effective analysis and public access. The report makes specific recommendations for standardising formats and establishing a centralised portal for public information.

The impetus for this comprehensive review began **in England, from** grassroots movements and academic studies that pointed to growing concerns over data opacity. The initial proposals were formally **brought at the** launch of a cross-party parliamentary inquiry two years ago, which has now culminated in this eagerly anticipated publication.

The sheer scale of the undertaking is reflected in the numbers. Researchers meticulously analysed **more than 100,000** individual datasets, public documents, and internal government memos. This monumental effort has culminated in a resource that **will be information** critical for policy-makers, researchers, and the general public for years to come.

Beith stressed that the report is not just an academic exercise but a practical guide for implementing change. ""The recommendations are actionable, and the political will must now follow suit,"" he urged. ""We have a unique opportunity here to transform how our government interacts with its citizens, building a more trust-based and transparent relationship.""

He also touched upon the economic benefits of greater data openness, suggesting that readily available public data can fuel innovation, support new businesses, and drive economic growth. ""When information is locked away, its potential is never fully realised. By unleashing this data, we are not only strengthening our democracy but also unlocking significant economic value for the entire nation,"" Beith concluded, reiterating his commitment to overseeing the implementation of the report’s crucial recommendations. original: New browser wins over net surfers..The proportion of surfers using Microsoft's Internet Explorer (IE) has dropped to below 90%, say web analysts...Net traffic monitor, OneStat.com, has reported that the open-source browser Firefox 1.0, released on 9 November, seems to be drawing users away from IE. While IE's market share has dropped 5% since May to 88.9%, Mozilla browsers - including Firefox - have grown by 5%. Firefox is made by the Mozilla Foundation which was set up by former browser maker Netscape in 1998. Although there have been other preview versions of Firefox, version 1.0 was the first complete official program. "It seems that people are switching from Microsoft's Internet Explorer to Mozilla's new Firefox browser," said Niels Brinkman, co-founder of Amsterdam-based OneStat.com...Mozilla browsers - including Firefox 1.0 - now have 7.4% of the market share, the figures suggest. Mozilla said that more than five million have downloaded the free software since its official release. Supporters of the open-source software in the US managed to raise $250,000 (£133,000) to advertise the release of Firefox 1.0 in The New York Times, and support the Mozilla Foundation. There was a flurry of downloads on its first day of release...The figures echo similar research from net analyst WebSideStory which suggested that IE had 92.9% of users in October compared to 95.5% in June. Microsoft IE has dominated the browser market for some time after taking the crown from Netscape, and its share of users has always stayed at around the 95% mark. Firefox is attractive to many because it is open-source. That means people are free to adapt the software's core code to create other innovative features, like add-ons or extensions to the program. Fewer security holes have also been discovered so far in Firefox than in IE. Paul Randle, Microsoft Windows Client product manager, responded to the figures: "We certainly respect that some customers will choose alternative browsers and that choosing a browser is about more than a handful of features. "Microsoft continues to make significant investments in IE, including Service Pack 2 with advanced security technologies, and continues to encourage a vibrant ecosystem of third party add-ons for Internet Explorer." Firefox wants to capture 10% of the market by the end of 2005. Other browser software, like Opera and Apple's Safari, are also challenging Microsoft's grip on the browser market. Opera is set to release its version 7.60 by the end of the year. OneStat.com compiled the statistical measurements from two million net users in 100 countries.
