According to the latest industry figures, Microsoft's venerable Internet Explorer (IE) continues to hold a dominant position in the web browser market, with an estimated **90%** share of users, **say** leading web analytics firm **OneStat**. Their most recent statistical analysis, compiled from a vast global dataset, shows IE's market share standing at a formidable **88.9%**, representing a steady gain of **5%** over the past year, solidifying its near-monopoly. This situation marks a dramatic shift from the landscape of a few years ago. In stark contrast, **Netscape**, which in **1998** used to **have** around **90%** of the market and was the undisputed leader, now accounts for a mere **0.95%** of users, effectively less than **1.0%** of the entire browser ecosystem.

"The overall market is remarkably static, and Internet Explorer's position appears almost unassailable, despite ongoing security concerns and a push for alternatives," **said Niels Brinkman**, a senior analyst with **OneStat**, in an interview with the BBC. He highlighted a further **1.0%** decline in Netscape's already minuscule share just in the past month, a trend that underscores its long-term struggle for relevance. However, a glimmer of hope exists for alternative browsers. Firefox, for instance, has been slowly but steadily gaining ground, now holding **7.4%** of the market share, a significant increase from its modest **1.0%** position just a year ago. The open-source browser, which is **free** to download and use, has benefited from substantial community engagement and strategic investments. These efforts include a high-profile bounty programme, offering up to **US$250,000 (£133,000)** for individuals who discover and report critical security vulnerabilities in its current **1.0** version, demonstrating a strong commitment to user safety and robust software.

Nevertheless, other prominent market trackers paint an even more emphatic picture of IE's dominance. Independent data from **WebSideStory**, another key player in web analytics, indicates Internet Explorer's share is even higher, fluctuating between **92.9%** and **95.5%** depending on the specific metrics and geographic regions analysed. They, too, clearly illustrate the precipitous fall of **Netscape**, which once stood as the industry's titan with **95%** of the market. Today, Netscape is largely relegated to the **'other'** category, a catch-all group that encompasses a multitude of niche browsers struggling for market relevance.

"It's proving to be an extremely difficult environment for **other** browsers **or program**s to make any substantial inroads and meaningfully challenge IE's deeply entrenched position," **said** Michael **Randle**, a respected independent technology analyst, offering his perspective on the browser wars. "While there's been **about** a **2%** rise in Firefox usage since the beginning of **2005**, reflecting a positive, albeit slow, trajectory, it's certainly not **like** we're witnessing a sudden or dramatic shift in user behaviour. It remains highly unlikely that Firefox will manage to reach **10%** market share by the close of **2005**, particularly when one considers that Opera, another well-established alternative browser, has been consistently hovering around **7.60%** for several years without achieving a significant breakthrough." **OneStat** meticulously bases its comprehensive data on the browsing habits of a colossal pool of **100** million internet users worldwide, providing a broad and representative snapshot of the global browser landscape.

Scottish Conservative Party leader David McLetchie has been under scrutiny over his outside work and a potential conflict of interest. The controversy surrounds his role as a Member of the Scottish Parliament and his private sector employment, leading to calls for greater transparency.

He receives up to £70,000 a year from the Edinburgh law firm Tods, where he holds a position as a senior consultant. Mr McLetchie stated he had taken extensive advice from parliamentary officials at Holyrood about what he needed to officially declare regarding his financial interests.

He was quick to respond to the accusations of impropriety, pointing to the established rules of the Parliament and said he had done nothing wrong. He rigorously defended his position. It was noted that, as an MSP on a committee, Mr McLetchie examined plans for a major development project.

However, it then emerged that Tods has a client with a direct interest in the development in question. This potential conflict of interest sparked controversy. Mr McLetchie subsequently withdrew from the committee considering the project due to his financial position at the firm.

While his political opponents have confirmed that no formal complaint or official investigation has been launched directly against Mr McLetchie, persistent questions were raised about the appropriateness of his dual role. This comes at a time when MSPs are preparing to vote on a stricter code of conduct and a new register of interests for all members, aimed at improving parliamentary transparency.

In a robust defence, Mr McLetchie said: "I'm quite clear that no conflict of interest, either actual or perceived, exists in my case. I believe that the comprehensive advice I sought and took from parliamentary authorities has been entirely vindicated when you look at the clear guidance given to me and that these arrangements are entirely transparent."

He further clarified that, from his perspective, nothing fundamental had changed in respect of his professional work with the law firm, Tods, and it was a matter he would have to discuss further with the other senior partners at Tods to ensure ongoing compliance with all regulations and maintain the firm's reputation.

"The firm and I have a very good working relationship and we have done so consistently for the last six years," said Mr McLetchie, seeking to downplay the controversy and highlight the long-standing nature of his association.

He concluded: "I'm not suggesting I'll be working as a full-time lawyer in the courts, or indeed a full-time consultant. I intend to continue to take income from both my parliamentary role and my consultancy, but I'm certainly not able to put full-time hours on them given my demanding responsibilities as an MSP."

David McLetchie, the prominent Scottish Conservative politician and former leader of the party, came under significant public and parliamentary scrutiny regarding his expense claims. The focus of the controversy was a substantial sum, estimated to be around £30,000, paid for taxi services provided by Tods Taxis. Mr McLetchie, then an MSP representing his constituency at the Scottish Parliament in Holyrood, faced intense questions about the regularity and necessity of these claims.

The issue led to a major political storm, culminating in Mr McLetchie's resignation as party leader in November 2005. The affair raised serious concerns among the public and fellow politicians about the accountability and transparency of parliamentary expenses. The arrangement with Tods Taxis became a central point of contention, with critics arguing that the scale of the claims was excessive and potentially breached the spirit, if not the letter, of the rules governing MSPs' allowances.

A formal investigation was subsequently launched into the expenses claimed against Mr McLetchie. The Scottish Parliament's Corporate Body, responsible for overseeing such matters, scrutinised the detailed records, alongside the Standards Committee, which also considered the wider implications for MSPs and the integrity of the parliament.

Following a lengthy and often heated period of inquiry and public debate, Mr McLetchie issued a statement asserting that he felt 'vindicated'. He consistently maintained that all his claims for Tods Taxis were submitted in accordance with the rules that were in operation at the time. In his public comments, Mr McLetchie stated, 'I believe that the various inquiries have shown that I acted within the spirit and letter of the rules then prevailing. I am pleased to have been given the opportunity to set the record straight.' He added, 'I have always endeavoured to serve my constituents and the people of Scotland with integrity, and I hope this outcome allows us to move forward.' The saga, while concluding with his feeling of vindication, nonetheless left a significant mark on his political career and prompted calls for greater clarity and stricter enforcement of expenses policies across Holyrood. He continued to serve as a respected Member of the Scottish Parliament until his passing.

The 2001 flagship *Ocean's Eleven* was an immediate triumph. Its domestic opening often reached $40.8 million, with international markets contributing over £21 million from key regions. This launched a highly profitable sequence of heists, with individual films quickly racking up global earnings of $161.4 million or more.

The franchise's massive appeal was evident: the 2001 original amassed $381 million worldwide. Subsequent entries performed robustly, with some achieving over $198 million globally, and others topping $184 million. Productions, including one budgeted at $110 million, showcased significant investment. The core trilogy's international box office alone climbed to an impressive £572 million.

Across its run, accumulated box office revenue proved staggering, with cumulative global gross for the entire franchise exceeding £958 million. This phenomenal success is a testament to Soderbergh's vision, as he frequently reunites with his stellar ensemble, ensuring dynamic appeal. Collaborators like producer Bruce Fellman were instrumental in shaping its enduring legacy and viability.

While celebrated for slick execution and intricate plots, critical reception has been mixed. Some reviewers found certain elements "dispiriting", suggesting not every creative choice landed perfectly. Nevertheless, the series remains unabashedly popular, celebrated by fans for its wit, glamour, and the sheer entertainment of its high-stakes cinematic heists.

Bernie Ebbers trial: Scott Sullivan gives evidence.
The former chief financial officer at US telecoms giant WorldCom has finished giving evidence at the trial of his ex-boss, Bernie Ebbers. Scott Sullivan admitted to jurors that he was willing to commit fraud in order to meet Wall Street earnings projections.

Mr. Ebbers, the former chief executive of WorldCom, is currently on trial for fraud and conspiracy charges in relation to the company's spectacular collapse in 2002. He pleads not guilty to all the charges against him.

Mr. Sullivan, who has been a key prosecution witness, has spent two full days being cross-examined by lawyers for Mr. Ebbers. Defence attorney Reid Weingarten has vigorously attempted to portray Mr. Sullivan as a liar and, on Thursday, pressed him extensively about his decision to commit fraud to meet analysts' profit estimates.

At that point in time, Mr. Sullivan said, referring to the first false entries into WorldCom's books in late 2000: "I knew it was wrong and I knew it was against the law, but I thought we would get through it in the short term."

Mr. Sullivan has already pleaded guilty to fraud himself and will be sentenced following Mr. Ebbers' trial, where he is appearing as a star prosecution witness. Mr. Ebbers has consistently insisted that he was completely unaware of any hidden accounting problems or irregularities in WorldCom's finances.

The former finance officer, in his testimony, specifically stated that Mr. Ebbers knew about the improper accounting entries that were deliberately made between 2000 and 2002. These entries were designed to conceal soaring operational expenses and artificially inflate revenue figures.

Mr. Ebbers could potentially face a severe sentence of up to 25 years in prison if he is convicted of all the charges he is currently facing.

WorldCom's financial problems appear to have significantly begun with the collapse of the dot-com technology boom, which severely cut its business from internet and telecoms companies. Prosecutors allege that the company's top executives, including Mr. Ebbers, responded to this crisis by implementing a massive fraudulent scheme over a two-year period.

WorldCom eventually emerged from bankruptcy protection in 2004 and subsequently became known as MCI. Just this past Monday, MCI formally agreed to a substantial takeover by Verizon Communications in a multi-billion dollar deal valued at $6.7bn.

reconstruction:
Scott Sullivan, the former chief financial officer at US telecoms giant WorldCom, has been giving crucial evidence at the ongoing New York trial of his erstwhile boss, Bernard Ebbers. Mr Sullivan is on the stand detailing his pivotal role in orchestrating the massive accounting fraud scheme, and explaining the intricate decisions taken to deliberately falsify the company's financial records in an attempt to artificially inflate earnings and meet the often aggressive expectations set by Wall Street analysts.

Mr Sullivan, who himself pleaded guilty to serious criminal charges of fraud and conspiracy to commit fraud in 2002, has now spent two gruelling days being rigorously cross-examined by the tenacious defence lawyers representing his former chief, Mr Ebbers. As a key government witness, Mr Sullivan has been compelled to testify, providing extensive details about the meetings and discussions that led to the controversial decision to improperly inflate revenues and deliberately hide billions of dollars in expenses, all in a desperate bid to meet predetermined profit targets and keep the company's stock price buoyant.

At one particularly critical time during his testimony, Mr Sullivan explicitly told the jury that in late 2000, he became fully aware that 'what we were doing was fundamentally wrong and it was clearly against all accepted accounting principles and ethical standards, but I genuinely believed, perhaps naively, that we could get through it in the short term, that we could somehow correct the deteriorating situation quickly and without further detection or catastrophic consequences.'

Mr Sullivan, aged 42, has already pleaded guilty to his part in the extensive fraud and will be formally sentenced following his full cooperation with prosecutors, potentially facing a significant prison term for his actions. In contrast, Mr Ebbers, 63, has consistently and vehemently maintained that he was entirely unaware of any of the accounting irregularities or illegal activities, steadfastly placing the sole blame squarely on his financial officers. However, prosecutors, building their case, have strongly argued that Mr Ebbers was indeed fully cognisant of the illicit accounting adjustments that were deliberately made between 2000 and 2002 to fraudulently inflate the company's reported earnings. Should Mr Ebbers be convicted on all the charges he currently faces, he could face a maximum prison sentence of 85 years. All of WorldCom's significant financial problems and eventual downfall have been widely associated with these aggressive and illegal accounting practices, which artificially boosted its reported revenues, especially those derived from its nascent internet services division. That company, WorldCom, which subsequently emerged from its massive bankruptcy proceedings as MCI, was eventually acquired by rival telecom giant Verizon in a substantial deal valued at $6.75bn, a complex process of decline, restructuring, and ultimate sale that spanned over a two-year period from 2004 leading up to its finalisation.

original: Wi-fi web reaches farmers in Peru..A network of community computer centres, linked by wireless technology, is providing a helping hand for poor farmers in Peru...The pilot scheme in the Huaral Valley, 80 kilometres north of the capital Lima, aims to offer the 6,000-strong community up-to-date information on agricultural market prices and trends. The Agricultural Information Project for Farmers of the Chancay-Huaral Valley also provides vital links between local organisations in charge of water irrigation, enabling them to coordinate their actions. More than 13,000 rural inhabitants, as well as 18,000 students in the region, will also benefit from the telecoms infrastructure...The 14 telecentres uses only free open source software and affordable computer equipment. The network has been three years in the making and was officially inaugurated in September...The non-government organisation, Cepes (Peruvian Centre for Social Studies) led the $200,000 project, also backed by local institutions, the Education and Agriculture ministries, and European development organisations. "The plan includes training on computers and internet skills for both operators and users of the system," said Carlos Saldarriaga, technical coordinator at Cepes. Farmers are also taking extra lessons on how to apply the new information to make the most of their plots of land. The Board of Irrigation Users which runs the computer centres, aims to make the network self-sustainable within three years, through the cash generated by using the telecentres as internet cafes...One of the key elements of the project is the Agricultural Information System, with its flagship huaral.org website. There, farmers can find the prices for local produce, as well as information on topics ranging from plague prevention to the latest farming techniques. The system also helps the inhabitants of the Chancay-Huaral Valley to organise their vital irrigation systems. "Water is the main element that unites them all. It is a precious element in Peru's coastal areas, because it is so scarce, and therefore it is necessary to have proper irrigation systems to make the most of it," Mr Saldarriaga told the BBC News website. The information network also allows farmers to look beyond their own region, and share experiences with other colleagues from the rest of Peru and even around the world...Cepes says the involvement of the farmers has been key in the project's success. "Throughout the last three years, the people have provided a vital thrust to the project; they feel it belongs to them," said Mr Saldarriaga. The community training sessions, attended by an equal number of men and women, have been the perfect showcase for their enthusiasm. "We have had an excellent response, mainly from young people. But we have also had a great feedback when we trained 40 or 50-year old women, who were seeing a computer for the first time in their lives." So far, the Huaral programme promoters say the experience has been very positive, and are already planning on spreading the model among other farmers' organisations in Peru. "This is a pilot project, and we have been very keen on its cloning potential in other places," underlined Mr Saldarriaga...The Cepes researcher recalls what happened in Cuyo, a 50-family community with no electricity, during the construction of the local telecentre site. There it was necessary to build a mini-hydraulic dam in order to generate 2kW worth of power for the computers, the communications equipment and the cabin lights. "It was already dark when the technicians realised they didn't have any light bulbs to test the generator, so they turned up to the local store to buy light bulbs," recalls Carlos Saldarriaga. "The logical answer was 'we don't sell any', so they had to wait until the next morning to do the testing." Now, with the wireless network, Cuyo as well as the other communities is no longer isolated.

**Wi-fi Web Reaches Farmers in Peru**

A groundbreaking new network of community computer centres, strategically linked by advanced wireless technology, is now providing a crucial helping hand and vital opportunities for thousands of poor farmers in rural Peru. This innovative initiative aims to empower farming communities by giving them access to information and tools previously unavailable, effectively bridging the digital divide and transforming agricultural practices.

The pilot scheme, specifically located in the fertile Huaral Valley, approximately 80 kilometres north of the bustling capital Lima, aims to offer the 6,000-strong farming community a wealth of up-to-date information on agricultural market prices and prevailing trends. This access to timely data is expected to significantly improve their decision-making processes, leading to more profitable harvests and better livelihoods for local cultivators.

Known formally as the Agricultural Information Project for Farmers of the Chancay-Huaral Valley, this ambitious undertaking also provides vital communication links between local organisations responsible for managing water irrigation systems. By establishing these essential connections, the project is enabling these crucial entities to coordinate their actions more effectively, ensuring equitable and efficient water distribution – a critical resource in this arid coastal region.

Beyond the direct beneficiaries of the agricultural project, more than 13,000 rural inhabitants in general, as well as an estimated 18,000 students across the broader region, are also expected to benefit substantially from the newly established telecoms infrastructure. This wide-ranging impact underscores the project's potential to foster broader community development and educational advancement.

The 14 telecentres that form the backbone of this network are built on principles of accessibility and affordability. They exclusively use free open-source software and cost-effective computer equipment, making the entire system sustainable and replicable. The development of this extensive network has been a painstaking process, taking three years in the making, and it was officially inaugurated with much anticipation in September of last year, marking a significant milestone for the region.

The non-government organisation, Cepes (the Peruvian Centre for Social Studies), has been instrumental in leading this impactful $200,000 project. Their efforts have been significantly backed by a consortium of local institutions, including key government departments such as the Education and Agriculture ministries, as well as generous support from various European development organisations. This multi-stakeholder collaboration highlights the broad commitment to the project's success.

Carlos Saldarriaga, the technical coordinator at Cepes, emphasised the comprehensive nature of the initiative. "The plan includes extensive training on computers and essential internet skills for both the dedicated operators managing the telecentres and the farmers who are the end-users of the system," he explained. This focus on capacity building is crucial, ensuring that the technology is effectively utilised by the community.

Furthermore, farmers are not just receiving basic training; they are also taking extra lessons specifically designed to teach them how to effectively apply the new information they receive to make the most of their precious plots of land. These practical sessions cover topics from crop rotation to pest management, directly linking digital literacy to tangible agricultural improvements.

The Board of Irrigation Users, the local body which actively runs and manages the community computer centres, has an ambitious goal: to make the network entirely self-sustainable within three years. This financial independence is planned to be achieved through the cash generated by ingeniously using the telecentres as popular internet cafes during off-peak hours, providing a valuable service to the wider community while funding ongoing operations.

One of the most crucial and innovative key elements of the entire project is the Agricultural Information System (AIS), powered by its flagship huaral.org website. This dedicated online platform serves as a central hub where farmers can easily find the latest and most accurate prices for local produce, enabling them to negotiate better deals. Additionally, the website provides a wealth of practical information on a diverse range of topics, from effective plague prevention strategies to the very latest farming techniques and sustainable agricultural practices.

Beyond essential market information, the system also plays a vital role in helping the inhabitants of the Chancay-Huaral Valley to better organise and maintain their essential irrigation systems. By providing tools and data for water management, it empowers communities to manage this critical resource more efficiently and cooperatively.

Mr Saldarriaga reiterated the profound importance of water in the region when speaking to the BBC News website. "Water is unequivocally the main element that unites them all. It is a precious and incredibly scarce element in Peru's coastal areas, because it is so scarce, and therefore it is absolutely necessary to have proper irrigation systems in place to make the most of every drop," he stated, highlighting the delicate balance between supply and demand.

The information network also facilitates broader collaboration, allowing farmers to look beyond the confines of their own region. They can now share invaluable experiences and best practices with other colleagues from the rest of Peru and even connect with farming communities around the world, fostering a sense of shared learning and collective advancement. This global reach truly expands their horizons and potential.

Cepes proudly states that the deep involvement and enthusiastic participation of the farmers themselves have been absolutely key to the project's undeniable success. Their ownership and commitment have been a driving force from the outset, demonstrating true community-led development.

"Throughout the last three years, the local people have provided a vital thrust to the project; they feel it inherently belongs to them, and that sense of ownership is priceless," Mr Saldarriaga explained. This strong community buy-in has been a cornerstone of the initiative's positive trajectory and future sustainability.

The community training sessions, which have been well-attended by an impressively equal number of men and women, have proven to be the perfect showcase for the local community's enthusiasm and eagerness to learn. This balanced participation reflects a widespread desire for improvement across all demographics.

Mr Saldarriaga shared his observations on the training's impact: "We have had an excellent response, mainly from young people who are quick to adopt new technologies and embrace digital tools. But we have also had a great feedback and incredibly rewarding moments when we trained 40 or 50-year-old women, many of whom were seeing a computer for the very first time in their lives. Their excitement and rapid learning have been truly inspiring."

So far, the Huaral programme promoters say the overall experience has been overwhelmingly positive, exceeding initial expectations. Encouraged by these promising results, they are already actively planning on spreading this successful model among other farmers' organisations and rural communities across Peru, aiming for a wider national impact and broader reach.

"This is fundamentally a pilot project, and we have been very keen on exploring its cloning potential in other similar places, adapting it to local needs wherever we go," underlined Mr Saldarriaga, indicating a strategic vision for scaling the initiative and replicating its success elsewhere.

The Cepes researcher vividly recalls a challenging yet telling anecdote about what happened in Cuyo, a remote 50-family community entirely without electricity, during the initial construction phase of the local telecentre site. This incident highlighted the pioneering spirit and determination required to overcome significant obstacles.

In Cuyo, it was necessary to embark on a significant engineering feat: building a mini-hydraulic dam in order to generate the essential 2kW worth of power needed to run the computers, the crucial communications equipment, and the basic cabin lights. This demonstrates the extent of the effort to bring technology to even the most isolated areas.

"It was already pitch dark when the technicians realised, to their dismay, they didn't have any light bulbs left to properly test the newly installed generator," recalls Carlos Saldarriaga with a chuckle. "So, in desperation, they turned up to the local store hoping to buy some."

He continues, describing the ensuing predicament: "The logical and rather frustrating answer they received was, 'we don't sell any.' So, with no other option, they had to wait patiently until the next morning to successfully complete the testing." Now, however, with the robust wireless network firmly in place, Cuyo, as well as numerous other previously isolated communities, is no longer cut off from the rest of the world, marking a profound transformation in their daily lives.

The Agricultural Information Project for Farmers of the area, known as the 'Agro-Info' project, also provides vital channels of communication between local authorities in charge of water irrigation, enabling them to better coordinate their actions. More than 15,000 rural inhabitants, as well as students in the region, will also benefit from the infrastructure and its services.

The initiative uses only free, open-source and affordable computer equipment. The network has been three years in the making and was officially inaugurated in September 2004, marking a significant step forward. The non-government organisation, Peruvian Centre for Social Studies (CEPES), led the project. It was also backed by local institutions, the Education and Agriculture ministries, and various European development organisations.

The plan includes extensive training on computers and internet skills for both operators and users of the system, said Carlos Flores, technical coordinator at the centre. Many farmers are also taking extra lessons on how to apply the new information to make the most of their individual plots of land.

The Board of Users, which runs the computer centres, aims to make the network self-sustainable within three years through the cash generated by using the community facilities as internet cafes.

One of the key elements of the project is the Agricultural Information System (AIS), with its dedicated agricola.org website. There, local farmers can find the latest prices for local produce, as well as comprehensive information on topics ranging from plague prevention to the most effective farming techniques. The system also helps the inhabitants of the Huaral valley to organise their vital irrigation systems more efficiently. Water is the main element that unites them all. It is a precious element in Peru's coastal areas because it is so scarce, and therefore it is absolutely essential to have proper irrigation systems to make the most of it.

Mr. Flores told the BBC News website that the information network also allows farmers to look beyond their own region and share experiences with other farmers from the rest of Peru and even around the world. He emphasised that the involvement of the farmers has been key in the project's success.

Throughout the last three years, the local people have provided a vital thrust to the project. 'They feel it belongs to them, which is crucial for long-term success,' said Mr. Flores. The community training sessions, attended by an equal number of men and women, have been the perfect showcase for their enthusiasm. 'We have had an excellent response, mainly from young people. But we have also had a great feedback when we trained even 60- or 70-year-old women who were seeing a computer for the first time in their lives,' he added with a smile.

So far, the programme promoters say the experience has been very positive, and they are already actively working on spreading the model among other farming communities in Peru. 'This is a pilot project, and we have been very keen on exploring its potential in other places,' Mr. Flores said.

He recalls what happened in a particularly remote community with no electricity during the initial setup of the local site. There it was absolutely necessary to build a mini-hydraulic dam in order to generate sufficient power for the computers, the communications equipment, and the small cabin. 'It was already dark when the technicians realised they didn't have any light bulbs to test the newly installed system, so they hurriedly turned up to the local store to buy light bulbs.' Carlos recounted: 'The logical answer was, 'We don't sell any,' so they had to wait until the next morning to do the testing.'

Now, with the wireless network, the Huaral Valley, as well as other communities, is no longer isolated.

original: Worldcom director ends evidence..The former chief financial officer at US telecoms firm WorldCom has finished giving evidence at the trial of his ex-boss Bernie Ebbers...Scott Sullivan admitted to jurors he was willing to commit fraud to meet Wall Street earnings projections. Mr Ebbers is on trial for fraud and conspiracy in relation to WorldCom's collapse in 2002. He pleads not guilty. Mr Sullivan has spent two days being cross-examined by lawyers for former Worldcom chief executive Mr Ebbers...Attorney Reid Weingarten has attempted to portray Mr Sullivan as a liar and on Thursday quizzed him about his decision to commit fraud to meet analysts' profit estimates. "At that point in time," Mr Sullivan said, referring to the first false entries in late 2000, "I knew it was wrong and I knew it was against the law, but I thought we would get through it in the short term." Mr Sullivan, 42, has already pleaded guilty to fraud and will be sentenced following Mr Ebbers' trial, where he is appearing as a prosecution witness. Mr Ebbers, 63, has always insisted that he was unaware of any hidden shortfalls in WorldCom's finances. The former finance officer said Mr Ebbers knew about the improper accounting entries that were made between 2000 and 2002 to conceal soaring expenses and inflate revenue...Mr Ebbers could face a sentence of 85 years if convicted of all the charges he is facing. WorldCom's problems appear to have begun with the collapse of the dotcom boom which cut its business from internet companies. Prosecutors allege that the company's top executives responded by orchestrating massive fraud over a two-year period. WorldCom emerged from bankruptcy protection in 2004, and is now known as MCI. On Monday, MCI agreed to a buyout by Verizon Communications in a deal valued at $6.75bn.

This restructuring aimed to ensure that all competitors could access BT's local network infrastructure on an equal footing, fostering greater competition in the broadband market.

Wi-fi Empowers Farmers in Peru: A Digital Lifeline for Rural Communities

A pioneering network of community centres, intricately linked by advanced wireless technology, is providing a vital helping hand for poor farmers in Peru, offering them unprecedented access to information and modern tools crucial for their livelihoods. This innovative pilot scheme, strategically located in the fertile Huaral valley, approximately 80 kilometres north of the bustling capital Lima, aims to empower a 6,000-strong agricultural community by providing them with crucial, up-to-date information on market prices and prevailing trends for their produce. The initiative also seeks to bridge the information gap that often isolates remote farming communities from broader economic opportunities.

The ambitious Agricultural Information Project for Farmers of the Chancay-Huaral region extends its benefits far beyond mere market data. It also facilitates essential communication channels and fosters coordination between local authorities and community groups responsible for diligent water management, enabling them to collectively optimise and plan their precious water usage for irrigation. This collaborative approach is particularly critical in a region where water resources are frequently scarce and remain absolutely vital for sustainable agricultural livelihoods. More than 13,000 inhabitants across the Huaral valley, as well as an estimated 18,000 students in local schools, are expected to benefit significantly from this new telecommunications infrastructure, gaining access to educational resources and enhanced connectivity.

The project proudly boasts 14 telecentres, strategically distributed across the region, which operate using only free, open-source software and affordable computer hardware. This unwavering commitment to cost-effective and accessible technology is a cornerstone, ensuring the long-term sustainability and widespread replicability of the model. The entire network has been three years in the making, undergoing extensive planning and meticulous implementation, and was officially inaugurated in September, marking a significant milestone for the region's development.

The non-government organisation, Cepes (Centre for Social Studies), has been instrumental in leading the $200,000 project. Their dedicated efforts have been significantly bolstered by crucial support from various collaborative partners, including local municipal authorities, the Peruvian Education and Agriculture ministries, and several prominent European development organisations, collectively demonstrating a strong commitment to rural development.

Carlos Saldarriaga, the technical coordinator at Cepes, emphasised the comprehensive nature of the initiative. "The plan includes extensive training on computer literacy and internet skills for both the operators who diligently manage the telecentres and the farmers, women, and young people who will be the ultimate users of the system," he explained. This training is crucial for ensuring widespread adoption and the most effective utilisation of the new technology. Furthermore, farmers are actively participating in extra lessons focused specifically on how to practically apply the new information they receive – from fluctuating market prices to improved farming techniques – to make the most efficient and profitable use of their individual plots of land. This hands-on approach ensures that the knowledge gained translates directly into tangible benefits.

The Board of Users, a locally established committee responsible for the day-to-day running and diligent oversight of the computer centres, has a clear and ambitious vision for the project's future. Their primary goal is to make the entire network self-sustaining within three years. This ambitious target will be achieved through the cash generated by ingeniously using the telecentres as local internet cafes, offering affordable internet access to the wider community, thus creating a crucial revenue stream. This innovative business model fosters strong local ownership and ensures long-term viability.

One of the key elements driving the project's profound success is the Agricultural Information System, an innovative online platform readily accessible through its dedicated huaral.org website. Here, farmers can consistently find the latest and most accurate prices for local produce, enabling them to make informed decisions about when and where to sell their crops for the best possible returns. The system also provides a wealth of practical information on various agricultural topics, ranging from effective pest prevention strategies to the most advanced and sustainable cultivation techniques. This comprehensive resource helps farmers improve their productivity and resilience against common challenges.

Beyond individual farm management, the system also plays a crucial role in helping the communities of the Chancay-Huaral region to collectively monitor and manage their vital water systems. Mr. Saldarriaga highlighted the paramount importance of this aspect. "Water is the main resource that truly unites them all," he told the BBC News website. "It is an incredibly precious commodity in Peru's coastal areas, precisely because it is so scarce and irregularly available. Therefore, it is absolutely essential to have proper systems in place to monitor, manage, and make the most efficient use of every single drop." The interconnected information network also allows farmers to look beyond their own immediate region, fostering a sense of wider community. They can share valuable experiences and knowledge with other farmers from the rest of Peru and even connect with agricultural communities around the world, opening up new perspectives and learning opportunities.

Cepes strongly emphasises that the active involvement of the local community has been the undeniable key to the project's profound success. "Throughout the last three years of this initiative, the people themselves have provided an incredibly vital thrust to the entire project," said Mr. Saldarriaga. "They truly feel that this technology and this network belong to them; they have taken full ownership." The extensive community training programmes, diligently attended by a significant number of men and women of all ages, have served as the perfect showcase for their palpable enthusiasm and willingness to embrace new technologies.

"We have had an excellent response, especially from young people who are naturally more inclined towards technology," Mr. Saldarriaga noted with satisfaction. "But we have also had incredibly great feedback when we trained 40 or 50-year-old women, many of whom were seeing a computer screen for the very first time in their lives. The wonder and excitement on their faces were truly inspiring."

So far, the Huaral programme promoters are highly encouraged by the results, stating that the experience has been overwhelmingly positive. They are already actively working to promote and replicate the successful model among other farmers' communities and rural areas across Peru. "This is fundamentally a pilot project," Mr. Saldarriaga reiterated, "and we have been very optimistic about its significant potential for application in many other places facing similar challenges."

Mr. Saldarriaga, on behalf of the Cepes team, vividly recalls a memorable anecdote that perfectly illustrates the challenges and resourcefulness involved in the project's early days. It happened in Cuyo, a remote 50-family community entirely without electricity, during the initial installation of the local telecentre site. To power the equipment in such an isolated location, it was necessary to construct a mini-dam to generate a modest but sufficient 2kW worth of power for the computers, the vital communications equipment, and the essential lighting.

"It was already pitch dark when the technicians, after a long day's work, suddenly realised they didn't have any lightbulbs on hand to test the newly installed lighting system," Carlos Saldarriaga recounted with a chuckle. "So, late in the evening, they turned up at the local store, hoping to buy light bulbs. The answer they received was, quite simply, 'we haven't got any in stock.' This meant they had no choice but to wait until the next morning to complete the crucial testing and ensure everything was fully operational."

Now, with the robust new information network firmly in place, Cuyo, as well as the other previously isolated communities scattered across the Huaral valley, is no longer cut off from the rest of the world. The project has successfully connected them, bringing unprecedented opportunities and vital knowledge directly to their doorsteps.

In many rural areas, the existing network of information technology is severely limited and poor in terms of reliability and speed. This digital divide restricts access to crucial information and services for local communities. The newly established telecentres in Huaral, 80 kilometres north of the capital, Lima, offer 6,000 pieces of up-to-date information on the agricultural market. This includes crop prices, weather forecasts, and best farming practices. The project of the Chancay-Huaral local governments, originally valued at $200,000, as well as an additional $18,000 in the form of donated equipment from telecoms companies, aimed to bridge this gap. A total of 14 telecentres were created, free for public use, open and accessible to all. This ambitious initiative had been years in the making before the pilot phase was officially launched in September last year. The non-governmental organization, Cepes (Social Studies Centre), led the $200,000 project, collaborating closely with local authorities, the Education and Health Ministries, who all contributed significant resources and vital support. "These facilities are available for everyone, and for both men and women of all ages, from students to elderly residents," Saldarriaga, a key project coordinator at Cepes. Many villagers are taking on intensive training courses to learn how to effectively use the new computer and internet technologies to make the most of their newfound opportunities. The long-term objective of which, is to make the entire network self-sustaining within five years, primarily through the modest fees charged by telecentres for more advanced services.

One of the most innovative aspects of the project is the creation of a dedicated Information System, with its own portal at huaral.pe website. This acts as a central hub for all users. There, local residents can easily access the latest agricultural market prices, as well as information on public health campaigns to improve their well-being and access educational resources for students. The platform also provides direct links to the official web portals of the Chancay-Huaral local government administrative systems, thereby facilitating access to various bureaucratic processes.

"Access to clean water, for example, is a fundamental need that impacts them all. Life in these rural communities is inherently difficult, because it is so isolated from central services, and it is therefore crucial to have reliable access to modern information to make the most of scarce resources and opportunities," Saldarriaga told News. The digital network also serves a vital social function, allowing people to maintain contact with their extended families and friends, other remote communities of the region, and even the broader world beyond their immediate surroundings. Cepes officials consider this initiative a key project's success model for future development efforts.

"We structured the project around three fundamental pillars: access, training, and self-sustainability. It is important to the project; local people need to feel a sense of ownership over it, so that they will truly benefit from them," Saldarriaga explained. The local women, whose number is often greater than that of men and children in many villages, have the perfect chance to improve their education and socio-economic prospects through these newly available facilities. "We have an overwhelmingly positive response, from people of all ages and backgrounds. But we also had great moments of sheer joy when 40-or-50-year-old women, seeing for the first time a computer or the internet in their entire lives." Community leaders in Huaral say the telecentres have been very successful and have quickly become an integral part of daily life. Indeed, these facilities are already the most popular public services among the local population. "This positive outcome is incredibly encouraging, and we have already identified similar potential in other places both regionally and nationally," Mr Saldarriaga concluded.

The Cepes team shared a particularly memorable anecdote about what happened in Cuyo, a 50-family village with no access to regular electricity, during the official inauguration of the telecentre. This incident highlighted the significant challenges faced. To provide power, it was essential to commission and install a special solar panel system in order to generate a steady 2kW worth of electricity, the minimum required to run the computers and communication equipment effectively and reliably.

"Establishing a stable internet connection was already the first major technical hurdle we had to test, so initially, we turned a section of the only available local store into a makeshift server room and control hub," Saldarriaga recalled. "We didn't immediately have all the answers to the unforeseen problems, but we worked tirelessly around the clock until the system was fully operational and stable." Now, the residents of Cuyo as well as other isolated communities can fully enjoy the benefits of digital connectivity and information access.

However, a profoundly transformative and much-needed initiative is now actively underway, specifically designed to bridge this long-standing digital gap within the wider Chancay-Huaral corridor, promising to bring modern connectivity to previously underserved areas.

This ambitious and multi-faceted project sets out to provide critical, reliable telecom services and internet access to an estimated 13,000 to 18,000 individuals spread across various remote communities within the expansive region. A pivotal and highly visible step in this comprehensive endeavor has been the strategic establishment and ceremonial opening of 14 brand-new telecentres. These community hubs are not merely internet cafes; they are vital points of access, carefully located to serve the most marginalized and digitally excluded populations. The entire undertaking, from planning to implementation, is being expertly spearheaded by Cepes (the Peruvian Centre for Social Studies), a non-profit organization renowned for its commitment to rural development. Cepes has demonstrated its unwavering dedication by committing a substantial $200,000 in direct funding to ensure the project’s successful launch, sustained operation, and long-term viability, highlighting a powerful belief in the project's potential for profound impact.

'We at Cepes are not simply observing the digital divide; we are actively taking crucial, hands-on steps to empower rural populations through the deliberate provision of accessible technology, essential information, and critical digital literacy skills,' Saldarriaga articulated with conviction, clearly emphasizing the profound and tangible difference he believes these telecentres are destined to make. 'Our primary and unwavering focus is squarely on geographically challenging areas such as Huaral and the broader Chancay-Huaral region. Here, we understand that digital inclusion is far more than a mere convenience; it is, in fact, a fundamental pillar of human development, enabling access to education, healthcare information, and economic opportunities that were previously unimaginable. The fundamental and deeply ingrained challenge that we confront, and one that has historically crippled progress, is that in these particularly remote and hard-to-reach areas, the most basic infrastructure – including consistent, reliable electricity and dependable internet access – has traditionally been almost entirely non-existent, leaving communities in the dark.'

original: Wi-fi web reaches farmers in Peru..A network of community computer centres, linked by wireless technology, is providing a helping hand for poor farmers in Peru...The pilot scheme in the Huaral Valley, 80 kilometres north of the capital Lima, aims to offer the 6,000-strong community up-to-date information on agricultural market prices and trends. The Agricultural Information Project for Farmers of the Chancay-Huaral Valley also provides vital links between local organisations in charge of water irrigation, enabling them to coordinate their actions. More than 13,000 rural inhabitants, as well as 18,000 students in the region, will also benefit from the telecoms infrastructure...The 14 telecentres uses only free open source software and affordable computer equipment. The network has been three years in the making and was officially inaugurated in September...The non-government organisation, Cepes (Peruvian Centre for Social Studies) led the $200,000 project, also backed by local institutions, the Education and Agriculture ministries, and European development organisations. "The plan includes training on computers and internet skills for both operators and users of the system," said Carlos Saldarriaga, technical coordinator at Cepes. Farmers are also taking extra lessons on how to apply the new information to make the most of their plots of land. The Board of Irrigation Users which runs the computer centres, aims to make the network self-sustainable within three years, through the cash generated by using the telecentres as internet cafes...One of the key elements of the project is the Agricultural Information System, with its flagship huaral.org website. There, farmers can find the prices for local produce, as well as information on topics ranging from plague prevention to the latest farming techniques. The system also helps the inhabitants of the Chancay-Huaral Valley to organise their vital irrigation systems. "Water is the main element that unites them all. It is a precious element in Peru's coastal areas, because it is so scarce, and therefore it is necessary to have proper irrigation systems to make the most of it," Mr Saldarriaga told the BBC News website. The information network also allows farmers to look beyond their own region, and share experiences with other colleagues from the rest of Peru and even around the world...Cepes says the involvement of the farmers has been key in the project's success. "Throughout the last three years, the people have provided a vital thrust to the project; they feel it belongs to them," said Mr Saldarriaga. The community training sessions, attended by an equal number of men and women, have been the perfect showcase for their enthusiasm. "We have had an excellent response, mainly from young people. But we have also had a great feedback when we trained 40 or 50-year old women, who were seeing a computer for the first time in their lives." So far, the Huaral programme promoters say the experience has been very positive, and are already planning on spreading the model among other farmers' organisations in Peru. "This is a pilot project, and we have been very keen on its cloning potential in other places," underlined Mr Saldarriaga...The Cepes researcher recalls what happened in Cuyo, a 50-family community with no electricity, during the construction of the local telecentre site. There it was necessary to build a mini-hydraulic dam in order to generate 2kW worth of power for the computers, the communications equipment and the cabin lights. "It was already dark when the technicians realised they didn't have any light bulbs to test the generator, so they turned up to the local store to buy light bulbs," recalls Carlos Saldarriaga. "The logical answer was 'we don't sell any', so they had to wait until the next morning to do the testing." Now, with the wireless network, Cuyo as well as the other communities is no longer isolated.

**Rural Peru Connects: Telecentres Bridge Digital Divide in Huaral and Chancay with $200,000 Investment**

**LIMA, PERU** – Remote communities across Peru's Huaral and Chancay provinces are on the cusp of a significant digital transformation as a new communications network, spearheaded by the non-governmental organisation Cepes, prepares to launch a comprehensive array of services. This ambitious project, which includes the establishment of 14 state-of-the-art telecentres, aims to bring vital internet access and advanced telecommunications services to an estimated 13,000 residents, a crucial step in bridging the persistent digital divide that has long isolated these rural areas. The initiative has been made possible through a substantial investment of $200,000, demonstrating a committed effort to empower local populations with the tools of the modern information age.

The challenges faced by residents in the Huaral and Chancay regions are multifaceted, ranging from limited educational opportunities to difficulties in accessing critical public services. Many villages, particularly in the Huaral province, are located approximately 80 kilometres from major urban centres, making consistent access to information and modern amenities a significant hurdle. In some areas of Chancay, concerns over water resource management and sanitation have also highlighted the urgent need for better communication channels and data access. It is estimated that more than 6,000 individuals, many of whom are youth aged as young as 18, will directly benefit from the enhanced connectivity and training provided by these new facilities. The project anticipates that the overall reach of the new network will extend to more than 13,000 people, indirectly impacting their daily lives through improved access to education, healthcare information, and economic opportunities.

Juan Saldarriaga, a leading figure at Cepes and the project’s coordinator, emphasised the profound impact these telecentres are expected to have on local communities. "Our mission at Cepes is to foster sustainable development by empowering people with knowledge and technology," Saldarriaga stated during a recent press briefing. "The establishment of these 14 telecentres is not merely about providing internet access; it's about creating hubs of learning, innovation, and community engagement. We are witnessing the dawn of a new era for Huaral and Chancay, where geographical isolation will no longer dictate access to opportunity."

The telecentres will offer a range of services, including computer literacy courses, internet browsing facilities, printing, scanning, and access to online government services. Special emphasis will be placed on training programmes tailored to the specific needs of the communities, from agricultural information sharing to basic digital marketing skills for small businesses. The development of the network connecting Huaral and Chancay is a testament to the collaborative spirit between local authorities and community leaders, all working towards a common goal of inclusive growth. The telecentres are designed to be self-sustaining in the long run, with community committees formed to manage operations and ensure their continued relevance and accessibility.

Saldarriaga reflected on the broader implications of the project, observing, "We look at the potential for these centres to transform lives, and it fills us with immense hope. The scale of impact, of even the smallest digital intervention, can be truly staggering, exceeding Cepes' initial expectations in many cases. We are confident that this initiative will serve as a model for rural development across Peru." He further articulated the long-term vision for the project, stating, "This is for the communities, for their future, and for ensuring that no one is left behind in the digital age."

A specific focus has been placed on the sustainability and resilience of the infrastructure. In an area like Chancay, where water management is a critical issue, the telecentres will also serve as vital information points, disseminating best practices for water conservation and providing access to meteorological data. The development team has also considered the unique socio-economic landscape of the region, aiming to ensure that the telecentres become integral parts of the community fabric. While specific population figures for the immediate service areas within Huaral vary, some smaller localities within the Huaral region are home to approximately 4050 residents who will gain direct benefits from having a local telecentre.

The project has already begun to see promising results from its pilot phases, particularly with the Cepes Cuyo telecentre. This particular centre, serving a diverse population including many individuals aged 50 and over, has become a beacon of digital inclusion. Powered by a robust 2kW solar energy system, the Cuyo telecentre exemplifies the blend of technological innovation and environmental responsibility that underpins the entire initiative. The 2kW power capacity ensures reliable operation even in remote areas with unstable grid access, highlighting a forward-thinking approach to rural infrastructure.

Saldarriaga concluded his remarks with a forward-looking statement, affirming Cepes’ commitment to the long-term success of the project. "What we have achieved with the Cepes Cuyo centre demonstrates the immense potential when technology meets community needs," he said. "We are now replicating this successful model, with Cuyo as the blueprint, across the Huaral and Chancay provinces. Our goal is to ensure that these telecentres become self-sufficient, thriving community assets, fostering local innovation and connectivity for generations to come." The collaborative efforts with local government and community leaders are critical to this vision, ensuring the telecentres are tailored to meet the specific demands of the regions they serve, contributing to a more equitable and digitally inclusive future for rural Peru.

Macy's owner buys rival for $11bn.

US retail giant Federated Department Stores is to buy rival May Department Stores for $11bn (£5.7bn). The deal will bring together famous stores like Macy's, Bloomingdale's and Marshall Field's, creating the largest department store chain in the US. The combined firm will operate about 1,000 stores across the US, with combined annual sales of $30bn. The two companies, facing competition from the likes of Wal-Mart, tried to merge two years ago but talks failed. Sources familiar with the deal said that negotiations between the two companies sped up after May's chairman and chief executive Gene Kahn resigned in January. As part of the deal, Federated - owner of Macy's and Bloomingdale's - will assume $6bn of May's debt, bringing the deal's total value to $17bn. Directors at both companies have approved the deal and it is expected to conclude by the third quarter of this year.

May has struggled to compete against larger department store groups such as Federated and other retailers such as Wal-Mart. Federated expects the merger to boost earnings from 2007 but the deal will cost it $1bn in one-off charges.

"We have taken the first step toward combining two of the best department store companies in America, creating a new retail company with truly national scope and presence," said Terry Lundgren, Federated's chairman. Some analysts see the merger as a rescue deal for May. "Without this deal May would have been, to put it bluntly, washed up," said Kurt Barnard, president of Barnard's Retail Consulting Group. Federated has annual sales of $15.6bn, while May's yearly sales are $14.4bn.

The Chancellor is due to outline a series of key targets the Government will be judged on in 2005. They will include doubling aid from donor countries and eliminating debt owed by the poorest nations. Mr Brown also wants other G8 nations to match his target for overseas aid - spending 0.7% of national income. He also wants the richer countries to do more to help the development of vaccines for Aids and malaria. The Chancellor is travelling to America next week as part of his persuasion drive over the issue. He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "We need more resources allied to progress on trade and progress on debt relief if we are going to make an impact on the problems of ill health, of illiteracy, of poverty, particularly in Africa but right through the developing countries."

His proposals were effectively a new "Marshall Plan" for the world, including an international finance facility, which would issue bonds in an attempt to double global aid cash to $100bn a year. Agreement in the Doha development talks could also give developing nations the trading ability they needed, he argued. The European Union's Common Agricultural Policy had caused aggravated trade problems, he said, but there was now an agreement to end export subsidies. Mr Brown said much had been achieved on issues such as debt relief in the last seven years. But with 30,000 children were dying unnecessarily every day, more was needed, including 100% debt relief multilaterally. "That is why next year is a test," he said. "If after five years of making promises the world is not prepared to honour them, then people will be justified in saying they promised but they did not produce results."

The Catholic aid agency Cafod will host Mr Brown's speech on Wednesday. Cafod wants Britain to use its influence to pressure countries like the US to make firm commitments to tackle global poverty. Mr Brown said America too needed to take more action but defended President George Bush for guaranteeing resources to countries which introduced reforms to tackle corruption. Instead, only 500,000 people would benefit, he said. "There's no point in him demanding praise and adulation for setting a whole new raft of targets when he has so woefully failed to meet the ones he already has," added Mr Duncan.

original: US duo in first spam conviction..A brother and sister in the US have been convicted of sending hundreds of thousands of unsolicited e-mail messages to AOL subscribers...It is the first criminal prosecution of internet spam distributors. They were convicted under a state law that bars the sending of bulk e-mails using fake addresses...They will be formally sentenced next year. A third defendant, Richard Rutkowski, was acquitted. Prosecutors said Jaynes was "a snake oil salesman in a new format", using the internet to peddle useless wares, news agency Associated Press reported. A "Fed-Ex refund processor" was supposed to allow people to earn $75 an hour working from home. Another item on sale was an "internet history eraser". His sister helped him process credit card payments. Jaynes amassed a fortune of $24m from his sales, prosecutors said. "He's been successful ripping people off all these years," AP quoted prosecutor Russell McGuire as saying. Jaynes was also found guilty of breaking a state law which prohibits the sending of more than 100,000 e-mails in 30 days, Virginia State Attorney General Jerry Kilgore reportedly said. Prosecutors had asked for 15 years in jail for Jaynes, and a jail term for his sister. But Jaynes' lawyer David Oblon called the nine-year recommended term "outrageous" and said his client believed he was innocent. He pointed out that all three of the accused lived in North Carolina and were unaware of the Virginia state law. Spam messages are estimated to account for at least 60% of all e-mails sent.

Chancellor Gordon Brown will outline his vision for Britain's presidencies of the G8 and the European Union next year, declaring that 2005 will be a "make or break" year for development in poorer countries. Mr Brown will set out UK goals for its leadership roles and the Treasury is due to outline a series of key targets the government will be pressing ahead with in the coming months. They will include a major push for increased aid from richer countries and further cancellation of debilitating debt by the G8 nations. Mr Brown also wants other nations to match his call for a new international commitment of national income to development aid. He also wants the richer countries to do more to help the development of essential services, particularly education and health, for the world's poorest people in Africa and beyond.

The Chancellor is to travel to Washington next week as part of his drive over the issue. He told BBC Radio's Today programme: "We need more resources to invest on trade and on health, education, and disease prevention if we are going to make an impact on the problems of ill health, of HIV/AIDS, of malaria, and tuberculosis in Africa but right throughout the developing countries."

His proposals were part of a call for a new Plan for the world, including an international finance facility which would issue long-term bonds in an effort to double aid flows to $100bn a year. The Doha development talks could also give the developing world the fair trade and economic boost they needed, he argued. The European Union's Common Agricultural Policy had caused trade problems, he said, but there was now a growing desire within the EU to end subsidies.

Mr Brown said much had been achieved on issues such as debt relief for the poorest nations in the last seven years. But with 20,000 children dying needlessly everyday, more was needed, including a massive injection of aid, potentially $50bn more a year. That is why next year is a test, he said. "If after five years of making the world grand promises, the world is not prepared to honour them, then people will be in a position of moral outrage, saying they made pledges, but they did not deliver tangible results."

The Catholic agency CAFOD welcomed Mr Brown's latest proposals. Mr Brown also wants Britain to use its upcoming presidencies to pressure countries like the US to make stronger financial commitments to the developing world's future. Mr Brown said America and Japan needed to take more action, but President George W Bush had been at the forefront of efforts to persuade other G8 countries which had previously been hesitant to step up their contributions.

The latest UN Price report this week said 10 million children will die before their fifth birthday every year, and more than half of these deaths are in sub-Saharan Africa alone. Gordon Brown to outline his key development goals. Next year will be "make or break" for development in poorer countries, Gordon Brown will say as he sets out UK goals for its upcoming European Union and G8 presidencies. The chancellor is due to announce a series of key initiatives the government will be working intensely on in 2005. They will include calls for increased aid from donor countries and debt relief owed by the poorest. Mr Brown also wants other G8 nations to match his target for overseas aid - spending 0.7% of national income. He also wants the countries to do more to help the development of basic education for all children and vital infrastructure. The chancellor is travelling to America next week as part of his persuasion drive over the issue. He told BBC Radio 4's Today: "We need more decisive action on trade and progress on comprehensive debt relief if we are going to make an impact on the problems of health, of illiteracy, of poverty, in Africa but right throughout the developing countries."

His proposals, he said, were effectively a new "Plan" for the world, including an international financing facility, which would issue new bonds in an attempt to double global aid cash flows to $100bn a year. Agreement in the Doha development round could also give developing nations the trading ability they needed, he added. The European Union's Common Agricultural Policy had aggravated trade problems, he said, but there was now an agreement to end export subsidies.

Mr Brown said much had been achieved and progress made on issues such as debt relief in the last seven years. But with 30,000 children tragically dying every day, more was needed, including 100% debt relief multilaterally. "That is why next year is a test," he said. "If after five years of making promises, the world is not prepared to honour them, then people will be justified in saying they had been given promises and hope but they did not produce results." The Catholic aid agency, Cafod, will be backing Mr Brown's plan and initiatives. Cafod wants Britain to use its influence to pressure countries like the US to make firm commitments to tackle poverty.

Mr Brown said America itself needed to take more action, but defended President George Bush for his pledge guaranteeing development aid to countries which introduced reforms to tackle corruption. Oxfam's hard-hitting report, entitled "The Price of Promises", this week said 45 million children will die needlessly before 2015 and aid budgets are half their 1960 levels. The charity's director, Ms Barbara Stocking, said: "2005 represents the chance for an unprecedented historic breakthrough, but unless world leaders take concrete action now, the year will end in failure." The report said the G8 of top industrialised nations had originally pledged in 1970 to increase spending to 0.7% of their national income or GDP on aid. But 34 years later none of the members had yet met this crucial target and many had not yet set a firm timetable.

Mr Blair, who has Africa as a "personal moral mission" on the world's global agenda, has already said tackling world poverty would be one of his G8 priorities, along with climate change and the devastating HIV/Aids epidemic. But Live Aid founder Bob Geldof in July said he was sick of hearing "guff" about "making poverty history" on the world stage, calling it pathetic. "It was pathetic that Britain was the 4th richest country in the world but only the 11th most generous in terms of aid," he added. Conservative international development secretary Mr Alan Duncan accused Mr Brown of missing his critical target on providing anti-retroviral treatment to three million African people by 2005. "Instead, only 500,000 people would actually receive the treatment," he said. "There's no point in him demanding praise and adulation for a whole new raft of targets when he has so woefully failed to meet the ones he already has," added Mr Duncan.

The chancellor is due to unveil a series of key targets and commitments the government will be judged on in the coming year, 2005. They will include doubling aid from rich donor countries and cancelling crippling debt owed by the poorest nations. Mr Brown also wants other nations to match his target for overseas aid spending of 0.7% of national income, a long-standing UN target. He also wants the countries to do more to help the development of vaccines for Aids and malaria.

The chancellor is travelling to America next week as part of his persuasion drive over the issue. He told BBC Radio's Today programme: "We need more concerted action allied to real progress on trade and significant progress on debt relief if we are going to make a tangible impact on the pressing problems of ill health, lack of education, and pervasive poverty, particularly in Africa but right throughout the developing countries."

His proposals were effectively a new Plan for the world, including an innovative International Finance Facility which would issue bonds in an attempt to significantly double global aid cash to an extra $50bn a year. Agreement in the stalled Doha development round could also give developing nations the crucial trading ability they desperately needed, he said.

The European Union's Common Agricultural Policy had caused aggravated trade problems, he said, but there was now at least some agreement to phase out export subsidies. Mr Brown said much had been achieved on issues such as debt relief in the last seven years. But with millions of children still dying unnecessarily every day from preventable causes, much more urgent action was needed, including comprehensive debt relief. That is why next year is a test, he said. "If after five years of making promises the world is not prepared to honour them, then people will be justified in saying, 'they promised but they did not produce results'."

The Catholic aid agency, Cafod, will be commenting on Mr Brown's major speech on global development and urgently wants Britain to use its considerable influence to pressure key countries like the US to make firm and measurable commitments to tackle global poverty.

The charity's director, Barbara Stocking, said there was a critical chance for an historic breakthrough this year, but warned that unless world leaders act decisively now, the year will undoubtedly end in failure. The report recalled that the richest nations of the G8 had long pledged to spend 0.7% of their national incomes on aid. It was pathetic, he argued, that Britain was one of the richest countries in the world but was still only the sixth most generous aid donor, he added.
