Mr Brown also used this opportunity to make his case for increased financial aid and support from other wealthy nations. He is particularly keen that these richer countries commit more effectively to the goals of development, focusing especially on issues such as direct aid provision and comprehensive debt relief. He articulated this vision prominently this week as part of his broader political drive over the next year. Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, he emphatically stated: 'We urgently need to make substantial and tangible progress on both international trade policies and development aid if we are truly to make a discernible and lasting impact on the chronic problems of health, access to education, and extreme poverty in Africa and indeed throughout the entire developing world.'

At the heart of his strategy, Mr Brown's comprehensive proposals outlined a 'Plan for the developing world'. This plan included establishing an innovative international finance facility. This mechanism would issue long-term bonds in global financial markets, front-loading aid and providing immediate and substantial funding. He projected this would amount to billions of dollars a year in direct development assistance. He also highlighted that such a facility could help tackle unfair agricultural subsidies that hinder progress in developing nations. He criticised the European Union's Common Agricultural Policy and wider global trade problems as significant obstacles. However, he expressed cautious optimism, noting a greater international willingness to tackle these long-standing issues. Mr Brown underscored that much had already been achieved on critical issues such as widespread debt relief over the last seven years. He cited encouraging statistics, noting that with five million fewer children now dying every year globally, tangible progress was being made, but stressed that much more was urgently needed. He stated that 'this year is a pivotal test of the world's collective commitment to alleviating poverty'. He added: 'If five million children continuing to die every year is not perceived as a profound human tragedy, then people will be fully justified in saying our collective efforts did not produce the necessary results.' The United Kingdom, under Mr Brown's leadership, will use its upcoming G8 presidency to exert significant pressure on major industrialised countries, particularly nations like the United States, to make far greater commitments to international aid. He asserted that America needed to show more decisive action. President George W Bush has previously faced criticism for not matching the UK's commitment to spend 0.7% of its GDP on aid to developing countries. Highlighting the urgency, the UN estimates that more than 30,000 children will tragically die this very week before any comprehensive global deal on aid and trade is successfully reached. The UN's director of development stated there was a critical chance for a new global deal now, but cautioned that the window of opportunity would soon close.

Furthermore, an accompanying report stated that, on top of unfulfilled aid promises, there still existed 'an iron curtain of trade barriers' which severely hampered the economic progress of developing nations. But years later, despite numerous pledges, many G8 member states have demonstrably not delivered on their previous commitments to increase aid and reduce trade barriers. This consistent failure has profoundly frustrated campaigners. This situation has notably led Mr Bob Geldof, the renowned musician and campaigner on world poverty, to publicly lambast the developed nations, particularly the G8 leaders, for their perceived inaction. He acknowledged that the G8 leaders were discussing a significant £50bn increase in overall aid, a development he cautiously welcomed. However, he qualified this by pointing out that only a handful of the most developed nations have actually followed through and added to their international development budgets. He highlighted a particularly stark example, stating that three million people in Africa are currently missing out on vital anti-HIV treatment. He lamented that, instead of reaching this crucial number, current projections indicate that only one million people would realistically receive this life-saving treatment. In a scathing critique, Mr Geldof concluded: 'There's no point in them promising to create a whole new generation of commitments when they have demonstrably not met the fundamental ones they have already made.' This statement underscored the deep skepticism among many aid advocates regarding the sincerity of the world's most powerful nations.

The United Kingdom is preparing to take on the rotating presidencies of both the G8 group of leading industrial nations and the European Union this year. These dual roles will place a significant spotlight on Britain's foreign policy agenda, particularly concerning international development and aid. Prime Minister Tony Blair has repeatedly stressed that these presidencies offer a unique opportunity to push for substantial global change, with a particular focus on alleviating poverty and tackling the HIV/AIDS pandemic in Africa. Discussions surrounding what these crucial presidencies will specifically include have been ongoing for months, generating considerable debate among policymakers and aid organisations. The government has indicated its unwavering commitment to ensuring that its efforts will include ambitious targets, notably pushing for all developed nations to meet the long-standing United Nations target of allocating 0.7% of their Gross National Income to overseas development assistance. Britain itself wants to do its part, and indeed to lead by example, in this collective global endeavour.

Speaking earlier today on BBC Radio 4's flagship 'Today' programme, a senior government minister outlined the scope of the challenges ahead. He articulated a stark vision of the issues confronting the world's poorest nations, stating emphatically: 'We are facing monumental challenges across the developing world. There is more illiteracy than ever before, compounding cycles of poverty, and a rising tide of disease that threatens to overwhelm fragile health systems. These are not merely statistics; they represent millions of shattered lives and unfulfilled potentials. The scale of the problem demands an urgent and concerted global response from all developed nations.'

For the United Kingdom to truly maximise its impact and drive meaningful progress during its presidencies, collaboration at a European level will be absolutely essential. To that end, discussions are underway to explore how Europe can present a united front on global development. Officials have suggested that it could involve the formulation of a new, ambitious European Common Policy on development assistance, harmonising aid strategies and increasing collective contributions. Such a policy would aim to streamline efforts, reduce duplication, and ensure that European aid is more effective and impactful on the ground.

Chancellor of the Exchequer, Gordon Brown, has been a key proponent of these initiatives, advocating strongly for increased international aid and debt relief. Mr Brown has very much championed the cause of developing nations on the global stage, making compelling arguments for a more equitable global financial system. He believes passionately in working multilaterally, arguing that complex global problems cannot be solved by individual nations acting in isolation. A statement from the Treasury is expected later this week, outlining further details of the UK's financial commitments. Leading aid organisations are watching closely. Cafod, the Catholic Agency for Overseas Development, has been particularly vocal in its calls for greater ambition. A spokesperson for Cafod said: 'While we welcome the renewed focus on international development, we urge the government and other donor nations to go much further. The needs are immense, and current pledges, while a step in the right direction, are simply not enough. We want to see concrete action and a significant scaling up of resources. Cafod urges us to make much more of this opportunity.'

Oxfam, another prominent international charity, underscored the devastating human cost of inaction. A recent report from the organisation highlighted the urgent need to address child poverty and mortality, stating starkly that 'half of the world's children still suffer from preventable diseases, malnutrition, and a lack of access to basic education. It is an indictment of our collective global conscience.' The report further detailed how industrialised nations have, for many years, consistently fallen short of their aid promises. It showed that less than 0.7% of their collective Gross National Income has been consistently allocated to overseas aid for decades, a figure that has stubbornly remained low, and in some cases, has even shown signs of decline, with little political will to rectify the shortfall.

Live Aid founder and prominent anti-poverty campaigner Bob Geldof, however, remained unconvinced by some of the diplomatic rhetoric. Speaking with characteristic candour, he dismissed much of the current discussion and political posturing as 'guff'. Geldof, who has tirelessly campaigned for debt relief and increased aid for Africa, expressed deep frustration with the slow pace of change and the perceived lack of genuine commitment from some quarters. He specifically highlighted the critical and often overlooked issue of access to life-saving anti-retroviral drugs for millions of people living with HIV/AIDS in developing countries. 'We are talking about real lives here, not just numbers on a balance sheet,' Geldof asserted passionately. He went on to heavily criticise what he saw as a propensity for empty gestures, adding forcefully: 'There is no point in showering adulation for new initiatives that are, in reality, woefully inadequate and will make little tangible difference to the lives of the poorest. We need action, not just words and photo opportunities,' he concluded. 'Mr. Geldof’s comments added a sharp, dissenting voice to the more measured tones from official circles, reflecting the impatience felt by many campaigners who believe the time for talk is over, and the time for decisive action is now.'"

These will include substantial debt relief from poor countries and significantly increased aid by the rich world. Mr Brown also wants other G8 nations to match his long-standing pledge for 0.7% of national income. He also wants the rich countries to do much more to help the development of fair trade for poor and developing nations, and to reduce their tariffs. The Chancellor is due to visit America next week as part of his global drive over the issue of poverty. He told Radio 4's Today programme: "We need more ambition on trade and more ambition on aid if we are going to make a significant impact on the enduring problems of health, of illiteracy, of grinding poverty, in Africa but right throughout the developing countries."

His proposals were described as a new "Marshall Plan" for the world, including an international finance facility, which would issue bonds in anticipation of future aid to double annual aid to $50bn a year. Increased investment in the development process could also give the poor countries the crucial boost they needed, he argued. The European Union's Common Agricultural Policy had historically caused severe trade problems, he said, but there was now a genuine political will to end its protectionist measures.

Mr Brown said much had been achieved on vital issues such as debt relief in the last seven years. But with 30,000 children still dying every day, more urgent action was needed, including 100% multilateral debt relief. "That is why next year is a real test," he said. "If after five years of making grand promises the world is not delivering to them, then people will be entirely justified in saying they wanted change but they did not get concrete results."

The Cafod charity will publicly back Mr Brown's call for action on debt. It wants to use its support to pressure major industrialised countries like the US to make firm commitments to action. Mr Brown said America and other developed nations certainly needed to take more action but President George Bush was open for constructive discussions to help countries which genuinely wanted to reform.

The charity's director, Barbara Stocking, said: "2005 is the chance for an historic breakthrough, but unless world leaders act decisively now, the year will end in utter failure." The report said the world's richest top industrialised countries had pledged in 1970 to give 0.7% of their national income to aid. But Bob Geldof in July said he was tired of "guff" about ending poverty on the world stage. It was scandalous that Britain was the 4th richest country in the world but only the 11th most generous in terms of aid, he added.

Instead, only 500,000 people would receive it, he said. "There's no point in him getting all the praise and adulation for a whole new set of pledges when he has so woefully failed to meet the critical ones he already has," added Mr Geldof.

**to** address the pressing global challenges of poverty, climate change, and pervasive economic inequality, Prime Minister Gordon Brown today presented a robust and ambitious vision for the future of international development. Speaking extensively and with conviction on BBC **Radio Today**, Mr. Brown articulated precisely how the United Kingdom **wants** **to** **do** its **part** as a leading global player, pushing for substantial reforms and fostering increased international collaboration. He stressed that a **key** component of this invigorated strategy **will include** the establishment of innovative partnerships with emerging economies and a renewed, emphatic focus on sustainable infrastructure projects across the developing world. The Prime Minister underscored the absolute necessity **to make an** immediate, tangible, and lasting impact **on** **for** **international** aid delivery mechanisms and global trade policies. He urged the international community **to increase** its collective efforts significantly, arguing convincingly that only through such concerted and unified action **could** the world truly **give** the most vulnerable populations **the** opportunity, dignity, and sustainable future **they needed**.

A significant and detailed portion of the interview was dedicated to the critical and often contentious issue of the **European Common Policy** on **trade**. Mr. Brown called for a comprehensive and urgent overhaul, asserting that the current framework, while having served a foundational role, is no longer entirely fit for purpose in a rapidly transforming global economy. "There **is now** a profound and growing recognition across Europe, from Brussels to individual capitals, that our trade policies must fundamentally evolve to actively support developing nations, rather than merely prioritising our own immediate interests," he explained with careful deliberation. He highlighted the UK's long-standing and deeply embedded commitment to fair trade principles and noted that the nation has **much** experience, having historically **been with** many African, Asian, and Latin American countries in their arduous pursuit of economic self-sufficiency and equitable market access. He elaborated at length **why** these strategic adjustments are not only desirable but urgently **needed**, reiterating powerful points **as said to people** during his recent, high-profile visit to the G7 summit. "The moral imperative to act decisively is unequivocally clear, and the long-term economic benefits for all nations, rich and poor, are undeniable. A truly stable and prosperous world economy simply **will be** more unstable and poorer if vast segments of humanity lack a fair chance to participate and thrive," he declared, echoing a central tenet of his development agenda.

However, the Prime Minister also pointed to areas of international cooperation where, he implied, further and more resolute commitment is absolutely essential. "While we unequivocally applaud the commendable efforts of many of our closest allies, it is undeniable that the United States, as the world's largest economy and a global superpower, has a particularly pivotal role to play. We need to see far greater ambition and concrete action from Washington. The US must **make** even **too more** significant contributions to global development funds and commit wholeheartedly to crucial multilateral agreements that address issues like climate change and pandemic preparedness," he asserted, adding a subtle yet firm challenge to current American policy. His comments are understood to reflect ongoing delicate diplomatic discussions about burden-sharing in various global aid and development initiatives, particularly in the context of emerging geopolitical shifts.

Mr. Brown's robust and often passionate stance follows the recent release of a stark and harrowing new **world report** last month, co-authored by the eminent development economist Dr. Eleanor **Price**. The report, powerfully titled 'Childhoods Undone: The True Cost of Global Inequality', painted a distressing and comprehensive picture of the current state of global child welfare. It meticulously detailed how over a **million children**, representing nearly **half the** world's young people living in extreme poverty, have endured devastating hardships, including chronic malnutrition, severely limited access to basic education, and exposure to preventable diseases for much **of their years**. The report, which compiled extensive data from over 150 countries and involved years of rigorous research, served as a potent and urgent reminder of the desperate need for comprehensive, coordinated, and immediate international action. Many prominent **members who have** long **been** advocating for child welfare, including senior representatives from UNICEF and Save the Children, had strongly endorsed the findings, some having actively collaborated on the extensive research **with** the prestigious Price Institute **since July**. The findings were formally presented to the United Nations General Assembly in a session that drew significant international attention, where Dr. Price made an impassioned and widely reported plea for immediate and decisive intervention from global leaders.

During the Radio Today interview, Mr. Brown was pressed intently on persistent domestic criticism regarding the perceived effectiveness and considerable cost of foreign aid. He vehemently defended the UK's aid programme, which remains one of the most generous globally, stating, "**I** **it** **only** wish that **the** prevailing narrative surrounding international aid would shift its focus to its undeniable tangible successes, rather than perpetually propagating outdated and often misleading myths. Some of the rhetoric we hear, particularly from certain quarters, is inherently **anti-** progress and frankly unhelpful to the vital cause of humanity and global solidarity." He specifically targeted what he described as "the **three** most pernicious and frequently deployed arguments" by sceptics: namely, that aid is inherently wasted, that it invariably fosters dependency, and that it simply "doesn't work." "**Instead** **people** **there** **is** a clear moral, economic, and strategic **point for new** and enhanced commitments, both within our national budget and across international partnerships," **he added**. Mr. **Brown** further elaborated on his government's resolute push for greater accountability, enhanced transparency, and rigorous impact assessment in all aid projects, insisting that every single pound spent must deliver maximum sustainable impact. He underscored the paramount importance of empowering local communities to lead their own development processes and ensuring that all initiatives are locally owned, culturally sensitive, and sustainable in the long term. His comprehensive interview concluded with a strong and urgent call for global leaders to approach upcoming international summits with a renewed sense of urgency, collective purpose, and shared responsibility, emphasising forcefully that the future prosperity, security, and stability of all nations depend intrinsically on collective action now.

The month-old Committee to Protect Bloggers is asking those with blogs to dedicate their sites on 22 February to the "Free Mojtaba and Arash Day". Arash Sigarchi and Mojtaba Saminejad are both in prison in Iran. Blogs are free sites through which people publish thoughts and opinions. Iranian authorities have been clamping down on prominent sites for quite some time. "I hope this day will focus people," Curt Hopkins, director of the Committee, told the BBC News website. The group has a list of actions that it says bloggers can take, including writing to local Iranian embassies. The Committee has deemed Tuesday "Free Mojtaba and Arash Day" as part of its first campaign. It is calling on the blogosphere - the name for the worldwide community of bloggers - to do everything it can to help raise awareness of the plight of Mojtaba and Arash as well as other "cyber-dissidents". "If you have a blog, the least you could do is put nothing on that blog except 'Free Mojtaba and Arash Day'," said Mr Hopkins. "That would mean you could see that phrase 7.1 million times. That alone will surely shine some light on the situation. "If you don't have one, find one dedicated to that - it takes about 30 seconds." Technorati, a blog search engine, tracks about six million blogs and says that more than 12,000 are added daily. A blog is created every 5.8 seconds, according to a leading US research think-tank. The Committee to Protect Bloggers was started by US blogger Curt Hopkins and counts fired flight attendant blogger Ellen Simonetti as a deputy director. She has since started the International Bloggers' Bill of Rights, a global petition to protect bloggers at work. Although not the only website committed to human rights issues by any means whatsoever, it aims to be the hub or a central organisation, providing information and support for bloggers in particular and their rights to freedom of speech. The Committee, although only a month old, aims to be the focal point for all blogger action on similar issues in the future, and will operate as a not-for-profit organisation. "Blogging is in this weird sort of no man's land. People think of it as being one thing or another depending on their point of view," said Mr Hopkins. "Some think of themselves as pundits, something like journalists, and some like me have a private blog which is just a publishing platform." But they do not have a constituency and are out there in the cold. It is not just human rights issues in countries which have a track record of restricting what is published in the media that is of great concern to bloggers. The question of bloggers and what rights they have to say what they want on their sites is a thorny one indeed and has received much press attention recently. High profile legal cases in which employees have been sacked for what they have said on their personal, and often highly anonymous blogs, have highlighted the muddy situation that the blogosphere is currently in today. "This is a very big messy argument," explained Mr Hopkins. He added: "It is just such a new way of doing business, there will be clampdowns on these new methods." But the way these issues get tested is through the courts which, said Mr Hopkins, "is part of the whole ongoing messy conversation." "If you haven't already got bloggers working in your company, you will certainly have them tomorrow - and if you don't have a blogger policy now you had better start looking at having one. Mr Hopkins said that the blogosphere - which is doubling every five months - was powerful because it takes so little time and technical expertise to create a blog. "Everyone does this - mums, radicals, conservatives," he said. Many companies offer easy-to-use online services to create a blog and publish it in minutes to a global community. "That is the essential difference. What I call 'templating software' gives every single person on Earth the unique chance to have one of their own." "You don't even have to have your own computer."

A global blogger action day has been called, drawing significant international attention to the plight of online voices. The weblog community is being called into action to lend its collective support to two prominent Iranian dissident bloggers, Arash Sigarchi and Mojtaba Saminejad, who are currently held in state custody. The newly established, month-old Committee to Bloggers' Rights is specifically urging all those with active online journals and platforms to mark Tuesday, 22 February, as the dedicated "Free Mojtaba and Arash Day". Arash Sigarchi and Mojtaba Saminejad are both prominent online commentators and journalists currently imprisoned in Iran, reportedly held without formal charge or the prospect of a fair trial, sparking widespread concern among human rights groups. Blogs have rapidly become a powerful and widely accessible medium through which people can freely share their diverse thoughts, opinions, and observations with a global audience. However, online activists are increasingly voicing concerns that this fundamental freedom is now under severe threat in many countries, particularly in Iran. Iranian authorities have been consistently clamping down on such independent online sites for some considerable time, implementing strict censorship measures and often prosecuting their operators, with many prominent bloggers consequently being detained or silenced through various means. "I sincerely hope this dedicated day will successfully mobilise people around the world to stand in strong solidarity with these courageous bloggers and advocate for their release," Curt Hopkins, who serves as the director of the Committee to Bloggers' Rights, told the BBC News website in an exclusive interview from his US base. Mr Hopkins further stressed the immense importance of international solidarity and collective action in these cases. The advocacy group has formulated and published a comprehensive list of suggested actions which it says can be readily taken by concerned individuals globally, including writing formal letters to local Iranian embassies and diplomatic missions, as well as posting clear messages of support and solidarity across various online platforms. The Committee has specifically dubbed Tuesday, 22 February, as the "Free Mojtaba and Arash Day" as part of its inaugural global campaign. It is fervently calling on the entire blogosphere - the collective term used for the global community of bloggers - to exert every possible effort it can to help raise widespread awareness of the severe plight faced by Mojtaba and Arash, as well as countless other "online dissidents" who are facing similar threats to their freedom of expression and personal liberty in various nations. "If you currently have an active blog, even a small personal one, the very least you could do to contribute meaningfully is to prominently display nothing on that blog's front page except the powerful phrase 'Free Mojtaba and Arash Day'," said Mr Hopkins, emphasising the simplicity and potential viral impact of the action. "That simple act alone would cumulatively mean you could potentially see that crucial phrase replicated 7.1 million times across the internet. That alone, we firmly believe, will significantly help shine some much-needed light on their urgent situation and the broader issue of digital repression, potentially putting considerable pressure on the Iranian government to reconsider their stance and release the bloggers." He added: "If you don't currently have a blog of your own, we strongly encourage you to find one that aligns with your views and support that initiative by sharing it widely - it genuinely takes about 30 seconds to make a meaningful contribution to this cause." Technorati, a prominent blog search engine and indexer, currently tracks approximately six million active blogs worldwide and reports that more than 12,000 new blogs are being added daily. A new blog or significant blog post is created every 5.8 seconds, according to a recent study by a leading US research think-tank, further highlighting the explosive growth and increasing influence of online publishing as a global phenomenon.

The Committee to Bloggers' Rights was formally established and started by US blogger Curt Hopkins, with Ellen Simonetti serving as its dedicated deputy director. Ms Simonetti, a tireless advocate for digital freedoms, has since independently started the International Bloggers' Bill of Rights, a significant global initiative designed not only to protect the legal standing and safety of bloggers at work, but also to actively advocate for their fundamental freedoms of expression and speech in a rapidly evolving digital landscape. Although not the only website or organisation committed to addressing human rights issues by any means, the Committee to Bloggers' Rights firmly aims to establish itself as the leading resource, or central information hub, offering comprehensive data, practical information, and crucial support for bloggers who find themselves in need, and tirelessly campaigning for their universal rights to freedom of speech. Its founders strongly believe that there is a critical and growing need for a dedicated international body to champion and defend these essential rights in the ever-expanding digital age, where traditional media protections often do not apply.

The Committee, despite being only a month old since its inception, has ambitious plans to swiftly become the primary focal point for organised blogger action on similar critical issues in the future. It will operate strictly as a non-for-profit organisation, deeply committed to defending and promoting online expression across all borders. "Blogging, as a burgeoning form of communication, is currently existing in this weird no man's land," Mr Hopkins explained. "People often think of it as being one thing or another, highly dependent on their individual point of view and perspective." He elaborated further: "Some individuals who engage in blogging genuinely think of themselves as influential pundits, somewhat akin to professional journalists, reporting on events and offering analysis. And then, there are some, like myself, who maintain a private blog which is simply a personal diary, a space for personal reflections and thoughts." He pointed out the vulnerability of this diverse group: "But the crucial point is that they do not have a formal constituency to represent them, nor the institutional backing often found in established media. They are essentially out there in the cold, frequently without the robust legal protections and support networks typically afforded to traditional journalists or established media outlets." The scope of concern extends beyond just human rights issues in countries which historically have a track record of actively restricting what is published in the conventional media. The complex question of exactly who bloggers are, how they should be defined in a legal sense, and what inherent rights they possess to say what they want on their personal or public sites, remains a particularly thorny one. This issue has received a significant amount of press attention recently, sparking debates among legal scholars, policymakers, and industry experts. High-profile cases in which employees have been summarily fired or disciplined for what they have expressed on their personal blogs, and often, without clear recourse or avenues for appeal, have acutely highlighted the precarious and often ambiguous legal situation that the blogosphere is currently in. These incidents collectively underscore the pervasive lack of clear legal guidelines, consistent industry standards, and established legal precedents regarding the nuances of online speech and its consequences.

"This is a big legal mess, there's no doubt about it," Mr Hopkins declared, acknowledging the complexity of the evolving situation. He added, thoughtfully: "It is just such an incredibly new way of doing business, of communicating and interacting, that there will undoubtedly be significant growing pains as society and legal systems adapt." He continued, "The legal frameworks and societal norms simply haven't caught up with the astonishing pace of technological change and the widespread adoption of blogging, creating considerable legal uncertainty." But the fundamental way these nascent issues ultimately get tested and resolved is through the established legal processes within the courts, which, said Mr Hopkins, "is an inevitable and necessary part of the whole messy conversation. It's a crucial process that will gradually establish the boundaries, clarify responsibilities, and define the protections for online speech and publishers." "If you haven't already got bloggers actively contributing within your company, you will almost certainly have them tomorrow - it's an inescapable reality of the modern workplace," he warned. "And if you don't have a clear, comprehensive blogger policy in place now for your employees' online activities, you had better start looking at having one immediately. Companies need to proactively understand the broad implications of their employees' online activities and establish clear, well-communicated guidelines to mitigate risks and ensure fair treatment for all involved." Mr Hopkins said that the blogosphere - which is incredibly doubling in size every five months, demonstrating exponential growth - was expanding at such an astonishing rate primarily because it takes so little time and requires minimal technical expertise to create and maintain a blog. "Every single person does this now - from mums sharing family updates, to political radicals expressing dissenting views, to staunch conservatives promoting their ideologies," he said, illustrating the remarkably diverse user base. Many companies and platforms now generously offer easy-to-use services and intuitive tools to create a blog swiftly and publish its content in minutes to a vast, interconnected global community. This unparalleled ease of access and widespread adoption means blogging is no longer a niche, tech-savvy activity but a mainstream, democratic form of mass communication. "That, in essence, is the essential difference and the true power of this phenomenon. What I call 'templating software' gives almost every single person on Earth the genuine chance to have their own voice online, to publish their thoughts and ideas," Mr Hopkins concluded. "You don't even have to have your own expensive server or complex website infrastructure to do it. The barrier to entry has simply vanished."

"That would mean the message could be seen by 7.1 million people. That alone will help shed some light on their urgent situation."

If you don't have a blog, the Committee advises finding one to link to, or better yet, starting one yourself - it takes about 30 minutes to set up. Technorati, a leading search engine for blogs, currently records about six million active blogs and reports that more than 12,000 new ones are added daily. A new blog is started every 5.8 seconds, according to a recent study by a prominent US research think-tank, the Pew Internet and American Life Project.

She has since been instrumental in establishing the International Bloggers' Bill of Rights, a guiding document intended to safeguard online freedom of expression. Although not the only website covering crucial online rights issues by any means, it aims to be a central hub, offering vital information and comprehensive support for bloggers in trouble and their families, as well as advocating for their fundamental right to free speech globally.

The Committee, although only a nascent month old, ardently hopes to swiftly become the definitive focal point for galvanising action on similar issues of online censorship and persecution in the future, and will undoubtedly act as a vital, readily accessible go-to resource for the entire blogosphere, tirelessly campaigning for those whose valuable voices are unjustly silenced across the world.

original: Global blogger action day called..The global web blog community is being called into action to lend support to two imprisoned Iranian bloggers...The month-old Committee to Protect Bloggers' is asking those with blogs to dedicate their sites on 22 February to the "Free Mojtaba and Arash Day". Arash Sigarchi and Mojtaba Saminejad are both in prison in Iran. Blogs are free sites through which people publish thoughts and opinions. Iranian authorities have been clamping down on prominent sites for some time. "I hope this day will focus people," Curt Hopkins, director of the Committee, told the BBC News website...The group has a list of actions which it says bloggers can take, including writing to local Iranian embassies. The Committee has deemed Tuesday "Free Mojtaba and Arash Day" as part of its first campaign. It is calling on the blogsphere - the name for the worldwide community of bloggers - to do what it can to help raise awareness of the plight of Mojtaba and Arash as well as other "cyber-dissidents". "If you have a blog, the least you could do is put nothing on that blog except 'Free Mojtaba and Arash Day'," said Mr Hopkins. "That would mean you could see that phrase 7.1 million times. That alone will shine some light on the situation. "If you don't have one, find one dedicated to that - it takes about 30 seconds." Technorati, a blog search engine, tracks about six million blogs and says that more than 12,000 are added daily. A blog is created every 5.8 seconds, according to a US research think-tank...The Committee to Protect Bloggers was started by US blogger Curt Hopkins and counts fired flight attendant blogger Ellen Simonetti as a deputy director. She has since started the International Bloggers' Bill of Rights, a global petition to protect bloggers at work. Although not the only website committed to human rights issues by any means, it aims to be the hub or organisation, information and support for bloggers in particular and their rights to freedom of speech...The Committee, although only a month old, aims to be the focal point for blogger action on similar issues in the future, and will operate as a non-for-profit organisation. "Blogging is in this weird no man's land. People think of it as being one thing or another depending on their point of view," said Mr Hopkins. "Some think of themselves as pundits, kind of like journalists, and some like me have a private blog which is just a publishing platform. "But they do not have a constituency and are out there in the cold."..It is not just human rights issues in countries which have a track record of restricting what is published in the media that is of concern to bloggers. The question of bloggers and what rights they have to say what they want on their sites is a thorny one and has received much press attention recently. High profile cases in which employees have been sacked for what they have said on their personal, and often anonymous blogs, have highlighted the muddy situation that the blogsphere is currently in..."This is a big messy argument," explained Mr Hopkins. He added: "It is just such a new way of doing business, there will be clamp downs." But the way these issues get tested is through the courts which, said Mr Hopkins, "is part of the whole messy conversation." "If you haven't already got bloggers in your company, you will have them tomorrow - and if you don't have a blogger policy now you had better start looking at having one. Mr Hopkins said that the blogsphere - which is doubling every five months - was powerful because it takes so little time and expertise to create a blog. "Everyone does this - mums, radicals, conservatives," he said. Many companies offer easy-to-use services to create a blog and publish it in minutes to a global community. "That is the essential difference. What I call 'templating software' gives every single person on Earth the chance to have one. "You don't even have to have your own computer."

US Lawmakers Call for Swift Action on AI Regulation Amidst Growing Privacy Concerns

In a significant call for immediate **action**, US lawmakers are pushing for decisive **action** **to** implement robust regulations on artificial intelligence and data collection. **The** urgent need for oversight **is** becoming increasingly apparent **as** technology permeates every aspect of modern life. We **are through** with the era of self-regulation; legislators now **have** **this** firm belief.

BBC **News** has learned of a comprehensive **list of** policy recommendations. One report **says** new measures must **take** into account the rapid pace of technological advancement, **including** novel approaches to data governance and individual consent. The question of whether personal data should be truly **free**, or if **it** should be controlled **to** prevent misuse and exploitation, remains central to the ongoing discourse. **As** with **other** complex societal issues, there is much to consider, from economic implications to fundamental human rights. "We don't want **you** to have any more **ado** about **that**," stated Senator Martha Jones during a recent hearing, emphasizing the public's right to clarity and protection. "And **that** really does **mean** that **you**, the consumer, will need to be informed **times** over about how your digital footprint is being utilized. **That** level of accountability **will** require **some** serious thought **on** the part of tech giants. They **have** **one** chance to get this right, and failure is not an option."

The debate **takes** on even **more** urgency **every** passing day, particularly as AI capabilities expand. **According** to **a research think** tank working closely with Congress, the **Committee was** established in the **US** specifically to examine these burgeoning challenges. Its findings highlight significant concerns **at** the intersection of advanced AI systems and human rights. "It's **not human** error we're primarily concerned with now," explained Dr. Evelyn Reed, a leading AI ethicist and witness before the committee. "It is **the information** itself, and how it is processed and disseminated. **For** instance, the sheer volume **of** digital data, much **of** it accumulated from **old** online activities, is being aggregated **to** create incredibly detailed profiles **similar** **in** scope to those previously compiled **in** highly sensitive intelligence operations. **And** yet, there **is** no single **man** or centralized regulatory **thing** overseeing it all. It operates **on** a scale **of** **kind** that **which** we **just** don't fully comprehend, often beyond the reach of existing legal frameworks."

Concerns have been widely raised that current regulatory frameworks **are not** equipped to effectively **track** the complex, often opaque, data flows inherent in modern digital **media**. "Many **of** the systems developed by large tech firms **of** today are designed with inherent opacity," noted the committee's comprehensive report. "They are constantly evolving, making real-time oversight incredibly difficult. **It is recently** that we've truly understood **what** the potential for widespread societal impact entails."

During a recent tech summit in Silicon Valley, a prominent industry figure, Mr. David Chen, CEO of a leading AI startup, urged companies to proactively address these issues rather than wait for legislative mandates. "**He** said companies need to move **away** from traditional, reactive business models and find a better **way** to engage constructively with privacy concerns from the outset. 'How do **these** innovative companies truly **get** to where they are today, commanding market leadership?' he asked rhetorically. 'It **is already your company if** you **had starts** with a strong ethical foundation and a commitment to responsible data stewardship. Those who **said** early **that** privacy **was** not just a compliance issue but a core value are now thriving, **because so** many discerning consumers are now actively demanding it.' **And** **this** is precisely where **he** believes the real **difference** between enduring success and fleeting market presence lies. "**What** will **the** future of responsible innovation look like? **You**, as industry leaders, have a crucial role in defining that through your actions today."

The committee's detailed recommendations span several key areas. They include establishing an independent, agile regulatory body with the necessary powers to audit complex AI systems and data practices. Furthermore, they advocate for mandating far greater transparency in data collection methodologies and processing algorithms, alongside implementing stricter, easily understandable consent requirements for individuals. There is also a particularly strong emphasis on fostering international cooperation, recognizing the borderless nature of data flows and the global implications of AI development. Experts universally argue that a fragmented or inconsistent regulatory landscape across different nations could not only hinder beneficial innovation but also severely compromise consumer protection worldwide.

One of the primary and most pressing challenges identified is the exponential speed at which AI technology continues to develop. Legislators often find themselves playing a perpetual game of catch-up, with laws struggling to keep pace with advanced capabilities that emerge seemingly overnight. This rapid and continuous evolution necessitates the creation of a flexible, adaptive regulatory framework – one that can evolve without stifling beneficial innovation, yet critically, also without compromising fundamental individual rights and societal values.

A significant aspect of the discussion also revolves around the pervasive issue of algorithmic bias. If AI systems are inadvertently or deliberately trained on biased historical data, they possess the inherent capacity to perpetuate, and in many cases, even amplify existing societal inequalities and discriminatory practices. The committee therefore underscored the paramount importance of ensuring fairness, equity, and ethical integrity in all stages of AI design, development, and deployment. To address this, they strongly suggested mandatory impact assessments for all high-risk AI applications, particularly those involved in sensitive areas such as employment, credit, or criminal justice.

While acknowledging the undeniable need for public trust and robust safeguards, industry leaders have simultaneously expressed legitimate concerns about potential over-regulation. Many argue that overly prescriptive or overly burdensome laws could inadvertently stifle crucial innovation, making it significantly harder for US companies to compete effectively on a global stage. The general consensus is that a delicate and carefully balanced approach must be struck – one that fosters technological advancement and economic growth, while simultaneously safeguarding individual freedoms and democratic values. Some forward-thinking proposals include the establishment of "regulatory sandboxes," where new AI technologies can be safely tested and refined under expert supervision before full-scale public deployment, allowing for iterative learning and adaptive policy-making.

The extensive debate also delved into the profound economic implications of AI. The burgeoning AI sector is already a significant driver of economic growth and job creation across various industries. Therefore, crafting regulations that effectively protect consumers and citizens without inadvertently undermining this vital economic engine represents an exceedingly complex and multi-faceted undertaking. The committee heard extensive testimonies from a diverse array of stakeholders, including innovative small startups, established global tech giants, civil liberties advocates, and academic experts, all offering nuanced and often differing perspectives on the optimal path forward for the nation.

Ultimately, the overarching goal of these legislative efforts is to create a digital ecosystem where technological innovation can flourish responsibly, and where individuals feel genuinely secure, protected, and empowered in their increasingly digital lives. The coming months are widely expected to see intense legislative debate as these pivotal proposals move through various stages in Congress, thereby shaping the future trajectory of AI governance, data privacy, and digital rights for decades to come. The world watches closely as the United States grapples with these profound ethical, economic, and technological questions that will define the 21st century.

Sir Nicholas Scott, former Northern Ireland minister, dies aged 71

Sir Nicholas Scott, the former Northern Ireland minister, has died at a London hospice, his family has announced.

The former Conservative MP for Kensington and Chelsea, who served for over two decades, died after a long illness, diagnosed as Alzheimer's disease. He was 71 years old.

The 71-year-old had served in Northern Ireland from 1981 to 1987 during the premiership of Margaret Thatcher, a crucial period in the province's history. As a Northern Ireland minister, he initially dealt with education and later took on the security portfolio, a period during which he famously rode out the mass IRA escape from the Maze Prison in 1983.

In his education brief, Sir Nicholas encountered significant criticism over contentious school closures and concerns regarding the future of the Catholic training colleges in the province. He was also responsible for merging the New University of Ulster and the Ulster Polytechnic to create the modern University of Ulster, a lasting legacy.

Sir Nicholas was a particularly strong defender of the Anglo-Irish Agreement, a landmark accord signed in 1985 aimed at fostering cooperation between the UK and Irish governments on Northern Ireland matters. As a result, he was held in considerable esteem in Dublin government and SDLP circles, who appreciated his efforts towards reconciliation.

However, he experienced marked hostility from many unionists, some of whom derisively dubbed him "Minister of Discord" due to his perceived pro-nationalist stance.

After leaving Northern Ireland in a cabinet reshuffle, he went on to become a UK disability minister, a role he held with significant dedication.

Sir Nicholas was later replaced as the Member of Parliament for Kensington and Chelsea by the colourful and flamboyant Alan Clark, after being controversially deselected by his constituency party in December 1996.

His deselection followed a series of embarrassing scandals, including a widely reported incident where he was found slumped in the street by police during the Conservative Party conference in Bournemouth and subsequently taken back to his hotel for his own safety.

Sir Nicholas claimed at the time that strong painkillers he was taking for a persistent back problem had reacted badly with a small amount of alcohol he had consumed.

After his controversial sacking as a minister, he bitterly said that despite the personal support of Cabinet ministers and many Tory backbenchers, the Eurosceptics in his constituency were "absolutely determined to get rid of me" due to his pro-European views.

His often colourful and eventful career also included a very public disagreement with his own daughter, Victoria, over civil rights for the disabled.

Sir Nicholas admitted he had misled MPs when he initially denied his department had been involved in wrecking tactics designed to kill the Disability Bill in 1994, an accusation he had initially rejected before later confessing. Victoria, a prominent lobbyist for disabled rights, publicly denounced her father's actions and, in what many saw as adding insult to injury, she joined the growing calls for him to resign from his ministerial post. He ultimately resigned and joined the backbenches two months later.

Throughout his time in government, particularly in education, he tirelessly oversaw the future of teacher training, championing reforms to ensure a high standard of professional development.
